## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The proposed statement is that for every pair of
smooth oriented knots $K_0,K_1\subset S^3$, a smooth diffeomorphism
$X_0(K_0)\cong X_0(K_1)$ implies that $K_0$ and $K_1$ are smoothly concordant.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the Conway knot $C$ and its Figure 2 trace partner $K_P$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written AC, is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] AC implies dependent choice and hence countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; this supplies every retained local countable-choice hypothesis. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[def-smooth-knot-concordance]]: a smooth concordance is a properly embedded smooth annulus in $S^3\times[0,1]$ with product collars.

[F2] [[lem-piccirillo-knot-lee-computations]] gives $s(C)=0$ by its direct Conway Lee computation. Only its Conway conclusion is used here.

[F3] [[lem-lee-cobordism-filtration-genus-bound]] gives $|s(K_1)-s(K_0)|\le2g$ for an actual smoothly properly embedded oriented genus-$g$ cobordism with product collars.

[F4] [[thm-piccirillo-conway-trace-partner-has-s-two]] proves under full AC that $X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P)$ and $s(K_P)=2$, using the retained local framed construction with its explicit published terminal input and the direct rational Lee calculation.


## Counterexample

1.1 The oriented knots $C,K_P$ of [F4] have diffeomorphic zero-traces. Suppose they were smoothly concordant. By [F1] the concordance is a properly embedded product-collared annulus, hence a genus-zero cobordism. [A1, A2, F1, F4, given, contradiction]

2.1 Apply [F3] with $g=0$. It gives $|s(C)-s(K_P)|\le0$, so the two invariants must agree. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 But [F2] and [F4] give $s(C)=0$, $s(K_P)=2$. Their difference has absolute value two, contradicting step 2.1. Thus these actual equal-zero-trace knots are not smoothly concordant, refuting the unchanged universal Statement. [A2, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, contradiction] ∎

## Definition

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

## Definition

A **finite triangulation of a compact PL surface** is a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex $K$ in which each edge is incident to one or two triangles and the link of each vertex is homeomorphic to a circle or a closed interval. Its realization $|K|$ is the surface; its boundary is the subcomplex formed by edges incident to one triangle and their vertices. If $V,E,F$ are the numbers of vertices, edges and triangles, its simplicial Euler characteristic is $\chi(K)=V-E+F$.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold whose boundary $M$ is a rational homology three-sphere, meaning $H_*(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$. The boundary intersection lattice has underlying group $L_W=H_2(W;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$. Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies each $x\in H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ with a class $\alpha_x\in H^2(W,M;\mathbb Z)$. Define $Q_W(\bar x,\bar y)=\langle\alpha_x\smile\alpha_y,[W,M]\rangle$, where $\smile$ is the relative cup product and $[W,M]\in H_4(W,M;\mathbb Z)$ is the relative orientation class; equivalently, this is the signed intersection number of interior two-cycle representatives. Its rank is $b_2(W)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_2(W;\mathbb Q)$. A nondegenerate positive-definite $Q_W$ is called a positive-definite filling lattice. It is not required to be unimodular; the boundary linking form can make its determinant have absolute value greater than one.

## Definition

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

## Definition

Let $K_0,K_1$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$, and let $I=[0,1]$. A smooth concordance from $K_0$ to $K_1$ is the image of a smooth proper embedding $f:S^1\times I\to S^3\times I$ whose lower and upper boundary circles are $K_0\times\{0\}$ and $K_1\times\{1\}$. The embedding has product collars at both ends: in a neighborhood of each boundary circle it is the corresponding knot embedding crossed with the interval coordinate. Orient the annulus so that its boundary, with the boundary-orientation convention, is $-K_0\times\{0\}\sqcup K_1\times\{1\}$. The knots are smoothly concordant when such an annulus exists.

## Example

Assume $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=e^{\alpha j}$, and $\sigma_j=e^{\beta j}$ in the Gaussian sequence detection experiment. A minimax separation rate over $\Theta_2(r)$ is
$$r_\varepsilon^*\asymp\varepsilon^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}.$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\alpha,\beta>0$, $q=2$, $a_j=e^{\alpha j}$, $\sigma_j=e^{\beta j}$, and the finite-support extremal profile for sufficiently small $r$. For this rate comparison, $X_\varepsilon\asymp Y_\varepsilon$ means the ratio is bounded above and away from zero by constants independent of $\varepsilon$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-ellipsoid-detection-boundary]]: $r^2=A J_1/J_2$, $u_\varepsilon^2=(r/\varepsilon)^4J_0/(2J_1^2)$, and the $u_\varepsilon$ boundary determines minimax distinguishability.

[F2] [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-exists-for-small-r]] and [[lem-ip-q2-ellipsoid-extremal-profile-is-minimizer]]: the active cutoff $m$ satisfies $A\asymp e^{-2\alpha m}$.

## Verification

1.1 Let $m$ be the largest active index and put $t=Ae^{2\alpha m}\in[e^{-2\alpha},1)$. For $j=m-\ell$, the profile factor is $\rho_\ell=1-te^{-2\alpha\ell}$. For every $\ell\ge1$, $1-e^{-2\alpha}\le\rho_\ell\le1$, while $0\le\rho_0\le1$. The sums for $J_1$ and $J_0$ are geometric in $\ell$; their $\ell=1$ terms give positive lower bounds and the full geometric sums give upper bounds, so $J_1\asymp J_0\asymp e^{4\beta m}$. In $J_2$, the summands are $t e^{-(2\alpha+4\beta)\ell}\rho_\ell e^{4\beta m}$; the $\ell=1$ term is bounded below by a positive constant times $e^{4\beta m}$, and the geometric series gives the matching upper bound. Thus $J_2\asymp e^{4\beta m}$. By [F1], $$r^2\asymp A\asymp e^{-2\alpha m},\qquad u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^4e^{-4\beta m}\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^{4+4\beta/\alpha}.$$ [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The last expression is comparable to $(r/\varepsilon^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)})^{4+4\beta/\alpha}$. Thus radii below the displayed scale by a factor tending to zero have $u_\varepsilon\to0$, and radii above it by a factor tending to infinity have $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$ when $r_\varepsilon\to0$. If $r_\varepsilon$ does not tend to zero, reduce to $\bar r_\varepsilon=\sqrt{r_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*}$. Nonempty alternatives satisfy $r_\varepsilon^2\le a_1^{-2}$ by the two q=2 constraints, so $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$ and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$. The inclusion $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_2(\bar r_\varepsilon)$ transfers consistent tests to the original class. The risk implications in [F1] establish the separation rate. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, where $\doteq$ denotes equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. Then $K$ has a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface $F$ and an ordered geometric basis, represented by embedded simple closed curves $s_1,\ldots,s_g,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_g$ for $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, such that $s_i\cdot_Fs_j=0=\ell_i\cdot_F\ell_j$ and $s_i\cdot_F\ell_j=\delta_{ij}$, and the Seifert matrix in this basis has block form
$$V=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_g+U\\U^T&W\end{pmatrix},$$
where $U$ is strictly upper triangular and $W$ is symmetric with zero diagonal. Such a geometric symplectic basis and block matrix are called a trivial Alexander basis.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and an oriented knot $K$ with $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the choice-function axiom used by the Seifert-form interfaces.

[F1] [[def-oriented-seifert-surface]]: A Seifert surface is connected, compact, smooth, oriented, and has boundary the given oriented knot.

[F2] [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]]: Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every smooth oriented knot bounds such a surface.

[F3] [[lem-alexander-one-seifert-form-is-s-equivalent-to-empty]]: The actual proof gives primitive kernel-vector splittings and exact integral inverse tube enlargements, rather than an unspecified stabilization.

[F4] [[def-seifert-form-s-equivalence]]: The displayed symmetric coupling enlargement is an allowed algebraic tube addition.

[F5] [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]: Its finite disk-and-band/polygon construction provides a geometric handle graph. On the supplied smooth surface, its finitely many piecewise smooth handle curves can be rounded in chart disks, preserving their finite transverse crossing pattern. Thus the finite twist construction below starts with actual smooth curves, not a claimed arbitrary TOP smoothing.


## Proof

1.1 Full AC implies Countable Choice, so choose the actual connected smooth Seifert surface supplied by [F2]. The proved reduction [F3] splits its given lattice by symplectic pairs and the exact inverse tube enlargements of [F4]. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, choose]

1.2 Reversing these reductions also produces the claimed trivial Alexander block. Keep all short vectors first and all long vectors second. A reverse tube addition introduces a new short x with zero column and only the entry 1 in its own long column, and a new long y with zero diagonal. Its couplings to earlier short vectors occupy precisely the new LAST column of U, so U stays strictly upper triangular. Its couplings to earlier long vectors give a symmetric new row/column of W, with zero new diagonal. Starting from the empty matrix therefore gives [[0,I+U],[U^T,W]] with exactly the advertised conditions. This is an integral symplectic basis of the original lattice; the finite construction below realizes it geometrically rather than assuming that arbitrary integral basis changes are surface homeomorphisms. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 Fix a standard geometric basis a_i,b_i on the actual compact oriented genus-g surface with one boundary circle. Its existence follows by cutting a finite disk-and-handle model of the surface, not from an arbitrary homology basis. Put omega(a_i,b_j)=delta_ij. An annular Dehn twist about an embedded curve v acts by the transvection T_v(z)=z+omega(z,v)v, choosing the twist sign accordingly. This formula is proved by cutting each transverse arc at the annulus: the twisted arc acquires one oriented copy of its core. Curves representing a_i+a_j, b_i+b_j and a_i+b_j for i≠j are embedded band sums on distinct handles. The joining arc lies in the complement of the other standard handles; the band gives the indicated homology class. Thus these transvections and their inverses are actual boundary-fixed surface homeomorphisms (smooth diffeomorphisms in the smooth model). [F5, construct]

1.4 For orthogonal u,v, direct expansion gives
T_(u+v) T_u^−1 T_v^−1(z)
=z+omega(z,u)v+omega(z,v)u. [F5, construct]

1.5 Taking u=a_i,v=b_j, i≠j, realizes the elementary block-GL operation a_j to a_j+a_i and b_i to b_i−b_j. Its powers realize arbitrary integral elementary additions. Handle permutations and simultaneous sign reversal of a_i,b_i are also realized; the latter is the square of the two-twist rotation on that handle. Euclidean elimination consequently realizes every block action (x,y) to (A x,A^−T y) for A in GL_g(Z). Likewise the a_i and a_i+a_j twists realize every symmetric upper shear, because the diagonal rank-one matrices and the identity (e_i+e_j)(e_i+e_j)^T−E_ii−E_jj=E_ij+E_ji generate all symmetric integral matrices; the b_i analogues realize every symmetric lower shear. [F5, construct]

1.6 Here is a complete generation argument, so this is not an appeal to mapping-class surjectivity. Given a primitive vector v=(x,y), first interchange the a and b directions on a handle if necessary to make x nonzero. A block-GL operation makes x=(d,0,...,0), d>0. If some y_j is not divisible by d, reduce d strictly: for j=1 use the ordinary Euclidean two-twist SL_2 algorithm on (d,y_1); for j≠1 an upper diagonal shear inserts y_j in x_j, then block-GL Euclidean reduction replaces d by gcd(d,y_j). Repeat. The positive integer d decreases until every y_j is divisible by d; primitivity then forces d=1. A lower symmetric shear with first column −y clears y while keeping x=e_1. Thus an actual finite product of the specified twists takes every primitive vector to a_1. [F5, construct]

2.1 Let A be an arbitrary symplectic integral matrix. Apply this procedure to its first column, so the resulting matrix fixes a_1. Its image of b_1 has the form b_1+c a_1+z, with z in the span W of the remaining handles. The displayed orthogonal-transvection combination for u=a_1 and each basis vector v of W fixes a_1. Its k-th power subtracts k v from that image of b_1 and only changes its a_1 coefficient in addition. Use these powers to clear all coordinates of z. Then a power of T_(a_1) clears c. The resulting matrix fixes both a_1,b_1, and hence restricts symplectically to W. Induct on g. We have reduced A to the identity by actual twists; reversing the finite list realizes A. In particular the symplectic lattice basis from the preceding primitive-vector/tube reduction is represented by an ACTUAL geometric basis, with disjoint short curves, disjoint long curves and exactly one transverse short–long intersection on each matching pair. ∎ [F5, construct]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated countable-choice hypothesis, fixed bridge pair $(K,S)$ and initial spanning disks, the specified two-puncture sphere $P$, and the two essential-annulus hypotheses.

[F1] A knot exterior is irreducible under countable choice. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]]

[F2] Smooth Schoenflies identifies both sides of a smooth sphere simultaneously with balls, by an ambient isotopy. [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]]

[F3] Supplied smooth ball windows admit collar-compatible attachment and removal. [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F4] A compact smooth embedding isotopy extends ambiently. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F5] The oriented factors obtained from a two-puncture sphere by boundary caps are the connected-sum factors, independently of the cap choices. [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]


## Proof

1.1 Write $B_+,B_-$ for the fixed bridge balls, $D_i^\pm$ for their spanning disks, and $T_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$. Arrange finite transverse intersections, with $P\cap S\cap K=\varnothing$, and take the knot tube sufficiently small and adapted to these intersections. A product neighborhood of each $D_i^\pm$ identifies a neighborhood of its bridge with the usual boundary-parallel ball-arc. Cutting $B_\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ along the disks $D_i^\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ gives a ball: successively slide each bridge along its displayed disk into a boundary collar, and remove its displayed half-tube; each cut opens that collar tunnel. These moves use disjoint same-side disk neighborhoods. In particular this is a *complete* meridian-disk system, not merely a collection of compressing disks. Throughout the proof the knot and $S$ themselves stay fixed; a puncture of $P$ is allowed to travel along the fixed knot. [given, F3, construct]

1.2 First remove compressions of $T_\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ in its bridge exterior. A compressing circle is nullhomotopic in $E$, hence in $A$ by the assumed injection; in an annulus it bounds a disk $E_0\subset A$. This disk must cross $S$, since otherwise the proposed compression was inessential on the relevant $T_\pm\setminus N(K)$. The compression disk and $E_0$ form a sphere in $E$ after rounding. Its ball from [F1] has no other part of $A$ inside: $A\setminus E_0$ is connected and reaches $\partial E$, whereas the ball is in the interior. Push $E_0$ across this ball to a parallel copy of the compression disk. This is an isotopy of $P$ supported off $K$, removes all the intersection circles lying inside $E_0$, and creates none. Thus each such operation strictly reduces $|P\cap S|$. After finitely many operations both punctured $T_\pm$ are incompressible. The same preparation can be repeated after a later pass. These are isotopies of the given sphere, so its oriented factors are preserved. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 Fix one side, temporarily written $B,T,\mathcal D$. Remove circle components of $T\cap\mathcal D$ by disk exchange: a circle innermost on a spanning disk bounds a disk on the punctured $T$ by its incompressibility; take one innermost among the disk-bounding circles on $T$. Its interior contains no intersection arcs, since those have endpoints on $\partial T$ or $K$, and contains no intersection circles by this choice. Replace the disk of the spanning disk bounded by that circle by a nearby copy of this disk on $T$. The replacement is embedded, misses every other spanning disk, keeps the bridge boundary arc fixed and reduces the total number of circles. Repeat finitely. Intersection arcs now have either one endpoint on $K$ and one on the disk's foot in $S$ (type I), or both endpoints on the foot (type II). An arc with both endpoints on $K$ would join the two punctures of $A$: choose the subdisk next to the segment of the bridge between those endpoints. It has no other intersection arcs, since that segment has no further punctures and its interior foot-free subdisk cannot contain an arc ending on $S$. After deleting circles, its part in $E$ would be a boundary compression along a spanning arc of $A$, contrary to hypothesis. This also shows $P\cap S\ne\varnothing$: if it were empty, after circle removal the two punctures would have to be joined by just such an arc. Thus every component of either unpunctured planar $T_\pm$ has nonempty boundary. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

2.2 Here are the three disk moves, including their supports. For an arc innermost next to a disk's foot, let $\Delta$ be its cut-off subdisk containing no other intersection arcs. A neighborhood of $\Delta$, with collars on its boundary intervals, is a standard disk times an interval. Pushing the surface band across $\Delta$ and a little through $S$ is a smooth embedding isotopy: in these coordinates translate the band in the interval direction, with a bump zero at the ends of the retained intervals, and round the two moving corners. The support can avoid the other same-side spanning disks. For a type-I arc this slides its puncture along the bridge through the adjacent endpoint on $S$; the velocity along $K$ is tangent to $K$, so the isotopy extends preserving $K$ setwise. It removes this puncture from the treated side and does not change the homeomorphism type of the **unpunctured** $T$. Call this move I. For a type-II arc essential in unpunctured $T$, the same band push cuts $T$ along that arc; call this move II. Both remove their chosen intersection arc and create no new intersections with the treated disk system. Their punctured-surface operations are boundary cuts. All isotopies can be stationary at their time endpoints and extended using [F4]. [given, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

2.3 The remaining move changes a spanning disk, not $P$. Suppose a type-II arc $\gamma$ cuts off a disk $E_0$ from $T\setminus N(K)$ with no other intersection arcs in its interior. On its spanning disk, retain the component of the cut along $\gamma$ containing the bridge, and replace the other component by a nearby copy of $E_0$. The union along $\gamma$ is a disk: two disks glued along one boundary interval. Its new foot is the old retained foot together with $\partial E_0\setminus\gamma$, pushed a little on $S$. Push its interior off $T$ on the retained disk's side and round the seam. Since $E_0$ has no punctures or other intersection arcs, the replacement misses $K$ except on its original bridge, is disjoint from all other same-side spanning disks, and deletes $\gamma$ and any intersections on the discarded part without adding any. This move III is valid even when $\gamma$ is not innermost on its spanning disk. In particular it is a disk replacement, not an unproved assertion that two disks in a knotted region are isotopic. [given, F3, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 If the treated disk system is still met, one of these moves is available. Here is the finite innermost argument for the only obstructed case. If neither I nor II is available, every arc innermost next to a foot is type II and cuts off a disk $E_0$ of the unpunctured surface $T$. Choose one such arc $\gamma$ and its foot-adjacent disk $\Delta$. If $E_0$ has no punctures, take an innermost subdisk of $E_0$ cut off by intersection arcs; it is empty and gives III. Otherwise a puncture of $E_0$ starts a type-I arc. The disk $Q=E_0\cup\Delta$, rounded at $\gamma$, is a proper disk in the bridge ball. It separates it into two balls: cap by either boundary disk on $\partial B$ and apply [F2], retaining the actual collars. Call the side away from the bridge on the spanning disk of $\gamma$ the inside. Follow the type-I arc's spanning disk from its puncture towards its foot. If this arc were foot-innermost, I would be available. The arcs between it and the foot therefore contain an innermost type-II arc on the inside. Its disk cut off on $T$ is also on the inside: $T$ misses the interior of $\Delta$, and its only portion on $Q$ is $E_0$, so an arc or cut-off disk cannot leave the inside without crossing $E_0$ or $\Delta$; if it lies on $E_0$, use its subdisk there and push its collar inward. Its own foot-adjacent disk together with that cut-off disk now cuts off an inside ball contained in the previous one. The bridge-containing side is again discarded. This is a strict descent in the finite set of intersection arcs contained on or inside these disks: the previous delimiting arc is outside the next inside ball. Repeat if its cut-off disk has a puncture. A strict descent cannot continue indefinitely. It ends with a puncture-free disk, and an innermost subdisk in it is the empty disk required for III. This proves availability without assuming an arbitrary boundary compression has the required foot. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct]

3.2 Perform available moves on this one side. Each deletes at least one arc of the treated system, and creates none there, so this inner process is finite. If necessary remove circles as in step 2.1. The punctured surface remains incompressible after a move I or II. To verify the usual boundary-cut assertion here, reverse its band in the empty disk-product neighborhood of step 2.2. Put a proposed compression disk transverse to the band cocore and remove its outermost intersections in that product; a surviving essential compression would give a compression of the old surface. If its boundary bounds a disk on the old surface, that disk is disjoint from the cut arc: a proper arc cannot enter the interior of a disk bounded by a disjoint interior circle without crossing that circle. It is therefore also a disk on the cut surface. Any sphere produced in removing the outermost intersections bounds a ball, since a bridge exterior cut from a ball along trivial-arc tubes is a handlebody; its sphere bounds a ball on the side not meeting the boundary by the same [F2] argument as in [F1]. Thus it cannot supply an exceptional compression. Move III does not change the surface. At termination $T$ misses both $K$ and the complete disk system. It lies in the cut-open ball of step 1.1 and is a union of disks: for a nondisk planar component an innermost boundary curve on that ball's sphere gives, by a small boundary-collar push, a compression, contrary to incompressibility. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, construct]

4.1 We give the strict count rather than infer it from the number of punctured boundary curves. For an unpunctured planar surface with $b$ boundary curves and $c$ components, set $z$ equal to its number of nondisk components. Moves I and III do not change this surface's topology. Every move II cuts an essential proper arc. A nonseparating such cut reduces the total $\sum(b_j-1)=b-c$ by one; a separating cut leaves this total unchanged and creates no disk, since the arc was essential. At the end this total is zero, so there were exactly $b-c$ nonseparating cuts. Each creates at most one new disk; initially there were $c-z$ disks. Hence the number $d$ of final disks satisfies $d\le(c-z)+(b-c)=b-z$. Their boundaries are precisely the *new* circles $P\cap S$. If the treated side had a nondisk component, $z\ge1$, and a complete pass strictly decreases the number of circles from $b$ to $d$. This is the planar hierarchy count used here. Punctures do not occur in $b$. [step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.2, algebra]

4.2 Repeat the compression cleanup of step 1.2 and then a complete pass on either side that has a nondisk component. Cleanup and every such pass strictly decrease the positive integer $|P\cap S|$, so the outer process is finite. At its end every component of both $T_+$ and $T_-$ is a disk. The dual graph of the circles cutting the sphere $P$ is connected; every vertex is now a disk and has degree one, so that graph has just one edge. Consequently $P\cap S$ is exactly one circle. Each operation on $P$ was an embedding isotopy through spheres meeting $K$ in exactly two points, preserving $K$ setwise; each other operation changed only a spanning disk. The specified oriented factors are therefore still the same by [F5]. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.1 Each $T_\pm$ is now a single disk. Apply I and III on the upper side until it has no punctures or disk intersections; II is unavailable on a disk. The two punctures then lie in the lower disk. Apply I and III below only until one of its punctures has passed to the upper disk. There is now one puncture in each disk, and the intersection circle has not changed. In a disk a nonempty finite family of type-II chords cuts off at least two outermost disks; at least one of those contains no puncture. Choose an innermost empty subdisk if further intersection arcs lie in it and apply III. Repeating removes all type-II arcs, without changing $P$ or either puncture. Circles have already been removed. Each remaining puncture is on exactly one spanning disk on its own side, and a type-I arc has just one puncture endpoint. There are therefore exactly two type-I arcs in total. Their other endpoints are on $P\cap S$, away from $K$, and can be taken distinct by a small foot perturbation on $S$. Thus their union consists of two disjoint embedded arcs, as asserted. All choices and all moves after the stated smooth suppliers were finite. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 4.2, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $S=|K|$ be a connected compact surface with nonempty boundary, where $K$ is a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex, each edge lies in one or two triangles, and each vertex link is a circle or interval. If its simplicial Euler characteristic is $\chi(K)=1$, then $S$ is homeomorphic to a closed disk.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite triangulation $K$ of $S$ and its boundary subcomplex.

[F1] [[def-finite-triangulated-compact-surface]]: each edge has one or two incident triangles, vertex links are circles or intervals, and nonempty boundary contains a boundary edge.

[F2] [[def-simplicial-euler-characteristic]]: $\chi(K)=V-E+F$ for the finite triangulation.


## Proof

1.1 Form the finite dual graph with one vertex for each triangle, an additional outside vertex, an edge between two triangle vertices for each shared interior edge, and an edge from the outside vertex for each boundary edge. This graph is connected: a path in the connected surface between triangle interiors can be moved off the finitely many vertices and then crosses a finite sequence of edges; every triangle can also be joined to the outside vertex through a path to the nonempty boundary. Fix a spanning tree rooted at the outside vertex by choosing the first one in the finite lexicographic ordering of edge subsets. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Process the triangle vertices in increasing distance from the root. For a triangle whose parent is the outside vertex, use its corresponding boundary edge; otherwise use the edge shared with its parent triangle. The parent has already been removed, so the chosen edge is now incident to this triangle alone. Remove the open triangle and that free edge. This is an elementary collapse: it is a deformation retraction and removes one $2$-cell and one $1$-cell, preserving both connectedness and Euler characteristic. After all triangles are removed, the remaining finite connected complex is a graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=\chi(K)=1$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct]

3.1 A connected finite graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges has a spanning tree with $V-1$ edges. Since $V-E=\chi(G)=1$ by [F2], it has exactly $V-1$ edges, so every edge belongs to that spanning tree and $G$ itself is a tree. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Reverse the collapses in reverse order, starting with a regular neighborhood of the tree $G$ from step 3.1. A regular neighborhood of a finite embedded tree is a disk: attach a small disk at each vertex and one rectangular band for each tree edge, adding a leaf edge and its new vertex one at a time. At each reversed collapse the removed triangle is restored along its two retained edges; these form the exposed side of one embedded boundary arc of the current neighborhood, because its third edge was the free edge removed in that collapse and the parent triangle is not yet restored. Attaching a disk along a single boundary arc enlarges a disk without adding a handle. Induction restores all triangles and the boundary collar, so $S$ is a disk. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots, and use the epsilon sign convention from the preceding definition. If their knot Floer complexes are stably filtered equivalent, meaning that there are totally acyclic bifiltered complexes $A$ and $B$ with $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A$ filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(J)\oplus B$, then $\epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)$. The acyclic summands here need not be acyclic after taking either associated-graded filtration.

The invariant satisfies $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$, $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$, and the tensor rules
$$ \epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(K),\qquad \epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(J). $$
The converse of $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$ fails: the knot $T_{2,5}\#-T_{4,5}\#T_{2,3;2,5}$ has $\tau=0$ and $\epsilon=1$, where $T_{p,q}$ is the positive $(p,q)$ torus knot and $T_{2,3;2,5}$ is the $(2,5)$ cable of the right-handed trefoil with longitudinal winding two. Epsilon is not an integer-valued homomorphism on the smooth concordance group: the right-handed trefoil has $\epsilon=1$ and its connected sum with itself also has $\epsilon=1$, not $2$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The actual normalized finite free Maslov-graded bifiltered complexes of the knots, with the supplied geometric tensor and duality identifications. Every newly used finite operation below is over $\mathbb F_2$.

[F1] [[def-epsilon-from-filtered-knot-floer-complex]] defines $F_s,G_s$ and epsilon. Its supplied two-hook argument proves the three cases are exhaustive and the two maps cannot both vanish.

[F2] [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]] supplies actual reverse-mirror duality, conjugation and normalized horizontal homology. The vertical and horizontal homologies at level zero are each one-dimensional, in Maslov degree zero.

[F3] [[lem-tau-connected-sum-filtered-tensor-product]] supplies the actual normalized filtered tensor identification and additive vertical threshold; the finite field-complex Kunneth calculation also follows by splitting boundary pairs.

[F4] [[lem-epsilon-stable-core-from-finite-filtered-splittings]] supplies stable-core invariance of the vertical threshold and both hook-map zero patterns, allowing arbitrary totally acyclic stabilizers without assuming their vertical or associated-graded complexes acyclic.

[F5] [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] supplies the actual normalized grid comparison. In particular tilde homology is hat knot Floer homology tensored with $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$, where $V$ has degrees $(0,0),(-1,-1)$. Its grid, differential, scalar and analytic suppliers are reused as proved interfaces.

[F6] [[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]] identifies oriented decorated diagrams with the same signed rotation/strand code and selected outer face. [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] fixes the positive Clifford-torus convention. The five-grid with $O=[4,3,2,1,0]$ and $X=[2,1,0,4,3]$ is identified with the positively oriented right-handed trefoil in step 4.3 below; its three crossing signs are all positive.

[F7] The grid coordinate and orientation conventions are [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]; the finite signed visit, crossing-rotation and face-selector data are [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]].


## Proof

1.1 In the finite-rank free Maslov-graded knot Floer category, [F4] proves the stable-equivalence conclusion directly. Its finite endomorphism matrices strictify homotopy idempotents and give a unique non-acyclic indecomposable core up to filtered homotopy. The rank-one vertical homology of each original knot complex forces its internal acyclic complementary summands to have acyclic vertical complexes. Consequently its vertical threshold and the zero/nonzero patterns of $F_\tau,G_\tau$ are precisely those of that core. Stable equivalence identifies the two cores even if the externally added acyclic summands have nonzero vertical or associated-graded homology. Thus the three-case epsilon values in [F1] agree. This argument does not apply the epsilon definition to the stabilized complexes themselves. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 First reduce a finite based Laurent complex by explicit filtered contractions. If a differential coefficient preserves both coordinates, homogeneity makes it a single Laurent monomial; translate its target so that it is $1$. Write $da=b+r$ with $a,b$ at the same bifiltration and replace $b$ by $b'=da$. This is a filtered homogeneous basis change with inverse $b=b'+r$. For every other basis element $c$, subtract the coefficient of $b'$ in $dc$ times $a$ from $c$; this is filtered since the relevant copy of $a$ has the coordinates of the corresponding copy of $b'$. The new differentials contain no $b'$, and their $a$ coefficients vanish by $d^2=0$. Thus the pair $a\to b'$ splits off. Inclusion $I$, projection $P$ and $H(b')=a$, zero on all other generators, satisfy $PI=1$ and $IP+1=dH+Hd$, with $H$ preserving both filtrations and of Maslov degree $+1$. Finitely many repetitions give a reduced complex with no equal-bifiltration arrow. Tensoring these identities with another complex preserves them: the extra differential terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Dualizing likewise preserves them. This supplies all reduction inverse maps and homotopies used below, including their tensor compatibility. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Let $s=\tau(C)$ and choose a Maslov-zero vertical cycle $z$ at $j\le s$ representing its distinguished class. Its corner part $z_c$ is nonzero, or the threshold would be smaller. If $F_s=0$, choose a Maslov-one northeast-hook chain $b$ with $d_Nb=z_c$ and split it into strictly upper, corner and strictly right parts $b_+,b_0,b_r$. The strictly upper part of $d_vb_+$ is zero, since the other parts cannot reach it. Hence $z'=z+d_vb_+$ is another distinguished vertical cycle supported at $j\le s$. Put $q=b_0+b_r$. Its horizontal boundary $h=d_hq$ has no strictly right component, and its corner is $z'_c$, by the corner equation of $d_Nb=z_c$. Then $x=z'+h_{\mathrm{left}}$ is supported in $i\le0,j\le s$, its vertical projection represents the distinguished class, and its horizontal projection is the boundary $h$. Conversely, if such an $x$ has horizontal part $d_hq$, project $q$ to the northeast hook: its strictly left part cannot reach the corner or right ray, and the remaining boundary is precisely $x_c$, with no upper component. Thus $F_s=0$. This proves the exact boundary-representative alternative, rather than assuming a simultaneous simplification theorem. [F1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 If $G_s\ne0$, choose a Maslov-zero southwest-hook cycle mapping to the distinguished vertical class. In the reduced complex it is $x=z+\ell$, with $z$ on the lower vertical ray, including the corner, and $\ell$ strictly left at $j=s$. The two retained boundary equations are exactly $d_vz=0$ and $d_h(z_c+\ell)=0$: a lower ray cannot reach the other ray, and the corner has no equal-bifiltration differential. Conversely these two equations give a southwest-hook cycle mapping to the vertical class. Therefore $G_s\ne0$ is exactly the existence of this simultaneous vertical/horizontal cycle representative. If also $F_s\ne0$, its horizontal cycle is not a boundary, by step 2.2. Each constructed $x$ extends to a homogeneous filtered Laurent basis: choose a nonzero original corner coordinate $e$, whose coefficient is $1$, and replace $e$ by $x$. Homogeneity excludes any other power of that same basis element, and all other terms are no higher in either filtration, so the inverse is the same filtered elementary substitution. These are the needed distinguished representative normal forms. A chosen horizontal noncycle alone is not used as an epsilon test. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

2.4 The dual vertical threshold is $-s$. Indeed, if $B$ is the vertical boundary space, the distinguished cycle $z$ is not in $B+V^{\le s-1}$, since such an expression would give a lower-level cycle representing it. Finite-dimensional basis extension gives a cocycle functional annihilating that subspace and taking $z$ to $1$; its dual filtration is at most $-s$. A dual cocycle at level at most $-s-1$ vanishes on every cycle at level $s$ and hence on the one-dimensional vertical homology, so it is a dual boundary. The finite perfect pairing identifies the dual of the northeast hook at $s$ with the southwest hook of $C^*$ at $-s$. The transpose of $F_s(C)$ is $G_{-s}(C^*)$, and the transpose of $G_s(C)$ is $F_{-s}(C^*)$: quotient/inclusion maps reverse under this pairing. Duality of finite-dimensional homology preserves zero/nonzero. Thus $\epsilon(C^*)=-\epsilon(C)$; [F2] identifies this with $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Normalize Laurent bases at $i=0$. The vertical slice of $C\otimes D$ is the ordinary field tensor of the vertical slices, with differential $d_v\otimes1+1\otimes d_v$; no term lowering algebraic level can survive there. Similarly horizontal slices at levels $s,t$ tensor to the horizontal slice at $s+t$. Splitting a finite field complex into boundary pairs and homology representatives proves the field Kunneth assertion directly: a boundary pair tensored with anything is contractible by its pair homotopy. In particular the tensor of distinguished vertical cycles represents the distinguished tensor class. Its threshold is $s+t$ by [F3]. All representatives used in steps 2.2–2.3 are supported southwest, so their vertical and horizontal projections tensor exactly to the projections of their tensor. [F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

3.2 If both epsilon values are $1$, choose the boundary representatives of step 2.2. Both horizontal parts are cycles; if $x_h=d_ha$, then $(x\otimes y)_h=d_h(a\otimes y_h)$. Its vertical part is the distinguished tensor class, so the converse in step 2.2 gives $F_{s+t}=0$, and epsilon of the tensor is $1$. The same proof works when one factor has epsilon zero and the other has epsilon $1$, using a cycle representative from step 2.3 for the zero factor. If both factors have epsilon zero, tensor their southwest-hook lifts to obtain $G_{s+t}\ne0$. Their duals also have epsilon zero by step 2.4; applying the same lift construction to the dual tensor gives its $G_{-(s+t)}\ne0$, hence $F_{s+t}\ne0$ on the original tensor. Its epsilon is therefore zero. Dualizing the already proved positive cases proves the negative/negative and zero/negative cases. Together with [F3], these are exactly both tensor rules in the Statement, with actual representatives and compatible homotopies. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 We next admit the actual complexes used for the geometric examples. Use the following marking-cell arrays, rows ordered bottom to top: for positive $T_{2,5}$ take $n=7$, $O=[6,5,4,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,3,2,1,0,6,5]$; for positive $T_{4,5}$ take $n=9$, $O=[8,7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,3,2,1,0,8,7,6,5]$. The first has five positive crossings and oriented over/under word $A^+B^-C^+D^-E^+A^-B^+C^-D^+E^-$, where superscripts indicate over/under and all crossing signs are positive. The explicit positive torus curve $(r e^{2it},s e^{5it})$, $r=s=1/\sqrt2$, has this identical code in stereographic projection: its planar angle is $2t$, radius $r/(1-s\sin5t)$, height $s\cos5t/(1-s\sin5t)$, and crossing parameters $t/(2\pi)=0,1/10,\ldots,9/10$. Equal projections force parameter difference $\pi$ and $\sin5t=0$. At the overparameter the radial derivative is positive and at the underpartner negative, so the oriented crossing determinant is positive. The angular derivative is nonzero, and there are no triple points. Thus [F6] admits this grid as the actual positive $T_{2,5}$. [F6, given, construct, algebra]

4.2 Following oriented strands in the nine-grid gives fifteen positive crossings and the full signed rotation/strand code of the closure of the four-strand positive word $121321321121321$, after a cyclic starting-point change and reversal of the knot orientation. This is an explicit finite code equality: enumerate crossings in each row and column interval, then follow each row $O\to X$ and column $X\to O$; on the braid follow the strand permutation through each listed crossing, taking the top-right strand over to bottom-left. The exact words and crossing correspondence are recorded in the finite certificate named in Remarks. Commutations $13=31$ and braid relations $121=212$, $232=323$ give the successive words $123121321121321$, $123123121121321$, $123123121212321$, $123123121213231$, $123123121231231$, $123123121231213$, $123123121232123$, $123123121323123$, $123123123123123$. Each is a local disjoint-strand isotopy or oriented R3, so their closures are equivalent. The last is $(123)^5$. To identify its torus embedding, cut the Clifford curve $(r e^{4it},s e^{5it})$ by the disk coordinate $\arg(z_1)=\theta$: its four disk points have arguments $5(\theta+2\pi k)/4$. A generic phase makes one quarter-turn's braid $132$, which becomes $321$ by moving the first generator past the closure cut, and then $123$ by reversing the four disk positions via the half-turn conjugation. Five quarter-turns give the last closure. Finally simultaneous complex conjugation is an ambient SO(4) isotopy endpoint and sends this curve to its orientation reverse: rotate its two imaginary axes through $\pi$. Thus the code reversal preserves oriented knot type, and [F6] proves the actual positive $T_{4,5}$ admission. [F6, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

4.3 Verify the trefoil grid in [F6] directly. Use row indices $0,1,2,3,4$ from bottom to top and column indices from left to right, as in [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]], and draw the standard planar grid realization using the in-square mark-to-mark intervals. Following the grid orientation gives the single cycle
$$O_{0,4}\to X_{0,2}\to O_{2,2}\to X_{2,0}\to O_{4,0}\to X_{4,3}\to O_{1,3}\to X_{1,1}\to O_{3,1}\to X_{3,4}\to O_{0,4}.$$
The horizontal and vertical intervals meet away from their endpoints at exactly three crossings: $c_1=(\text{row }1,\text{column }2)$, $c_2=(\text{row }2,\text{column }1)$, and $c_3=(\text{row }3,\text{column }3)$. Traversing the component from $O_{0,4}$ encounters $c_1$ over, $c_2$ under, $c_3$ over, $c_1$ under, $c_2$ over, and $c_3$ under. At $c_1$ and $c_2$ the oriented projected tangents $(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ are $((0,1),(-1,0))$; at $c_3$ they are $((0,-1),(1,0))$. Each determinant is $+1$ by [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]. Thus its signed oriented Gauss code is $1_O,2_U,3_O,1_U,2_O,3_U$ with crossing-sign vector $(+1,+1,+1)$. This code is also obtained by traversing the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$: its first braid strand encounters the three positive half twists over, under, over, and the returning strand encounters them under, over, under. The signed visit data determine the same crossing rotation and strand code, hence identify the face-permutation cycles. Retain the grid diagram's outer-face cycle and choose the corresponding face of the braid-closure diagram. To make this chosen face outer, compactify the projection plane to the oriented sphere $S^2$ and choose a point $q$ in that face, away from the diagram. An orientation-preserving rotation of $S^2$ sending $q$ to the projection point at infinity makes precisely this face outer. Realize the diagram lift in a product collar of the equatorial $S^2$ in $S^3$; the rotation extends by the same rotation on the first three coordinates and the identity on the normal coordinate. Its path of rotations is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy of $S^3$ preserving the crossing heights and oriented strand data. The two resulting plane codes now have the same selected outer face, so [[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]] identifies their diagrams up to planar isotopy. Thus the original grid and braid closure represent the same oriented knot even if their initially chosen planar outer faces differ. The braid closure lies on the standard unknotted torus with slope $2\alpha+3\beta$ (equivalently the swapped slope $3\alpha+2\beta$ under the orientation-preserving torus-coordinate swap), so it is $T(2,3)$ by [[def-coprime-torus-knot]]. The grid therefore represents the right-handed trefoil with its positive orientation, and its writhe is $+3$. [F6, F7, algebra]

4.4 For the cable take $n=10$, $O=[8,9,7,6,4,5,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,5,2,3,0,1,8,9,6,7]$. Here is an explicit preferred-framing admission independent of any Floer calculation. Double each row and column of the admitted positive trefoil five-grid in [F6]. At an old corner let $h,v\in\{\pm1\}$ be the directions toward its horizontal and vertical partner. A diagonal two-mark block for $hv=1$ and an antidiagonal block for $hv=-1$ give exactly two crossing-free parallel corners; checking the four quadrants verifies this and the oriented attachments. Only at the $O$ corner $(\text{row }0,\text{column }4)$, where $h=-1,v=1$, use the opposite diagonal block. It introduces one crossing of sign $hv=-1$. The listed ten-grid is precisely these ten corner blocks, and its component cycle visits rows $0,4,9,2,7,1,5,8,3,6,0$, hence it is one knot. Away from the exceptional block it follows two blackboard parallel copies of the trefoil. The blackboard longitude has linking number equal to writhe $+3$, so $\lambda_{\mathrm{bb}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{pref}}+3\mu$. The one negative half-twist therefore gives slope $2\lambda_{\mathrm{bb}}-\mu=2\lambda_{\mathrm{pref}}+5\mu$, with longitudinal orientation inherited from the original trefoil. This is exactly $T_{2,3;2,5}$ in the Statement; it is not identified from a polynomial or a candidate matrix. [F6, step 4.3, given, construct, algebra]

5.1 Compute the tilde groups of these three new grids by the following finite exact procedure. Enumerate the $n!$ state permutations $p$. For each ordered pair $a\ne b$, take the positive cyclic row interval $a\to b$ and column interval $p(a)\to p(b)$. Its initial corners are southwest and northeast, and the two row orders give the two directed rectangles for each unordered pair. Retain the rectangle exactly when its cell support contains no $O$ or $X$, and no state point lies in the product of its strict interior intervals. Its target swaps $p(a),p(b)$; equal targets cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Compute each state's degrees directly from $M_O=I(p,p)+I(O,O)-I(p,O)-I(O,p)+1$ and $A=(M_O-M_X-(n-1))/2$. In a column, use the largest target permutation index as pivot. If that pivot has an existing stored column, take symmetric difference with it; otherwise store the column there. A replacement is an invertible field-column operation and strictly lowers the pivot, so distinct stored pivots give precisely the rank. For each grade, homology dimension is basis count minus outgoing rank minus incoming rank. The completed exact computation over all $5040$, $362880$, $3628800$ states respectively gives tilde dimensions $320$, $1792$, $2560$ and the graded polynomials recorded in Remarks. The implementation and full pivot checkpoints are finite arithmetic certificates of this explicit calculation; its square-zero input is the already supplied grid differential, not an unproved reconstruction theorem. [F5, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3, step 4.4, construct, algebra]

5.2 By [F5], divide only the tilde HOMOLOGY dimension polynomial by $(1+m^{-1}a^{-1})^{n-1}$. Its quotient is unique by successively subtracting the largest-Maslov nonzero monomial times this factor. For $T_{2,5}$ the normalized hat degrees, each of rank one, are $(M,A)=(0,2),(-1,1),(-2,0),(-3,-1),(-4,-2)$; for $T_{4,5}$ they are $(0,6),(-1,5),(-2,2),(-5,0),(-6,-2),(-11,-5),(-12,-6)$; for the cable they are $(0,4),(-1,3),(-2,0),(-7,-3),(-8,-4)$. Now reduce the actual singly pointed CFK-infinity model supplied by [F5] using the contractions in step 2.1. Its Laurent basis at $i=0$ has exactly these reduced hat groups: every canceled equal-bifiltration pair is a graded boundary pair, and the reduced corner differential is zero. This step does not cancel $V$ in a chain category or tensor homology through a nonflat quotient. [F5, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

5.3 These exact degree profiles determine the full differential; no general inference from hat ranks to a full staircase is needed. List their generators in the displayed order as $e_0,e_1,\ldots$. A possible term $U^ke_j$ in $de_i$ must satisfy $k=(M_j-M_i+1)/2\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and $A_j-k\le A_i$. Exhausting these inequalities gives the following COMPLETE lists, with $v(i,j)$ denoting coefficient $1$ and $h(i,j;k)$ coefficient $U^k$ preserving horizontal level. For $T_{2,5}$: $v(0,1),v(1,2),v(2,3),v(3,4)$ and $h(1,0;1),h(2,1;1),h(3,2;1),h(4,3;1)$. For $T_{4,5}$: $v(0,1),v(1,2),v(3,4),v(5,6)$ and $h(1,0;1),h(3,2;2),h(5,4;3),h(6,5;1)$. For the cable: $v(0,1),v(1,2),v(3,4)$ and $h(1,0;1),h(3,2;3),h(4,3;1)$. Every allowed arrow is axial; there is no diagonal term. Homogeneity fixes each monomial, and its remaining coefficient is zero or one. [step 5.2, construct, algebra]

5.4 The normalized vertical homology in [F2] is one-dimensional in Maslov degree zero. Thus the only degree-zero candidate $e_0$ survives and $v(0,1)=0$. In the first list, absence of degree $-1$ homology forces $v(1,2)=1$, square-zero forces $v(2,3)=0$, and absence of degree $-3$ homology forces $v(3,4)=1$. In the other lists the remaining disjoint vertical pairs must all be present. ## Statement

For every valid connected one-component oriented planar knot code with $n$ crossings together with a specified polygonal realization $P$ whose regular projection has that code, there is an explicit finite combinatorial construction of a triangulated $S^3$ containing that same $P$ as a subcomplex. An abstract valid code can first be realized by the stated reconstruction procedure and then used as $P$. A **good exterior triangulation** is the triangulation inherited on the complement of the interior of a regular neighborhood made from one fixed ball around each vertex of $P$ and one fixed tube block along each edge, with its boundary torus triangulated and a meridian path marked. The construction gives a good exterior triangulation with at most $C(n+1)$ tetrahedra for one universal constant $C$, and the marked meridian is a path of at most $C(n+1)$ boundary edges. At $n=0$ the construction uses a fixed solid-torus exterior triangulation.

A local crossing is lifted by separating the over- and under-strands in the interval direction; the schematic below records only the projected crossing, with the continuous strand passing over the gapped strand.

The picture records only the planar local incidence. The proof constructs disjoint arcs in a three-dimensional crossing block and does not infer embeddedness from the drawing.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid connected one-component oriented planar knot code with $n$ crossings and a specified polygonal realization $P$ of that code.

[F1] [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]: the code gives a finite connected four-valent graph, directed strand pairings, over/under data and a face permutation.

[F2] [[lem-planar-diagram-code-realizability-and-face-validation]]: when $V-E+F=2$, the rotation system has a spherical polygonal realization with disk faces.

[F3] [[alg-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction]]: a passing code yields one crossing disk per crossing, one edge band per edge, and one cap per face, with recorded ports and face cycles.

[F4] [[thm-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-reconstruction-procedure-properties]]: the output gluing record represents the oriented link diagram described by the input code.


## Proof

1.1 If $n>0$, there are $4n$ darts and $2n$ paired edges. The connected crossing graph has $V=n$, $E=2n$, and hence $F=2-V+E=n+2$ faces by [F2]. The sum of face-boundary port occurrences, counted with multiplicity, is $2E=4n$. Choose disjoint small disks around the graph vertices and disjoint narrow rectangular bands along its edges, attached in the prescribed cyclic order. Their union $N(G)$ is a connected planar subsurface of the sphere; each boundary component is one face cycle, and the closure of each complementary component is a disk. The total number of vertex-disk ports, band sides and boundary occurrences is bounded by a universal constant times $n$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Triangulate each vertex disk and edge band by fixed templates. Subdivide every side occurrence on each complementary face boundary circle by a fixed number of new vertices and cone the resulting simple polygon to one interior vertex. Each face of boundary length $d$ contributes at most $c_0d$ triangles for a fixed $c_0$, and $\sum d=O(n)$ by step 1.1. Since the face boundary circles of $N(G)$ are embedded circles with port occurrences kept distinct, these are regular disk triangulations; matching subdivisions along shared ports and one fixed barycentric subdivision give a genuine finite simplicial triangulation of the projection sphere with $O(n)$ triangles. [step 1.1, F3, construct]

3.1 Take the product of this triangulated sphere with an interval. Each triangular prism is split into three tetrahedra by the fixed staircase subdivision; cap the two ends by fixed triangulated balls to obtain a triangulated $S^3$ with $O(n)$ tetrahedra. In each crossing disk, place the over- and under-strand arcs at distinct interval heights and connect each pair of opposite ports; along each edge band connect its end ports by a linear arc whose height interpolates between the endpoint heights. In a crossing block the two arcs are disjoint because their heights differ; interiors of distinct edge blocks are disjoint, and every edge arc joins only its designated crossing ports. A fixed subdivision of each crossing and edge block makes these finitely many local arc templates subcomplexes. Their number per block is bounded independently of $n$, so the resulting polygonal knot $P$ lies in the 1-skeleton and has exactly the given projection and over/under data by [F4]. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Around each vertex and edge of the 1-subcomplex $P$, take the fixed ball and tube blocks from the definition of a good exterior triangulation. Choose a normal 2-frame at one point, extend it across the finitely many edge and vertex blocks, and adjust the final frame along the last edge by a path of rotations in $SO(2)$ to agree with the initial frame. Thus their union is the product $S^1\times D^2$, a solid torus with triangulated boundary. The number of blocks and tetrahedra per block is constant, so removing its interior leaves a compact triangulated exterior with $O(n)$ tetrahedra. At an interior point of a chosen knot edge, the fixed local tube template has a meridian circle using a fixed number of boundary edges; mark that path. [step 3.1, F4, construct]

5.1 If $n=0$, use the standard genus-one product decomposition of $S^3$ into two solid tori and the fixed product triangulation of the exterior solid torus as a triangle times a three-edge circle. Splitting its three triangular prisms into three tetrahedra each and marking the three-edge fibre meridian gives a fixed-size model. Increasing $C$ to dominate this model and all fixed local template constants in steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 yields both stated $C(n+1)$ bounds. All code-dependent choices use the finite label and port order, so the construction is explicit. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. Let $S\subset M$ be a connected, two-sided, properly embedded incompressible surface with nonempty boundary contained in $\partial M$. Then either $S$ is boundary-incompressible, or $S$ is an annulus boundary-parallel into $\partial M$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact connected orientable irreducible smooth manifold with torus boundary and the connected two-sided proper incompressible surface $S$ with nonempty boundary.

[F1] The geometric disk obstructions and boundary-parallelity are [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition.

[F2] Disjoint essential smooth torus circles bound parametrized smooth annulus strips, without choice ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-curves-and-annulus-strips]], Statement).

[F3] A proper incompressible annulus with a boundary compression in this manifold is boundary-parallel, by the primitive-winding marked-ball construction ([[lem-boundary-compressible-annulus-is-boundary-parallel]], full proof).

[F9] Every compact smooth boundary-preimage surface has a boundary-fixed smooth embedding neatification with an explicit topological ambient extension. The actual smooth disk obstructions and boundary-compressing witnesses transport as stated in the endpoint-witness supplier. Products here are the products in the original Definition; on a broad nonneat input their pullbacks are topological products, not newly asserted smooth collars. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]] [[lem-angular-boundary-neatification-preserves-smooth-disk-obstructions]]


## Proof

1.1 First apply [F9] to the given surface, fixed pointwise on its boundary. The resulting surface is neat. Incompressibility passes to it, and a boundary-compressing witness passes in either direction; absence of boundary compressions therefore passes as well. Work with this neat representative for the following smooth collar constructions. The boundary-fixing topological ambient extension pulls any resulting boundary-parallel product back to the actual original surface. Thus this preparation does not add a neatness hypothesis to the Statement. If $S$ is boundary-incompressible, the first conclusion holds. Otherwise choose a boundary-compressing disk $D$, with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$ and $\alpha$ an essential proper arc of $S$. A boundary disk on a torus whose interior misses $\partial S$ can be pushed inward to compress $S$, unless $S$ is itself a disk: a boundary circle bounding a disk on the connected surface forces the surface to be that disk. An innermost choice among the finitely many inessential boundary circles provides such a boundary disk. But a disk has no essential proper arc. Therefore every boundary circle of $S$ on the torus $T$ containing $\beta$ is essential. By [F2] its complementary regions are annulus strips. The arc $\beta$ lies in one of them. If both endpoints lie on the same boundary copy of that strip, it cuts off a disk there. Gluing this disk to $D$ gives a disk with boundary $\alpha$ and an interval of $\partial S$; incompressibility of $S$ forces that circle to bound a disk on $S$, so $\alpha$ would cut off a disk on $S$, contrary to essentiality. Thus $\beta$ spans its annulus strip $A_0$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The two endpoints of $\alpha$ lie on distinct actual boundary circles of $S$. The only alternative after step 1.1 would be that the two ends of $A_0$ are the two copies of one circle $c$, with $c$ the only boundary circle of $S$ on $T$. Two-sidedness rules this out. Along the connected arc $\alpha$, the interior of $D$ lies on one fixed normal side of $S$. Along $c$, that same side restricts to one fixed side of $c$ in $T$, since the proper surface is two-sided. Hence $\beta$ must approach the same side of $c$ at both endpoints; a spanning arc of $T$ cut along $c$ approaches opposite sides. This contradiction proves the assertion. Let $P$ be a small regular neighborhood in $S$ of $\alpha$ and its two incident boundary circles. It is a pair of pants. Its third circle $d$ bounds a disk just off $S$: boundary-compress the annulus strip $A_0$ along $D$ and push the resulting disk a little inward. Its interior misses $S$, because the interior of $A_0$ misses $\partial S$ and the interior of $D$ misses $S$. Incompressibility makes $d$ bound a disk on $S$. This disk is on the side opposite $P$: if it contained $P$, the two boundary circles of $S$ in $P$ would lie in the interior of that disk, contrary to the surface half-space charts. Gluing the disk to $P$ fills a whole connected component of $S$, so $S$ is an annulus. The original $D$ is its boundary compression. Apply [F3] to get the second conclusion. Every neighborhood and disk surgery used only finitely many explicit surface and quadrant charts; [F2] and [F3] introduce no choice assumption. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $D,D'$ be finite regular oriented link diagrams related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move. Let $\bar C(D)$ be the integral signed state cube before the writhe shifts, with cohomological degree $|v|$ and quantum degree $|v|+\sum\deg(a)$, and normalize it by $C(D)=\bar C(D)[n_-]\{2n_--n_+\}$ to obtain the state degrees $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$. Before normalization, a positive type-I curl gives $\bar C(D_+)\simeq\bar C(D)\{1\}$, a negative type-I curl gives $\bar C(D_-)\simeq\bar C(D)[-1]\{-2\}$, a type-II move gives $\bar C(D_{II})\simeq\bar C(D)[-1]\{-1\}$, and a type-III move gives an unshifted equivalence. Consequently the normalized complexes are bigraded chain homotopy equivalent. If $D,D'$ are based knot diagrams and the move disk is disjoint from the basepoint, the same chain homotopy equivalence descends to their reduced quotient complexes, equivalently to the cut-tangle complexes with interval module $M=\mathbb Z$, $X\cdot1=0$.

[F2] A state with $r$ coordinates equal to $1$ is shifted by $r$ in quantum degree, and its edge signs are $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F3] The raw state complex becomes normalized by cohomological shift $[n_-]$ and quantum shift $\{2n_--n_+\}$; in the convention $C[s]^i=C^{i+s}$ and $M\{s\}_j=M_{j+s}$ these shifts give exactly $i=|v|-n_-$ and $j=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$ ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F4] For a based knot, the quotient removes the based-circle $X$ label and is identified statewise with the interval module $M=\mathbb Z$, $X\cdot1=0$. Local maps commuting with $X_p$ descend to this quotient, including when a local saddle meets the distinguished resolution component ([[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]]).

[F5] The explicit four-face RII retraction, two signed RIII Gaussian cancellations, tensor-factor conventions, quantum degrees, and commutation with exterior saddle maps and $X_p$ are proved in [[lem-khovanov-signed-local-cancellation-models]] (local-map, cancellation-rule, RII, RIII, grading and exterior-differential proof paragraphs).

[F6] Reindexing the chain mapping cone of the identity by $C_n=K^{-n}$ gives the cochain identity cone with degree-$i$ term $K^{i+1}\oplus K^i$ and differential $d(x,y)=(-d_Kx,x+d_Ky)$ ([[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]).

[F7] In the run's positively oriented crossing chart put $NW=(-1,1)$, $NE=(1,1)$, $SE=(1,-1)$ and $SW=(-1,-1)$. The overbranch is $SW$--$NE$ and the underbranch is $NW$--$SE$; A pairs $(NW,SW)$ and $(NE,SE)$, while B pairs $(NW,NE)$ and $(SW,SE)$.
