## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in $S^3$, and let $r:S^3\to S^3$ be an orientation-reversing reflection. Give $r(K)$ the image orientation, and let $-K$ denote reversal of the knot orientation. Then $g(K)=g(r(K))=g(-K)=g(-r(K))$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$, a smooth oriented knot $K$, and a smooth reflection $r$ of $S^3$.

[F1] Knot genus is the minimum genus among connected compact smooth oriented surfaces whose oriented boundary is the knot. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]])

[F2] For a connected compact orientable surface with one boundary component, reversing its orientation or applying a diffeomorphism preserves its genus. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

[A1] AC$_\omega$ is the sequence-choice principle. ([[def-countable-choice]])


## Proof

**Given:** The knot $K$, reflection $r$, and AC$_\omega$.

1.1 If $F$ is any spanning surface for $K$, its image $r(F)$ is a connected compact smooth surface with boundary $r(K)$. Push the orientation of $F$ forward to orient $r(F)$; reversing the boundary orientation instead is achieved by reversing the orientation on $r(F)$. By [F2], all these surfaces have genus $g(F)$. Thus every genus admissible for $K$ is admissible with the same value for $r(K)$ and $-K$. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct]

2.1 Apply the same argument using $r^{-1}=r$ and orientation reversal again. This gives the reverse inclusion of the sets of admissible genera, so their minima agree for all four knots. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be a null-homologous knot in a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$, let $F$ be a genus-$g$ Seifert surface, and let $(M,\gamma)$ be the balanced sutured manifold obtained by cutting the compact exterior of $K$ along $F$. For a surface-adapted admissible sutured Heegaard diagram, the generator correspondence between the top Alexander summand of the knot Floer complex and the sutured Floer disk-count module identifies their disk-count differentials. Under the hypotheses of a horizontal decomposition, the induced chain map realizes Ni's horizontal decomposition formula. Under the hypotheses of a separating product annulus with connected $R_+$ and $R_-$, the induced chain map realizes Ni's product-annulus tensor formula. These assertions use the specified basepoint domains, periodic-domain admissibility, and exact characteristic-product-region hypotheses; they make no claim that generic Heegaard disk existence alone supplies the decomposition maps.


## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-signed-relative-surface-cut-and-horizontal-decomposition]] gives actual adapted admissible nice diagrams, complete signed differential lifting with the specified character, and the horizontal graded tensor chain operation.

[F2] [[lem-signed-essential-product-annulus-decomposition]] constructs the actual closure marking, product one-handle and disk identifications, and the full essential separating-annulus tensor operation.

[F3] [[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology]] fixes the integral coefficient convention and Seifert-class normalization; [[lem-fiber-outer-grading-and-integral-cut-euler-matrix]] computes the absolute outer Chern anchor on an actually marked adapted diagram.


## Proof

**Given:** The stated null-homologous knot in an arbitrary closed connected oriented three-manifold, the specified genus-g Seifert surface, the meridional basepoint convention, and the stated decomposition hypotheses.

1.1 Construct the actual marked closure/adapted surface diagram from the relative Morse handles, carrying the page longitude and meridional boundary frame. Positive boundary fingers, the uniform relative windings, and permissible niceification give the admitted diagram. The Chern obstruction formula evaluates on minus F as minus 2g plus twice the number of interior polygon coordinates. Consequently its degree-g generators are exactly its outer generators. Each index-one disk is an exhausted embedded bigon or rectangle and lifts uniquely in the cut/double surface. The literal Fredholm conjugacies and the pullback of the specified periodic-domain orientation character align every coefficient after generator signs. Thus this generator correspondence identifies the full disk-count differentials over the integers. Signed relative moves transport the identification to the defining complexes, with their markings and coherent orientation classes. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 For a horizontal decomposition, the cut components are balanced. In its adapted diagram there is no reverse cross-family intersection from side two to side one; the equal row and column counts force every perfect-matching generator to avoid the polygon. Thus the whole complex is the outer complex. The cut surface is a disjoint union, so each index-one disk has exactly one nonconstant factor. Ordering determinant factors gives the Koszul differential ∂(x1⊗x2)=∂x1⊗x2+(−1)^|x1|x1⊗∂x2. This is the horizontal chain map and the complete integral chain formula. Taking homology over any field gives Ni's horizontal formula. Taking homology over the integers instead gives the Künneth exact sequence including Tor; no unqualified integral homology tensor formula is asserted. [F1, step 1.1]

1.3 For an essential separating product annulus with connected R+ and R−, form the two rounded horizontal surfaces from opposite boundary faces and the annulus. Their actual cobordism regions give the required relative class and their Euler sums give the horizontal equality. This reduces the operation to attachment of a product region. A rooted cut-arc forest removes a product region meeting the sutures by literal product-disk identifications. For an interior essential product region, the explicit once-punctured-torus block forces its two fixed coordinates and isolates the only possible extra genus-one two-corner domain, whose Maslov index is minus one; it cannot contribute. Both comparison diagrams therefore have precisely the same supported disks and conjugate oriented operators in the unchanged complement. The resulting integral chain identification, followed by the remaining product-disk cuts, gives the full separating-annulus graded tensor operation. It gives Ni's field formula and the integral Künneth/Tor formulation as above. All constructions keep the stated basepoint zero regions, actual periodic lattices and essential-annulus hypotheses. They apply when the specified characteristic product region supplies those actual surfaces; they do not infer its geometry from generic disk existence. [F2, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper disk, let $p$ be prime, $q=p^k$ with $k\ge1$, and let $\mathbb F_p$ be the field with $p$ elements. For the connected $q$-fold cyclic cover $X_{D,q}$ of the disk exterior, $H_0(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$, $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$, and $H_i(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$ for every $i\ge2$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth proper disk $D$, its exterior $X_D$, the infinite cyclic cover $X_{D,\infty}$ with deck generator $t$, and $q=p^k$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $H_0(X_D;\mathbb F_p)=\mathbb F_p$, $H_1(X_D;\mathbb F_p)=\mathbb F_p$ generated by the meridian, and $H_i(X_D;\mathbb F_p)=0$ for $i\ge2$. This follows from the integral homology of the exterior and the universal coefficient theorem for homology over a PID. [[lem-slice-disk-exterior-has-homology-of-a-circle]] [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-homology-over-a-pid]]

[F2] The infinite cyclic cover and its finite quotient are those defined by the positive-meridian deck action in [[def-infinite-cyclic-cover-of-a-slice-disk-exterior]]. Their chain groups give short exact sequences
$$0\to C_*(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\xrightarrow{t-1}C_*(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\to C_*(X_D;\mathbb F_p)\to0$$
and
$$0\to C_*(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\xrightarrow{t^q-1}C_*(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\to C_*(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\to0.$$
Each singular simplex has a free orbit of lifts; quotienting its orbit module by $t-1$ or $t^q-1$ gives the singular chains of the corresponding quotient cover. The long exact homology sequences are supplied by [[thm-long-exact-sequence-in-homology]].


## Proof

1.1 The deck transformation acts trivially on $H_0(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$ because the cover is connected. From the first sequence in [F2], its homology exact sequence and [F1] show that $t-1$ is an isomorphism on $H_i(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)$ for every $i\ge1$: for $i\ge2$ both neighboring homology groups of $X_D$ vanish, while in degree one exactness uses $H_2(X_D)=0$, $H_1(X_D)=\mathbb F_p$, and the zero map $t-1$ on $H_0(X_{D,\infty})$. Thus the degree-one quotient and kernel both vanish. [F1, F2, given, algebra, A1]

2.1 In characteristic $p$, repeated Frobenius gives $t^{p^k}-1=(t-1)^{p^k}$. Therefore $t^q-1$ is an isomorphism on every positive-degree homology group of $X_{D,\infty}$ and is zero on its degree-zero homology. The long exact sequence of the second sequence in [F2] now gives $H_1(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong H_0(X_{D,\infty};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$, while the quotient cover is connected and hence $H_0(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)\cong\mathbb F_p$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each $i\ge2$, both the cokernel on $H_i(X_{D,\infty})$ and the kernel on $H_{i-1}(X_{D,\infty})$ of $t^q-1$ vanish by step 2.1 and the isomorphisms of step 1.1. Exactness therefore gives $H_i(X_{D,q};\mathbb F_p)=0$. This includes all higher degrees and completes the calculation. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold other than $T^2\times I$ and the orientable twisted $I$-bundle over the Klein bottle. Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite family of connected, two-sided essential annuli in $M$ such that every boundary torus of $M$ contains a boundary circle of some annulus in $\mathcal A$. Then any two Seifert fibrations of $M$ induce isotopic regular-fiber slopes on each boundary torus.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a compact connected orientable Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold $M$ outside the two orientable exceptional manifolds in the Statement, a finite family $\mathcal A$ of essential annuli meeting every boundary torus, and two Seifert fibrations of $M$.

[A1] Full AC is the axiom that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], Definition).

[F1] An essential smooth boundary-preimage annulus in a Seifert piece can be isotoped through smooth embeddings to a vertical annulus for a given fibration; for neat annuli this is a smooth ambient isotopy, with a fibration change needed only in the exceptional underlying manifolds ([[lem-essential-annulus-in-seifert-piece-isotopic-to-vertical]], Statement).

[F2] [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]] defines the base surface, exceptional fibers, and regular-fiber slope.


## Proof

1.1 Fix an annulus $A\in\mathcal A$ whose boundary meets a chosen boundary torus $T$. Apply [F1] to the first fibration. Since $M$ is outside the exceptional cases, a smooth embedding isotopy makes $A$ vertical without changing that fibration. Its boundary circle on $T$ therefore represents the regular-fiber slope of the first fibration. [A1, F1, given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F1] to the second fibration. Again the annulus becomes vertical by a smooth embedding isotopy without replacing that second fibration. Restricting this embedding isotopy to the boundary gives a smooth isotopy of boundary circles on $T$, so it preserves the free isotopy class of its boundary circle on $T$, so that circle also represents the regular-fiber slope for the second fibration. The two primitive slopes are therefore isotopic on $T$. Repeating this argument for each boundary torus, using the annulus family $\mathcal A$, proves the claim for all boundary components. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $C$ and $D$ be finite integer-filtered chain complexes over $\mathbb F_2$, with increasing bounded exhaustive filtrations by subcomplexes and with $H(C)\cong H(D)\cong\mathbb F_2$. Give $C\otimes D$ the tensor differential and the convolution filtration
$$F_s(C\otimes D)=\sum_{p+q\le s}F_pC\otimes F_qD.$$
Then $H(C\otimes D)\cong\mathbb F_2$ and
$$\tau(C\otimes D)=\tau(C)+\tau(D).$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The complexes $C,D$ and their filtrations as in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau]]: $\tau(C)$ is the least integer $s$ for which $H(F_sC)\to H(C)$ has nonzero image, when $H(C)\cong\mathbb F_2$.


## Proof

1.1 Write $t=\tau(C)$ and $u=\tau(D)$. For each degree $n$, let $B_n=\operatorname{im}(\partial_{n+1})$ and $Z_n=\ker(\partial_n)$. Finite-dimensional linear algebra gives complements $H_n,L_n$ with $Z_n=B_n\oplus H_n$ and $C_n=Z_n\oplus L_n$; the differential maps $L_n$ isomorphically onto $B_{n-1}$. Thus each complex is the direct sum of homology representatives with contractible two-term complexes. If $h$ contracts one such summand $A$, then $h\otimes 1$ contracts $A\otimes E$: the two cross terms cancel by the graded tensor signs, while $(\partial h+h\partial)\otimes1=1$. Hence $H(C\otimes D)\cong H(C)\otimes H(D)\cong\mathbb F_2$. By [F1], choose cycles $x\in F_tC$ and $y\in F_uD$ representing the nonzero homology classes. Their tensor is a nonzero class in $H(C\otimes D)$ and lies in $F_{t+u}(C\otimes D)$, so $\tau(C\otimes D)\le t+u$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $n$ be the homological degree of $[x]$. The image of $H(F_{t-1}C)$ in $H(C)$ is zero by minimality of $t$, so every cycle in $F_{t-1}C_n$ is a boundary in $C$. The cycle $x$ cannot lie in $B_n+F_{t-1}C_n$; otherwise $x=b+v$ would make $v=x-b$ a cycle in $F_{t-1}C$ representing the same nonzero class. Extend the linear functional that is zero on $B_n+F_{t-1}C_n$ and one on $x$ to a functional $\lambda:C_n\to\mathbb F_2$. It vanishes on boundaries, so is a cocycle. Construct $\mu$ on the homological degree of $y$ in $D$ in the same way. The tensor cocycle $\lambda\otimes\mu$ evaluates to one on $x\otimes y$ and vanishes on every $F_{t+u-1}(C\otimes D)$: each summand $F_pC\otimes F_qD$ with $p+q\le t+u-1$ has either $p<t$ or $q<u$. Therefore no class in that lower filtration maps to the nonzero total homology class, and $\tau(C\otimes D)\ge t+u$. Together with step 1.1 this proves equality. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ and $q\ge2$, the first homology of the $q$-fold cyclic cover $M_{0,q}$ of zero surgery has an isomorphism of abelian groups
$$H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z,$$
where the free summand is generated by $\widetilde\mu$, the closed lift of the $q$-fold meridian loop $\mu^q$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth oriented knot $K$, the integer $q\ge2$, the exterior cover $E_q$, its meridional filling $\Sigma_q(K)$, and its zero-surgery filling $M_{0,q}$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The zero-surgery cover is obtained by filling the common exterior cover $E_q$ along a lift of the preferred longitude. Its filling solid torus has core represented by the closed lift $\widetilde\mu$ of $\mu^q$. [[def-cyclic-zero-surgery-cover]]

[F2] The branched cover $\Sigma_q(K)$ is obtained by filling the same $E_q$ along the closed lift of $\mu^q$. [[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot]]

[F3] The exterior homology is generated by the meridian; the preferred longitude is a degree-one peripheral curve nullhomologous in the exterior. The induced homomorphism $\ell_K:\pi_1(E_K)\to\mathbb Z$ sends $\mu$ to $1$ and is the meridian-coordinate map. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]

[F4] Every smooth oriented knot bounds a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface. Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of this supplier. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]] [[def-countable-choice]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F5] For a one-component knot, the total-linking homomorphism is the meridian-coordinate map $\ell_K$ from [F3]; it equals signed intersection with a Seifert surface. [[lem-total-linking-equals-intersection-with-link-seifert-surface]] [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]

[F6] Mayer–Vietoris computes the first homology of each filling from the common boundary torus, and the H0 map is injective because all three spaces are connected. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F7] The unbranched exterior cover is classified by the kernel of $\ell_K\bmod q$; a connected surface whose fundamental-group image lies in this subgroup lifts to the cover. [[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot]] [[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]

[L1] Conway's Lemma 2.31 states the same splitting and gives a Mayer–Vietoris proof. The complete proof in the retrieved §2.6 was read; the explicit meridian retraction below makes the splitting step transparent. [Anthony Conway, *Algebraic Concordance and Casson–Gordon Invariants*, §2.6, Lemma 2.31, pp. 23–24](https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000id_/https://www.unige.ch/math/folks/conway/Notes/AlgebraicConcordanceCassonGordon.pdf)


## Proof



1.1 Choose a Seifert surface for $K$ by [F4] and remove its boundary collar to obtain a properly embedded surface $F_0$ in the knot exterior. Its boundary is a degree-one longitude curve, hence represents the preferred longitude by [F3]. Each element of $\pi_1(F_0)$ has a smooth loop representative. Push that loop slightly to one side of the Seifert surface; the push is homotopic in the exterior and disjoint from the surface, so [F5] gives meridian coordinate zero. Thus $\ell_K\bmod q$ vanishes on $\pi_1(F_0)$, and [F7] lifts $F_0$ to each sheet of $E_q$. Each lifted copy has one boundary component over the preferred longitude, proving that every lifted longitude is nullhomologous in $E_q$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F7, given, construct]

1.2 In the branched filling, $\widetilde\mu$ bounds the attached solid torus's meridian disk and a longitude lift maps to its core generator. The same Mayer–Vietoris cokernel calculation [F6] gives $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)/\langle[\widetilde\mu]\rangle$. [F2, F6, algebra]

2.1 In the zero-surgery filling, the boundary-torus basis consists of the closed meridian lift $\widetilde\mu$ and a longitude lift $\widetilde\lambda$. The latter bounds a meridian disk in the attached solid torus and the former maps to its core generator. The Mayer–Vietoris cokernel in [F6] therefore eliminates the core generator and gives $H_1(M_{0,q};\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)/\langle[\widetilde\lambda]\rangle$. Step 1.1 makes this quotient $H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The cover subgroup is $\ker(\ell_K\bmod q)$ by [F7]. Thus $\ell_K(g)$ is divisible by $q$ for every $g\in\pi_1(E_q)$, and $g\mapsto\ell_K(g)/q$ is a homomorphism $\pi_1(E_q)\to\mathbb Z$. It descends to $r:H_1(E_q;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ and satisfies $r([\widetilde\mu])=1$, since $\widetilde\mu$ projects to $\mu^q$. Therefore $\mathbb Z[\widetilde\mu]$ is a direct summand and $H_1(E_q)\cong H_1(E_q)/\langle[\widetilde\mu]\rangle\oplus\mathbb Z[\widetilde\mu]$. Using step 1.2 and then step 2.1 proves the statement. [F3, F7, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $q$ be a prime power. If for every metabolizer $P$ of the torsion linking form on $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ there is a prime-power-order character $\chi:H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ vanishing on $P$ with $\sigma(K,\chi)\ne0$, then $K$ is not smoothly slice.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth oriented knot $K$, a prime-power degree $q$, the linking form on $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$, and the hypothesis that every metabolizer admits a character vanishing on it with nonzero signature defect.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For prime-power $q$, $H_1(\Sigma_q(K);\mathbb Z)$ is finite, and its torsion linking form is nonsingular. [[lem-prime-power-branched-cover-homology-is-finite]]

[F2] If $K$ is smoothly slice, a disk induces a metabolizer of this form. [[lem-slice-disk-induces-branched-cover-metabolizer]]

[F3] A knot is smoothly slice when it bounds a smooth proper disk in $B^4$. [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]]

[F4] A metabolizer is a subgroup equal to its orthogonal complement for the finite nonsingular linking form. [[def-finite-linking-form-and-metabolizer]]

[F5] A prime-power-order character is a finite-order homomorphism to $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ whose order is a prime power. [[def-finite-order-character-of-a-branched-cover]]

[F6] For a smooth slice disk and any prime-power-order character vanishing on its induced metabolizer, the specified Casson–Gordon signature defect vanishes; its proof constructs the actual extending disk-exterior coefficient system and proves the full Witt comparison. [[lem-casson-gordon-signature-defect-and-vanishing]]



## Proof

1.1 Prove the contrapositive. Suppose $K$ is smoothly slice, and choose its smooth proper disk $D$. By [F1] its prime-power branched-cover first homology is finite, and by [F2] the disk kernel $P_D$ is a metabolizer of its nonsingular linking form. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, contrapositive-reduce, assume-hyp, choose]

2.1 Every prime-power-order character vanishing on this particular $P_D$ has $\sigma(K,\chi)=0$ by the now proved vanishing statement [F6]. Therefore the universal metabolizer hypothesis in the Statement fails at $P_D$: there is no such character with nonzero defect. We have proved that smooth sliceness implies the negation of that hypothesis, so contraposition gives the stated obstruction. If the linking form has no metabolizer, smooth sliceness already contradicts [F2]; no independent existence of a metabolizer was assumed. All prime-power quantifiers and the stated smooth and AC scope are retained. [F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, discharge-contrapositive] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$ be the smooth knot concordance group, with addition induced by oriented connected sum and inverse represented by reverse mirror. The function $\epsilon: \mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}\to\{-1,0,1\}$ is well-defined and concordance-invariant, but it is not a homomorphism to $\mathbb Z$. The map
$$ \Upsilon:\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}\longrightarrow \mathrm{PL}([0,2],\mathbb R),\qquad [K]\longmapsto\Upsilon_K, $$
is a group homomorphism, where $\mathrm{PL}([0,2],\mathbb R)$ is the abelian group of continuous piecewise-linear real-valued functions under pointwise addition. For every representative $K$ and $0\le t\le1$, its value satisfies $|\Upsilon_K(t)|\le t\,g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth concordance group, the epsilon invariant, the Upsilon function, and the smooth four-ball genus with the conventions stated above.

[F1] [[thm-knot-concordance-is-an-abelian-group]]: in the smooth branch, the operation is oriented connected sum, the inverse is reverse mirror, and a class is zero precisely when represented by a smoothly slice knot. The smooth proof branch was inspected; the topological branch is not used.

[F2] The Upsilon supplier proves its model invariance, finite piecewise linearity, reflection, tensor additivity, mirror sign and initial slope. Its smooth four-ball genus clause uses the explicitly external OSS/Hom–Wu nu-minus bound recorded there. [[thm-upsilon-additivity-mirror-and-genus-bound]]

[F3] The completed epsilon supplier gives its actual stable-core/hook trichotomy, stable-equivalence invariance, normalized conjugation/dual sign and tensor rules, and admitted trefoil and torus/cable witnesses. In particular the trefoil and its double both have epsilon1, proving integer nonadditivity. This does not itself prove smooth-concordance descent. [[lem-epsilon-stable-equivalence-and-not-a-homomorphism]]

[F4] Smooth concordance implies stable filtered equivalence using the explicitly external Hom slice splitting and the preserved local finite tensor-stabilization argument. Its actual normalized model and tensor interfaces are supplied. [[thm-smooth-concordance-implies-stable-filtered-knot-floer-equivalence]]


## Proof

1.1 If $K$ and $J$ represent the same smooth concordance class, then $K\#(-J)$ is smoothly slice by [F1], so $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K\#(-J))=0$. The genus bound in [F2] gives $\Upsilon_{K\#(-J)}(t)=0$ for $0\le t\le1$; reflection gives the same for all $t\in[0,2]$. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 If $K$ and $J$ are smoothly concordant, [F4] gives stable filtered equivalence of their knot Floer complexes. Stable-equivalence invariance in [F3] then gives $\epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)$, so epsilon is well-defined on $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$. The trefoil witness in [F3] shows that it is not additive as a $\mathbb Z$-valued function. [given, F3, F4]

2.1 By additivity and reverse-mirror antisymmetry in [F2], $ 0=\Upsilon_{K\#(-J)}(t)=\Upsilon_K(t)-\Upsilon_J(t), $ so $\Upsilon_K=\Upsilon_J$ and the function is well-defined on smooth concordance classes. The same additivity identity on arbitrary representatives shows that $[K]\mapsto\Upsilon_K$ is a homomorphism to $\mathrm{PL}([0,2],\mathbb R)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every finite input code and either selected mode, the Haken–Jaco–Tollefson procedure terminates. It returns the prescribed first validation error for an invalid code, returns **not-a-knot** for a valid multi-component code, and for a valid one-component knot code returns either a finite normal-coordinate disk-candidate certificate or **no-candidate** after exhaustive search.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite tagged knot-code input and either Haken or JT mode.

[F1] [[alg-haken-jaco-tollefson-unknot-recognition]]: validation and component branching precede a finite exterior construction; Haken mode scans the finite coordinate box, and JT mode scans all subsets of $7t$ zero-coordinate constraints and performs finite exact linear algebra on each.


## Proof

1.1 The code and each encoded field are finite, so the planar-code validation procedure terminates. Its prescribed return is passed through unchanged; a valid multi-component code returns **not-a-knot** immediately. For a valid one-component code, the good exterior triangulation is a finite combinatorial output by [F1]. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 In Haken mode the integer bound $B=t2^{7t+2}$ is finite and nonnegative, so the lexicographic box contains exactly $(B+1)^{7t}$ vectors. Each matching, quadrilateral, and disk test scans finite coordinates and faces. Fundamentalness is decided by checking every coordinatewise split $v=x+(v-x)$; there are at most $\prod_i(v_i+1)$ such splits, each tested by finitely many integer comparisons. Therefore every loop and the complete Haken search terminate. [F1, algebra]

1.3 In JT mode there are exactly $2^{7t}$ subsets $Z$. For each, computing the rank and, when the nullity is one, an integer kernel generator by exact finite matrix operations terminates. Checking admissibility, deduplicating, and testing the boundary data are finite scans. Thus the complete JT search terminates. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The algorithm's ordered validation branch returns its first invalid result; its component branch returns **not-a-knot** exactly for a valid multi-component input. In either one-component mode, all candidates are drawn from the stated finite enumeration and a return of **no-candidate** occurs only after that enumeration ends. Steps 1.1–1.3 prove the stated termination and output form. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let X be a closed oriented smooth 4-manifold, Γ a discrete group, and φ:π₁(X)→Γ a homomorphism. Then the von Neumann signature of the NΓ-coefficient intersection form equals the ordinary signature:
sign_Γ^(2)(X,φ)=sign(X).


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the closed oriented smooth four-manifold $X$, the discrete group $\Gamma$, and the homomorphism $\phi$ of the Statement. AC is the standing convention of the coefficient Definition and the supplied smooth realization proof.

[A1] Full AC is already assumed by the coefficient Definition. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The signature in the Statement is the von Neumann inertia difference of the regular-coefficient middle intersection form. [[def-integral-half-solutions-strebel-and-l2-signatures]]

[F2] The smooth group-signature theorem constructs a coefficient-preserving smooth five-bordism after an injective acyclic-envelope enlargement, proves signature invariance across that actual bordism, and proves induction under group inclusion. Its closed smooth conclusion applies to arbitrary discrete target groups. [[thm-smooth-group-signature-defects-are-independent-and-uniformly-bounded]]


## Proof

1.1 Apply [F2] to the actual smooth manifold $X$ and $\phi$. More explicitly, its classifying-map and labelled-bordism arguments produce an acyclic-envelope classifying map and a labelled smooth five-bordism from $X$ with that map to the same $X$ with constant map. Its closed-manifold argument identifies the original $\Gamma$ intersection signature with the enlarged-target signature by regular-coset block induction and preserves that signature across this actual bordism. This is precisely the geometric intersection signature [F1], rather than a separate analytically defined quantity. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 With constant coefficients the finite intersection matrices are the ordinary complex matrices tensored with the regular module; every scalar positive or negative eigenspace has its ordinary multiplicity multiplied by the trace of the identity, namely one. Thus the constant-map signature is $\operatorname{sign}(X)$. The identifications in step 1.1 give $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(X,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}(X)$, for nononto maps and arbitrary target cardinality as included in [F2]. If $X$ is disconnected, compactness gives finitely many components and both signatures add; the empty case is zero. This proves the literal smooth Statement without an unproved analytic index or a TOP realization assumption. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every valid input of the colored-braid evaluation algorithm, where the braid word has $m$ letters and the total tensor-product dimension is $D$, the procedure terminates after exactly $m$ crossing-matrix updates and one finite pivotal-trace contraction. It returns the ribbon-category evaluation of that framed colored braid closure in the given matrix realization. The stated bound concerns the number of matrix updates; each update is a finite exact matrix multiplication over the effective field.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A valid effective matrix input, a color-preserving braid word of length $m$, and the algorithm specified above.

[F1] The algorithm initializes the identity matrix, multiplies the typed positive or inverse braiding matrix for each word letter, checks final color preservation, and returns the finite contraction $\operatorname{ev}_{W^\vee}((J_WM_\beta)\otimes1_{W^\vee})\operatorname{coev}_W$ ([[alg-ribbon-evaluation-from-colored-braid-word]]).


## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and [F1].

1.1 After $j$ updates, induction on $j$ shows that the running matrix is the composite of the first $j$ typed crossing maps in composition order. The base case $j=0$ is the identity of $W$; the update rule in [F1] composes exactly the next generator or its inverse, proving the induction step. There are precisely $m$ letters, so there are precisely $m$ updates. [F1, given, induction]

2.1 At $j=m$, [F1] identifies the matrix with $M_\beta$. Its final-color check makes it an endomorphism of $W$, and the output contraction is the categorical pivotal trace of that endomorphism, hence the defined closure evaluation. Every update is one finite matrix multiplication and the last contraction is finite; the effective-field procedures terminate, so the algorithm terminates and has the asserted value. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field and let $\mathcal C$ be a $k$-linear ribbon category with $k$-bilinear tensor product and $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)=k$. Let $X$ be absolutely simple, so its twist is $\theta_X=\lambda\operatorname{id}_X$ for a unique $\lambda\in k^\times$. For $n\ge1$ and $\beta\in B_n$, let $t_n(\beta)$ be the value of the blackboard-framed $X$-colored closure and let $w(\beta)$ be the exponent sum, with positive Artin generator and positive stabilization conventions fixed as in the supplied ribbon-trace formulas. Then
$$J_X(\widehat\beta):=\lambda^{-w(\beta)}t_n(\beta)$$
depends only on the oriented unframed link type of $\widehat\beta$ when every component has color $X$. This statement makes no normalization by the categorical dimension.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; the $k$-linear ribbon category and absolutely simple color in the Statement; a braid $\beta\in B_n$ with $n\ge1$.

[F1] The braid evaluation is $t_n(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(j_{X^{\otimes n}}\rho_n(\beta))$, where $j=u\theta$ is the ribbon-induced pivotal comparison ([[def-ribbon-evaluation-of-an-x-colored-closed-braid]]).

[F2] Categorical trace is cyclic: $\operatorname{Tr}_L(ac)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(c^{\vee\vee}a)$ for the stated typed morphisms ([[thm-basic-properties-of-the-categorical-trace]]).

[F3] The two stabilization values are $t_{n+1}(\iota_n(\beta)\sigma_n^{\pm1})=\lambda^{\pm1}t_n(\beta)$ when positive stabilization closes to the positive curl ([[lem-scalar-twist-controls-the-two-markov-stabilizations]]).

[F4] The exponent sum is unchanged by conjugation and satisfies $w(\iota_n(\beta)\sigma_n^{\pm1})=w(\beta)\pm1$ ([[def-exponent-sum-and-writhe-of-a-braid]]).

[F5] Two braids have equivalent oriented closures exactly when they are related by conjugations, stabilizations, and destabilizations ([[thm-markovs-closed-braid-equivalence-theorem]]).

[F6] The Axiom of Choice implies countable choice ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]).

[A1] Absolute simplicity means $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(X)=k\operatorname{id}_X$, so each automorphism of $X$ is a unique nonzero scalar multiple of the identity ([[def-absolutely-simple-object]]).

[A2] The Axiom of Choice is the assumption that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).


## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and [F1]–[F6], [A1]–[A2].

1.1 Fix $\gamma\in B_n$. Put $j=j_{X^{\otimes n}}$ and $\rho=\rho_n$. By [F1], $t_n(\gamma\beta\gamma^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_L(j\rho(\gamma)\rho(\beta)\rho(\gamma)^{-1})$. Apply [F2] with $a=j\rho(\gamma)$ and $c=\rho(\beta)\rho(\gamma)^{-1}$. Naturality of $j$ at $\rho(\gamma)^{-1}$ gives $(\rho(\gamma)^{-1})^{\vee\vee}j=j\rho(\gamma)^{-1}$, and a second use of [F2] then gives $t_n(\gamma\beta\gamma^{-1})=t_n(\beta)$. The exponent sum is also unchanged by [F4], so $J_X$ is invariant under conjugation. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 For a positive or negative stabilization, [F3] multiplies $t_n$ by $\lambda^{\pm1}$ and [F4] changes $w$ by $\pm1$. Hence $\lambda^{-w(\iota_n\beta\sigma_n^{\pm1})}t_{n+1}(\iota_n\beta\sigma_n^{\pm1})=\lambda^{-w(\beta)\mp1}\lambda^{\pm1}t_n(\beta)=\lambda^{-w(\beta)}t_n(\beta)$. The scalar is available because [A1] makes the invertible twist a unique $\lambda\in k^\times$; the positive sign is fixed by [F3]. Thus $J_X$ is invariant under both stabilizations and their inverses. [F3, F4, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F5], any two braids with equivalent oriented unframed closures are connected by finitely many conjugations, stabilizations, and destabilizations. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 preserve $J_X$ under each such move, so the corrected value depends only on the oriented unframed link type. The Axiom of Choice [A2] is used in [F5] and supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] by [F6]; no choice is used in the finite trace or scalar calculations. [F3, F4, F5, F6, A2, step 1.1, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be an unoriented link type in $S^3$. Its **crossing number** $c(K)$ is the least element of
$$\{\,n\in\mathbb N:\text{some regular diagram of }K\text{ has exactly }n\text{ crossings}\,\}.$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and an unoriented link type $K$ in $S^3$.

[F1] A link is a finite disjoint union of smoothly embedded circles in $S^3$, and it may be moved off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ before projection ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F2] A regular diagram is a finite planar projection with transverse double points, no triple points, and over-under data ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F3] Under countable choice, every oriented link admits a regular projection ([[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]).

[F4] Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

[A1] Countable choice, abbreviated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, selects one element from each member of a countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable-choice]]).


## Proof
1.1 Let $N(K)$ be the displayed set of crossing counts. By [F1], move an oriented representative off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$; [F3] and [A1] give it a regular diagram. Forgetting the diagram's strand arrows gives a regular diagram of the same unoriented type, so $N(K)\ne\varnothing$. [given, F1, F2, F3, A1, construct]

2.1 The set $N(K)$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so [F4] supplies its unique least element. Ambient-isotopic representatives have the same crossing-count set by definition of the underlying unoriented link type. This makes $c(K)$ well-defined. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1, choose] ∎

## Definition

An oriented link $L\subset S^3$ is **split** if a smoothly embedded sphere $S\subset S^3\setminus L$ has link points in both components of $S^3\setminus S$; otherwise $L$ is **nonsplit**.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A link $L\subset S^3$ as a finite disjoint union of embedded circles.

[F1] A link is a finite disjoint union of smoothly embedded circles in $S^3$ ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]).


## Proof
1.1 Forgetting the component orientations does not change the point set $L$ or the complementary regions of a sphere disjoint from it. Thus the split predicate depends only on the underlying unoriented link type, as required by [F1]. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Ambient isotopy carries any witnessing sphere and the two components of its complement to a sphere and two complementary components for the image link. The existence or nonexistence of a witness is therefore an ambient-isotopy invariant. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Example

For the right-handed trefoil and figure-eight knot, use their standard genus-one Seifert surfaces and the ordered bases whose positive-push Seifert matrices are, respectively,
$$V_T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V_8=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Their double branched covers have first homology $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, respectively. The double branched cover of the unknot is $S^3$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the matrices and knots specified in the Example.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom required by the double-cover presentation. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For a positive-push Seifert matrix $V$, $H_1(\Sigma_2(K);\mathbb Z)\cong\operatorname{coker}(V+V^T)$. [[lem-double-branched-cover-homology-from-seifert-matrix]]

[F2] A square integer matrix with nonzero determinant has finite cokernel of order the absolute determinant; unimodular row and column operations preserve the cokernel. [[lem-square-integer-cokernel-finiteness-and-order]]


## Proof

1.1 For the trefoil, $V_T+V_T^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$. Swap its columns, add twice the first row to the second, then add twice the first column to the second; the result is $\operatorname{diag}(1,-3)$. Each operation is unimodular, so [F1]–[F2] give $H_1(\Sigma_2(T))\cong\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 For the figure-eight knot, $V_8+V_8^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Swap its columns, subtract twice the first row from the second, then add twice the first column to the second; the result is $\operatorname{diag}(1,5)$. Thus its cokernel is $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For the unknot, the standard spanning disk has genus zero, so its Seifert matrix is empty and [F1] gives trivial first homology. To identify the whole cover, write $S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$ and define $f(z,w)=\bigl(z\sqrt{1+|w|^2},w^2\bigr)$. The image lies in $S^3$ because $|z|^2(1+|w|^2)+|w|^4=1$. Off $w=0$, each target point has exactly two preimages, corresponding to the two square roots of its second coordinate; on $w=0$ it has one. The involution $(z,w)\mapsto(z,-w)$ is the deck transformation, and in tubular coordinates about $w=0$ the transverse map is $w\mapsto w^2$. Hence $f$ is the connected double branched cover of $S^3$ over the unknot, so the cover is $S^3$. [F1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $u$ be a compactly supported distribution or a compactly supported distributional density on a real-analytic manifold. In each analytic chart use the Gaussian FBI packets of the preceding definition, paired with test densities in the first case and test functions in the second. The exponential-decay criterion is independent of the compact cutoff that equals one near the base point. It is also equivalent after an analytic chart change, with covectors transformed by the cotangent differential, and after replacing the standard Gaussian packets by their analytic pullbacks under that chart change. The latter equivalence is asserted only for the local packet and chart changes used on this page; it is the analytic-wavefront invariance needed to interpret the set geometrically.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A compactly supported distribution $u$, a point-covector pair, nested coordinate neighborhoods, and the Gaussian packet families in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-analytic-wavefront-fbi-transform]]: analytic regularity means a uniform exponential bound on localized Gaussian FBI pairings.

[F2] [[lem-ip-analytic-cutoff-sequence]]: smooth compact cutoffs can be chosen with $|\partial^\alpha\chi_N|\le C(CN)^{|\alpha|}$ for $|\alpha|\le N$.

[F3] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: scalar distributions act on test densities, while distributional densities act on scalar test functions; both are continuous with local fixed-support seminorm control.

[F4] [[thm-compactly-supported-distributions-are-tempered]]: compactly supported Euclidean distributions have unique tempered extensions.

[F5] [[lem-compactly-supported-distributions-extend-to-smooth-functions]]: compactly supported distributions act continuously on smooth functions by local cutoffs.

[F6] [[lem-ip-local-analytic-elliptic-packet-calculus]] proves bidirectional equivalence for normalized positive analytic phases and elliptic analytic amplitudes, including actual inverse and fixed-order exponentially small localization errors.


## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Fix one real-analytic chart and two smooth cutoffs $\chi,\widetilde\chi$ that both equal one on a neighborhood of the base point. Choose a smaller center neighborhood $U_0$ and a compact support neighborhood so that $|x-y|\ge d>0$ whenever $x\in U_0$ and $y\in\operatorname{supp}(\chi-\widetilde\chi)$. By continuity in the fixed-support topology [F3], in either distributional type the pairing is bounded by $C_0$ times the maximum of finitely many derivatives of its test object; a coordinate density factor, when present, has bounded derivatives on the compact chart support. Those derivatives of $(\chi-\widetilde\chi)e^{i\lambda(x-y)\cdot\omega-\lambda|x-y|^2/2}$ are bounded by $C_1(1+\lambda)^m e^{-\lambda d^2/2}$ uniformly for $x\in U_0$, directions near $\omega_0$, and $\lambda\ge1$. Since a polynomial times $e^{-\lambda d^2/2}$ is bounded by $C_2e^{-c\lambda}$ for any fixed $0<c<d^2/2$, replacing one fixed-chart cutoff by the other changes the FBI packet by an exponentially small term. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $\kappa$ be an analytic chart change. After shrinking to nested compact neighborhoods, $|\kappa(q)-\kappa(y)|\ge c|q-y|$ and $D\kappa(q)$ is invertible uniformly. The pulled-back packet has phase $ \phi(y,q,\omega)=\omega\cdot(\kappa(q)-\kappa(y))+\frac{i}{2}|\kappa(q)-\kappa(y)|^2. $ It is holomorphic after complexification, vanishes at $y=q$, and has derivative $-D\kappa(q)^T\omega$ there. First [F6] allows $\omega$ to range over a bounded open ball about its nonzero reference direction: its reference phase $(q-y)\cdot\omega+i|\omega||q-y|^2/2$ is exactly the unit-direction packet with parameter $\lambda|\omega|$, and [F6] equates this phase to the Gaussian of width $\lambda$ on that open ball. Apply the same reference criterion in the new chart before pulling its packets back. We may therefore reparameterize the open frequency ball by $p=D\kappa(q)^T\omega$; this is an analytic local diffeomorphism of open frequency parameters and is precisely the cotangent rule. The phase is now normalized and positive in the sense of [F6]. The Jacobian amplitude for scalar distributions is analytic and nonzero: the sign of the real determinant is constant on the smaller connected chart, so its absolute value has an analytic continuation. For distributional densities the amplitude is $1$. [F3, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Thus the exponential-decay criterion is independent of the fixed-chart cutoff. The finite-order sequence [F2] supplies the uniform localizers required when a distribution is restricted to a smaller chart; it avoids any use of compactly supported analytic bumps. For a distributional density $V$ in the fixed chart, define the scalar distribution $u_V$ by $\langle u_V,\varphi|dy|\rangle=\langle V,\varphi\rangle$. Continuity follows from [F3], and the vanishing-open sets of $u_V$ and $V$ agree because $|dy|$ is nowhere zero, so their supports agree. The packet pairings agree by definition. Hence [F4]–[F5] give the local Euclidean tempered and smooth-function realizations for either distributional type. This proves the cutoff and localization clauses without a choice axiom. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply [F6] to the standard and pulled-back packets on the smaller neighborhoods. It supplies actual transition representations in both directions, with polynomially bounded transition kernels and errors exponentially small in every fixed derivative; the finite distributional order from [F3] therefore preserves their exponential size after pairing. The known exponential estimate on the source parameter neighborhood transfers to the target one. Swapping the two families gives the converse. Step 1.1 removes all fixed cutoff choices, and step 2.1 covers both distributional conventions. This proves every invariance clause in the statement, with the exact cotangent transformation from step 1.2. [F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses and conventions of the Levine–Tristram form definition. At every root $\omega_0\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$ of $\Delta_K$, each one-sided limit of the nonroot signature as the parameter moves along the unit circle to $\omega_0$ exists and is an integer.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot, its Seifert matrix $V$, and an Alexander root $\omega_0\ne1$.

[A1] Full AC and the chosen surface/basis supply a finite real Seifert matrix. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $H_{e^{i\theta}}$ is a continuous Hermitian matrix family, and its singular parameters away from $1$ are exactly the zeros of a nonzero Alexander polynomial. [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]], [[lem-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-singular-set]], [[lem-square-seifert-presentation-and-alexander-normalization]]

[F2] Ordered Hermitian eigenvalues vary continuously, indeed Lipschitzly in operator norm. [[lem-complex-hermitian-eigenvalues-lipschitz]]

[F3] A continuous real function on an interval cannot take both positive and negative values without vanishing between them. [[thm-intermediate-value]]


## Proof

1.1 The entries of $H_{e^{i\theta}}$ are continuous functions of $\theta$. By [F2], each ordered eigenvalue $\lambda_j(\theta)$ is continuous. The determinant presentation in [F1] is a nonzero Laurent polynomial because its value at $t=1$ is $\pm1$; hence it has only finitely many roots on the unit circle. Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that each punctured one-sided arc $(\theta_0-\epsilon,\theta_0)$ and $(\theta_0,\theta_0+\epsilon)$ contains no other root. On each such arc, [F1] makes every eigenvalue nonzero. [A1, F1, F2, given, choose]

1.2 On either arc, a continuous real function $\lambda_j$ that never vanishes has constant sign: if it took both signs, [F3] would give a zero. Thus every positive/negative eigenvalue count is constant on each one-sided arc, and the signature there is a fixed integer. Each one-sided limit is that integer. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented $3$-sphere. With the normalized Conway polynomial $\nabla_K(z)=1+a_2(K)z^2+a_4(K)z^4+\cdots$ and the Seifert-form definition of $\operatorname{Arf}(K)$,
$$\operatorname{Arf}(K)=a_2(K)\pmod2.$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a smooth oriented knot $K$.

[A1] Full AC is the ambient hypothesis of the Seifert and Alexander conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The Seifert Arf invariant and normalized Conway coefficient use the conventions stated in their definitions. [[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form]], [[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization]]

[F2] The bridge theorem proves the claimed congruence and surface independence. [[thm-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-arf-bridge]]


## Proof

1.1 Apply [F2] to the knot $K$ with the definitions in [F1]. It gives exactly the displayed equality in $\mathbb F_2$; equality of two elements of $\mathbb F_2$ is the stated congruence. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 The bridge theorem already proves independence of the chosen surface and basis, so this corollary adds no new representative choice or normalization. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

For an analytic double fibration with incidence cotangent relation $C_Z\subset(T^*G\setminus0)\times(T^*X\setminus0)$, let
$$
\pi_L:C_Z\longrightarrow T^*G\setminus0,\qquad \pi_L(g,\eta;x,\xi)=(g,\eta).
$$
The double fibration satisfies the global Bolker condition if $\pi_L$ is an injective immersion. The Bolker condition holds at a specified point $c=(g,\eta;x,\xi)\in C_Z$ if the full fiber over its data covector is the singleton $\pi_L^{-1}(g,\eta)=\{c\}$ and $d\pi_L|_c$ is injective. Thus the pointwise condition has both a fiber-uniqueness clause, which excludes every other relation point over the same data covector even outside a chosen chart, and a local differential-rank clause.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An analytic double fibration and its incidence relation $C_Z$.

[F1] [[def-ip-analytic-double-fibration-transform]]: both incidence projections are analytic submersions and $C_Z$ is the relation of the transform.

[F2] [[def-ip-distributions-conormal-kernels-and-cotangent-relation]]: $C_Z$ consists of nonzero conormals with sign convention $(\eta,-\xi)$ and is independent of coordinates.


## Proof

**Given:** The incidence relation from [F2].

1.1 The relation is a smooth conic submanifold in local incidence coordinates: the conormal equations are smooth constant-rank linear equations in the covector variables, and the zero section is removed. Thus projection onto its first cotangent factor is a well-defined smooth map. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Global injectivity means that every data covector has at most one object covector paired with it; at a specified point $c$, the corresponding fiber condition is exactly $\pi_L^{-1}(\pi_L(c))=\{c\}$. Injectivity of the differential means that every tangent vector to $C_Z$ mapped to zero is itself zero. Both conditions are invariant under coordinate changes because [F2] makes $C_Z$ coordinate independent and cotangent coordinate changes are diffeomorphisms. This proves the two clauses in the definition. [F2] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

## Example

Let $U$ be the crossingless diagram of the oriented unknot, and choose any basepoint $p$ on its unique circle. For the normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex, $Kh^{0,1}(U)\cong\mathbb Z$, $Kh^{0,-1}(U)\cong\mathbb Z$, and all other unreduced groups vanish. For the reduced quotient convention that kills the based-circle $X$ label and lowers the quantum degree of the surviving label $1$ by one, $\widetilde{Kh}^{0,0}(U,p)\cong\mathbb Z$ and all other reduced groups vanish. Consequently the unreduced and reduced rank Euler polynomials are $q+q^{-1}$ and $1$, respectively.


## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The crossingless one-circle diagram $U$ and a basepoint $p$ on that circle.

[F1] The crossing set is empty, so there is one state and its state module is one copy of $\mathcal A$ in cohomological degree $0$; there are no edge maps ([[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]]).

[F2] The basis of $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ is $1,X$ with quantum degrees $1,-1$ ([[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).

[F3] The reduced quotient by the image of the basepoint action removes $X$ and shifts the surviving $1$ generator's quantum degree from $1$ to $0$ ([[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]]).


## Verification

1.1 By [F1], the zero-crossing cube has just $C^{0}(U)=\mathcal A$ and differential zero. Therefore its cohomology equals $\mathcal A$ in cohomological degree $0$. By [F2], the two basis elements give one free rank-one group in quantum degree $1$ and one in degree $-1$, with no other groups. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 In the based quotient, the image of multiplication by $X$ is $\mathbb Z\{X\}$, so the quotient of $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z\{1,X\}$ is freely generated by $[1]$. By [F3] its reduced quantum degree is $1-1=0$; the differential remains zero, so its only cohomology is $\mathbb Z$ in bidegree $(0,0)$. Summing the unreduced ranks with their quantum powers gives $q+q^{-1}$, and the reduced rank sum is $1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a finite tuple of finite signed Radon measures $\mu_i$.

[F1] For each coordinate, $|\mu_i|$ is a finite positive regular measure. ([[def-regular-complex-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]], [[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]])

[F2] Step 3.1 shows that $V$ is a regular Borel measure, with compact inner approximation on all Borel sets. ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]])


## Proof

**Given:** The open set $\Omega$ and finite signed Radon coordinate measures $\mu_i$.

1.1 For every Borel $A$ and every countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ of $A$, the Euclidean norm satisfies $|\mu(A_j)|\le\sum_{i=1}^m|\mu_i(A_j)|$. Summing over $j$ gives $V(A)\le\lambda(A)$ for $\lambda:=\sum_{i=1}^m|\mu_i|$, so $V$ is finite and $V(\Omega)<\infty$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $A=\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}E_k$ is a disjoint Borel union, then intersecting any partition of $A$ with each $E_k$ and using countable additivity of each coordinate shows $V(A)\le\sum_kV(E_k)$. Conversely, for fixed $N$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose for each of the finitely many $k\le N$ a partition of $E_k$ whose sum exceeds $V(E_k)-\varepsilon/N$. Their union, together with $A\setminus\bigcup_{k\le N}E_k$, is a partition of $A$, so $V(A)\ge\sum_{k\le N}V(E_k)-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and then $N\to\infty$ proves countable additivity. Thus $V$ is a finite positive Borel measure. [F1, step 1.1, given, choose]

2.2 For every $f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$ with $|f|\le1$, approximate $f$ uniformly by finite-valued Borel simple functions whose values have norm at most one. The partition definition bounds each simple integral by $V(\Omega)$, and finiteness of the coordinate measures lets the uniform errors tend to zero. Hence the displayed supremum is at most $V(\Omega)$. [step 1.1, given, choose]

3.1 Since $V\le\lambda$ and $\lambda=\sum_i|\mu_i|$ is a finite regular Borel measure by [F1], for every Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\lambda(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$, whence $V(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. There is also an open $G\supseteq A$ with $\lambda(G\setminus A)<\varepsilon$, whence $V(G\setminus A)<\varepsilon$. Thus $V$ is a regular Borel measure in the sense of [[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]], and in particular a Radon measure. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, given]

4.1 If $V(\Omega)=0$, the zero field proves the reverse inequality. Otherwise fix $0<\varepsilon<V(\Omega)/4$ and choose a countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ with sum greater than $V(\Omega)-\varepsilon$; truncate after $N\ge1$ so the tail is below $\varepsilon$. Omit indices with $\mu(A_j)=0$ or $V(A_j)\le\varepsilon/(4N)$; the sum of the omitted partition values is at most $\varepsilon/4$. For every retained index, compact inner regularity [F2] gives a nonempty compact $K_j\subset A_j$ with $V(A_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$. Since there are finitely many pairwise disjoint compact sets $K_j$ in the metric space $\Omega$, choose pairwise disjoint open neighborhoods $N_j$ with compact closures in $\Omega$. Outer regularity [F2] gives open $G_j\supset K_j$ with $V(G_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$. Put $U_j=G_j\cap N_j$. Then $K_j\subset U_j$, $V(U_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$, and the closures of the $U_j$ remain pairwise disjoint compact subsets of $\Omega$. Define $$\psi_j(x):=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega\setminus U_j)}{\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega\setminus U_j)+\operatorname{dist}(x,K_j)}.$$ This is continuous and compactly supported, equals one on $K_j$, and vanishes outside $U_j$. Set $e_j=\mu(A_j)/|\mu(A_j)|$ and $f=\sum_j e_j\psi_j$. The disjoint closures of the $U_j$ imply disjoint supports and $|f|\le1$. For bounded Borel vector fields, the partition definition and uniform simple-function approximation give $|\int g\cdot d\mu|\le\int|g|\,dV$. Thus replacing $e_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ by $e_j\psi_j$ loses at most $V(A_j\setminus K_j)+V(U_j\setminus K_j)$ for each retained $j$. Summing these errors, the omitted terms, and the tail gives $\int f\cdot d\mu>V(\Omega)-3\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the reverse bound. [F1, F2, step 3.1, choose, construct] ∎

## Statement

Fix even $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A$, the BHMV semisimplified category, and its quantum dimensions $d_j$ and twists $\theta_j$ for $0\le j\le r-2$. Put $\Omega_p=\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}d_jp_j$, $\Delta_+=\sum_jd_j^2\theta_j$, and $\Delta_-=\sum_jd_j^2\theta_j^{-1}$. The Statement asserts that both $\Delta_+$ and $\Delta_-$ are nonzero. For a finite integral framed link $L$ in the oriented three-sphere, color each surgery component by $\Omega_p$ and normalize the bracket evaluation by $\Delta_+^{b_+(L)}\Delta_-^{b_-(L)}$, where $b_\pm(L)$ are the positive and negative indices of the framing matrix. With the stated BHMV root and weighted anomaly convention, the resulting value is unchanged under framed isotopy, handle slides, and addition or deletion of a split $\pm1$-framed unknot.

## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The assertion that every generator-column deletion gives a defined Wada quotient for a based deficiency-one spine is false. Let $X$ be the standard unknot exterior, with its circle spine generated by a positive meridian $y$, and form a based simple expansion by adding a $1$-cell $x$ and a $2$-cell attached by the word $r=x$. This gives the based deficiency-one presentation $\langle x,y\mid x\rangle$. Use the trivial one-dimensional representation over $\mathbb Q$ and the full abelianization deck map $\psi(x)=1$, $\psi(y)=t$ into $H=\langle t\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$. For the $x$ column, the Fox minor is $0$ and the denominator is $0$, so that column's Wada quotient is undefined; for the $y$ column, the denominator is $t-1\ne0$ and the quotient is $1/(t-1)$. Thus the invalidity of one designated column does not imply that another column is inadmissible.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the standard solid-torus model of the unknot exterior; the based circle spine; the elementary expansion adding the pair $(x,r=x)$; the trivial representation; and the specified full abelianization map.

[A1] AC is inherited from the twisted-chain convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The Wada quotient for a selected generator column is defined only when its denominator $\det(\rho(x_j)\psi(x_j)-I)$ is nonzero; its numerator is the determinant of the Fox matrix with that block column deleted. [[def-knot-wada-quotient-for-deficiency-one-presentation]]

[F2] The based twisted differential for a generator $z$ is multiplication by $\rho(z)\psi(z)-1$, and acyclic based torsion is computed by the alternating determinant product. [[def-knot-twisted-chain-complex-and-reidemeister-torsion]]

[F3] The compact unknot exterior is a solid torus and retracts onto its core circle. [[def-knot-exterior]]

[F4] The positive meridian generates the first homology of a knot exterior. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]; [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]


## Counterexample



1.1 Under [A1], the circle spine of a solid torus has one $0$-cell and the single $1$-cell $y$. Attaching a $1$-cell $x$ at the vertex and a $2$-cell with attaching word $x$ is an elementary expansion: the new $1$-cell is a free face of the new $2$-cell, so collapsing this pair returns the original circle spine. Therefore $\langle x,y\mid x\rangle$ is a valid based deficiency-one spine of the same exterior. The relation kills $x$ in the fundamental group, so [F4] makes the full abelianization send $x$ to $1$ and the positive meridian $y$ to its generator $t$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 The Fox derivatives of $r=x$ are $\partial r/\partial x=1$ and $\partial r/\partial y=0$, so the row Fox matrix is $J=[1\quad0]$. By [F2], the $d_1$ blocks are $0$ for $x$ and $t-1$ for $y$, making the localized complex $0\to\mathbb Q(t)\xrightarrow{(1,0)}\mathbb Q(t)^2\xrightarrow{(0,t-1)^\mathsf T}\mathbb Q(t)\to0$ acyclic. Deleting the $x$ column leaves the zero $1\times1$ minor and gives denominator $0-1=0$, hence [F1] declares that quotient undefined. Deleting the $y$ column leaves minor $[1]$ and denominator $t-1$, so its quotient is $1/(t-1)$. This establishes the stated boundary case. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```


## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A nonempty finite regular oriented diagram $D$, a total order of its crossing set, and the operations displayed in the Definition.


## Proof

1.1 The quotient by the monic polynomial $X^2$ is the free abelian group with basis $1,X$. The displayed multiplication is the quotient-ring multiplication, so it is associative, commutative, and has unit $1$. On this basis, $\epsilon$ and $\Delta$ satisfy both counit identities; explicitly, $(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(1)=1$, $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta(1)=1$, and the same composites send $X$ to $X$. [given, algebra]

1.2 Cocommutativity follows by swapping tensor factors in the two displayed values of $\Delta$. For coassociativity, both $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(1)$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(1)$ equal $1\otimes X\otimes X+X\otimes1\otimes X+X\otimes X\otimes1$, and both composites send $X$ to $X\otimes X\otimes X$. Hence $(\mathcal A,m,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a commutative Frobenius algebra once the Frobenius compatibility is checked. [given, algebra]

2.1 On the ordered basis $1\otimes1,1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$ of $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$, each of $(m\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)$, $\Delta m$, and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes m)(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})$ has respective outputs $1\otimes X+X\otimes1$, $X\otimes X$, $X\otimes X$, and $0$. Thus the Frobenius identities hold. The degree shifts in the Definition give each edge map total quantum degree $0$; the quotient-ring construction and all checks are choice-free. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume full AC. Let $T$ be the standard right-handed trefoil, let $T^*$ be its image under a fixed orientation-reversing reflection of $S^3$, and let $-T^*$ denote reversal of that image's knot orientation. Then $g(T\#T)=2$ and $g(T\#(-T^*))=2$. The knot $T\#(-T^*)$ bounds a smooth ribbon disk in $B^4$, meaning a smooth properly embedded disk whose radial-height function has no interior local maxima; in particular it bounds a smooth properly embedded disk and is smoothly slice.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the standard right-handed trefoil, its reverse mirror, and the stated connected-sum operations.

[F1] The trefoil genus is exactly $1$. ([[lem-right-trefoil-has-genus-one]])

[F2] Genus is additive under connected sum. ([[thm-knot-genus-additive-under-connected-sum]])

[F3] Mirroring and reversing orientation preserve genus. ([[lem-knot-genus-invariant-under-mirror-and-reversal]])

[F4] The trefoil sum with its reverse mirror bounds a smooth ribbon disk. ([[lem-knot-reverse-mirror-connected-sum-is-ribbon]])

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[A2] Full AC implies AC$_\omega$. ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]])

[A3] The ribbon convention excludes interior radial maxima; index-zero minima and index-one saddles are allowed.


## Verification

**Given:** Full AC and the two connected sums in the statement.

1.1 By [F1], $g(T)=1$, and by [F3], $g(-T^*)=1$. Full AC implies the AC$_\omega$ hypothesis of [F2] by [A2], so additivity gives $g(T\#T)=1+1=2$ and $g(T\#(-T^*))=1+1=2$. [given, F1, F2, F3, A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $T\#(-T^*)$ bounds a smooth ribbon disk. A ribbon disk is in particular a smooth properly embedded disk, so the knot is smoothly slice. The explicit doubled-arc disk has no interior radial maxima, as required by the stated convention. [given, F4, A3] ∎

## Statement

Let $x$ be an invertible indeterminate and put $p=x-x^{-1}$. Every Laurent
polynomial $P(x)\in\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]$ has a unique expression
$$P(x)=a(p)+b(p)x$$
with $a,b\in\mathbb Z[p]$, where $\mathbb Z[p]$ is the ring of finite
integer-coefficient polynomials in the indeterminate $p$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The commutative polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Z[p]$, the monic polynomial $G(X)=X^2-pX-1\in R[X]$, and the Laurent polynomial ring $\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]$.

[F1] The polynomial ring $R[X]$ consists of finite-support coefficient sequences with coefficientwise addition and finite convolution multiplication ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

[F2] If $R$ is commutative, then $R[X]$ with these operations is a commutative ring ([[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]).

[F3] The ideal generated by $G$ is a two-sided ideal; the quotient ring consists of its additive cosets with multiplication induced from $R[X]$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]], [[def-quotient-ring]]).

[F4] Division by the monic degree-two polynomial $G$ gives each polynomial in $R[X]$ a unique remainder of degree less than two ([[thm-monic-polynomial-division]]).


## Proof

1.1 Let $Q=R[X]/(G)$. By [F1] and [F2], $R[X]$ is a commutative polynomial ring, and [F3] makes $(G)$ a two-sided ideal and $Q$ a quotient ring. Since $G$ is monic of degree two, [F4] gives every class in $Q$ a representative $a(p)+b(p)X$ of degree at most one in $X$. If two such representatives define the same class, their difference is a multiple of $G$ and has degree less than two; uniqueness in [F4] forces the difference to be zero. Thus this representative is unique. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 In $Q$, the relation $X^2-pX-1=0$ gives $X(X-p)=1$, so $X$ is invertible with inverse $X-p$. The homomorphism $Q\to\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]$ sending $p\mapsto x-x^{-1}$ and $X\mapsto x$ respects $G=0$. Conversely, sending $x\mapsto X$ defines a homomorphism $\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\to Q$ because $X^{-1}=X-p$. The composites fix the generators $p,X$ and $x$, respectively, so these homomorphisms are inverse. The unique representatives from step 1.1 therefore give the asserted unique Laurent decomposition. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with integer entries. Define $\operatorname{coker}(A)=\mathbb Z^n/A\mathbb Z^n$. Then $\operatorname{coker}(A)$ is finite if and only if $\det A\ne0$, and in that case its order is $|\det A|$. For the empty $0\times0$ matrix, take $\det A=1$ and $\operatorname{coker}(A)=0$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite square integer matrix $A$.


## Proof

1.1 If $n=0$, the codomain and image are both the zero group, so the cokernel is trivial and has order $1=|\det A|$. Now suppose $n>0$. Multiplication on the left or right by an integer matrix with determinant $\pm1$ preserves the isomorphism type of the cokernel and preserves the absolute determinant: left multiplication changes the basis of the target, and right multiplication changes the basis of the domain. [given, algebra]

2.1 Whenever the current remaining square submatrix is nonzero, among all matrices obtained from it by such row and column operations choose one whose least nonzero absolute entry is as small as possible; by swaps and a sign change, place that positive entry $d$ in position $(1,1)$. If any entry in its first row or column is not divisible by $d$, Euclidean division and a row or column subtraction produce a nonzero remainder strictly between $0$ and $d$, which contradicts the minimality of $d$. Clear the first row and column by subtracting multiples of the first column and row. If an entry $b$ in the remaining submatrix were not divisible by $d$, add its row to the first row, write $b=kd+r$ with $0<r<d$, and subtract $k$ times the first column from its column; swapping that column with the first would again give a smaller nonzero pivot. Hence $d$ divides the remaining submatrix. [given, step 1.1, choose, construct, algebra]

3.1 Apply the same finite pivot procedure to each remaining square submatrix. If a remaining submatrix is zero, stop and retain it unchanged as part of the zero block. Since every nonzero pivot removes one row and one column, induction gives a diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0,\ldots,0)$ with each $d_i>0$, obtained by unimodular row and column operations. Its cokernel is $\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/d_i\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z^{n-r}$. Thus it is finite exactly when $r=n$, equivalently when $\det A\ne0$; then its order is $\prod_i d_i=|\det A|$. The operations in step 1.1 preserve both conclusions for the original matrix. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ that bounds a smooth immersed disk in $S^3$ with only ribbon double arcs bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$ with boundary $K$. In particular, its smooth slice genus is zero.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** ACω, a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and a ribbon disk for $K$.

[F1] A ribbon disk is a smooth immersion of the oriented disk with embedded boundary $K$ and only finitely many ribbon double arcs, whose preimages are one proper arc and one interior arc. ([[def-ribbon-disk-and-ribbon-knot]])

[F2] Such an immersion has a smooth proper embedded resolution in $B^4$ fixed on its boundary. ([[lem-ribbon-singularity-local-resolution]])

[F3] The smooth slice genus is the minimum genus of a connected compact smooth oriented properly embedded surface in $B^4$ with boundary $K$; the disk has genus zero and all genera are nonnegative. ([[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]])

[A1] ACω is the sequence-choice axiom assumed in [F3]. ([[def-countable-choice]])


## Proof

1.1 Choose a ribbon immersion $f:D^2\to S^3$ for $K$ as in [F1]. Applying [F2] gives a smooth proper embedding $\widetilde f:D^2\to B^4$ that agrees with $f$ on $\partial D^2$; hence its boundary is exactly the oriented knot $K$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The image of $\widetilde f$ is a connected orientable disk, so its Euler characteristic is $1$ and its genus is $0$. By [F3], this disk is an admissible smooth spanning surface in the set defining $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$; since that set contains $0$ and consists of nonnegative integers, $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)=0$. Thus $K$ is smoothly slice. The argument from [F1] to [F2] itself is choice-free; ACω is present only for the library's slice-genus convention [F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume ACω. Let $T$ be the standard right-handed trefoil, represented by the closure of the standard two-strand braid with three positive half-twists, and let $T^\dagger$ be its reverse mirror. Choose the connected-sum balls on arcs colored $0$ in the Fox 3-colorings described below. The square knot $T\#T^\dagger$ is nontrivial, is ribbon, and bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** ACω, the standard right-handed trefoil $T$, its reverse mirror $T^\dagger$, and the connected-sum datum specified in the Example.

[F1] Under ACω, every smooth oriented knot $K$ has $K\#K^\dagger$ bounding a ribbon immersion in $S^3$, and separately bounding a smooth proper disk whose squared radial function is Morse with only index-$0$ and index-$1$ critical points. ([[lem-reverse-mirror-sum-has-a-ribbon-immersion]], [[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]])

[F6] Resolving a ribbon immersion gives a smooth proper disk with the same boundary. ([[lem-ribbon-singularity-local-resolution]])

[F2] The reverse mirror is reflection of the knot followed by reversal of its knot orientation, and the connected sum uses the fixed orientation-matching gluing convention. ([[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot]], [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[F3] A Fox 3-coloring assigns an element of $\mathbb F_3$ to each diagram arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing. ([[def-quandle-and-knot-coloring]], [[lem-dihedral-operation-is-a-quandle]])
