## Statement

Let $p\ge4$ be even, let $A$ be a primitive $2p$-th root of unity, and use the quantum integers and Temperley–Lieb loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$ specified above. Write $r=p/2$. The standard Jones–Wenzl recursion defines nonzero idempotents $p_n$ for $0\le n\le r-1$; their unnormalized closure traces are $[n+1]$. In particular, $p_{r-1}$ has trace zero and is negligible, while the next standard recursive formula for $p_r$ is undefined because its denominator is $[r]=0$. This statement concerns that recursion and does not assert that no differently constructed normalized idempotent can exist at rank $r$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An even integer $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A$, the BHMV loop value $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, and the standard recursive idempotents.

[F1] [[def-sl-two-root-of-unity-skein-parameter]]: $q=-A^2$, $q^2=A^4$ has order $r=p/2$, $[j]=(q^j-q^{-j})/(q-q^{-1})$, and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$.

[F2] [[def-temperley-lieb-jones-wenzl-recursion-over-unit-denominators]]: the recursive element $p_n$ is defined only when every denominator $[2],\ldots,[n]$ is a unit; the recursion for $p_{n+1}$ uses $[n+1]^{-1}$.

[F3] [[lem-temperley-lieb-jones-wenzl-partial-trace-and-uniqueness]]: if $[2],\ldots,[n]$ are units, then $p_n$ is a nonzero idempotent, $p_n\mathrm{TL}_np_n=\mathbb C p_n$, and its unnormalized closure trace is $[n+1]$.

[F4] [[lem-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-component-identities]]: $\operatorname{Tr}_n(xy)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(yx)$, including when $\delta=0$.

[F5] [[def-temperley-lieb-negligible-morphisms]]: an endomorphism $f:n\to n$ is negligible when $\operatorname{Tr}_n(g\circ f)=0$ for every $g:n\to n$.


## Proof

**Given:** The data and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Since $q^2$ has exact order $r$, for $1\le j<r$ one has $q^{2j}\ne1$. Also $q-q^{-1}\ne0$, because $q^2\ne1$. Thus $q^j-q^{-j}\ne0$ and $[j]\ne0$ for every $1\le j<r$. At $j=r$, $q^{2r}=1$, so $q^r=q^{-r}$ and $[r]=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $p\ge6$, one has $r\ge3$, so every denominator $[2],\ldots,[r-1]$ is nonzero and therefore invertible in $\mathbb C$. By [F2] and [F3], the recursion defines nonzero idempotents through $p_{r-1}$ and gives $\operatorname{Tr}_{r-1}(p_{r-1})=[r]=0$. For $p=4$, $r=2$ and $p_{r-1}=p_1=1_1$ is the initial projector; its closure is $\delta=[2]=0$, so the same conclusion holds without using a rank-two denominator. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, cases]

3.1 For any $g\in\mathrm{TL}_{r-1}$, [F3] gives $p_{r-1}gp_{r-1}=\lambda p_{r-1}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$. Cyclicity [F4] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(gp_{r-1})=\operatorname{Tr}(p_{r-1}gp_{r-1})=\lambda\operatorname{Tr}(p_{r-1})=0$. Thus $p_{r-1}$ is negligible by [F5]. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The recursive formula for $p_r$ requires the inverse of $[r]$, which does not exist because $[r]=0$. Therefore that formula has no value at this step; in particular, assigning a value by cancelling a zero denominator is not part of the recursion. This leaves open the separate existence question for normalized idempotents constructed by other methods. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, let $\Phi$ be holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of $\overline U$, and let $a\in C_c^\infty(U)$ have a holomorphic extension near $0$. Assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}a$, $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$, $d\Phi(0)=0$, and $d\Phi(x)\ne0$ at every $x\in\operatorname{supp}a\setminus\{0\}$. Let $H=-i\Phi''(0)$ be complex symmetric with positive-definite real part. Assume there are $r,c_0,d_0>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge c_0|x|^2 \quad(|x|\le r),\qquad \operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge d_0 \quad(x\in\operatorname{supp}a,\ |x|\ge r).
$$
Let $\chi_N$ be the finite-order cutoff sequence equal to one on a fixed neighborhood of $0$, with $0\le\chi_N\le1$, and supported where these phase hypotheses hold. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every $\lambda\ge1$, put $I_N(\lambda)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(x)}a(x)\chi_N(x)\,dx$. There are coefficients $c_j$ determined by the full Taylor series of the phase and amplitude at $0$ and constants $C,\delta>0$, independent of $N,\lambda$, such that
$$
I_N(\lambda)=e^{i\lambda\Phi_0}(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\lambda^{-j}\right)+E_N(\lambda),
$$
$$
|c_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,\qquad |e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)|\le C^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}+Ce^{-\delta\lambda}.
$$
The square-root branch is fixed by the preceding holomorphic Morse/Gaussian-contour lemma, and $c_0=a(0)$. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ for sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ makes the normalized remainder $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)=O(e^{-\delta_2\lambda})$ for some $\delta_2>0$. The expansion includes every coefficient through the stated truncation order; it is not only a leading-term estimate.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The phase, amplitude, cutoff sequence, stationary point, and positivity hypotheses in the statement.

[F1] [[lem-ip-holomorphic-morse-normalization-and-gaussian-contour]]: the phase is holomorphically reduced to a nondegenerate quadratic form, the Gaussian determinant branch is fixed, and admissible contours may be deformed when boundary terms vanish.

[F2] [[lem-ip-analytic-cutoff-sequence]]: $\chi_N$ equals one near $0$, is supported in $U$, and has finite-order derivative bounds.

[F3] [[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: analytic phase and amplitude germs extend holomorphically near $0$.

[F4] [[def-multivariable-power-series]]: convergent Taylor series converge absolutely on smaller polydiscs.

[F5] [[cor-cauchy-inequalities]]: a holomorphic function bounded on a polydisc has Taylor coefficients bounded by its supremum times inverse powers of the polyradius.

[F6] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: a $C^1$ map with invertible real derivative has a local real $C^1$ inverse.

[F7] [[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]]: the integral of a closed differential form over the boundary of a smooth chain is zero.


## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Choose $r>0$ so that $\chi_N=1$ on $B_{2r}(0)$ for every $N$, the phase and amplitude are holomorphic near $\overline B_{2r}(0)$, and the stated positivity holds. The positive-phase hypothesis and compactness of $\operatorname{supp}a\setminus B_r(0)$ give $\operatorname{Im}(\Phi-\Phi_0)\ge d>0$ there. Since $a$ is bounded and $\chi_N$ is bounded by one, the absolute value of that contribution after multiplication by $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}$ is at most $\|a\|_\infty |U|e^{-\lambda d}$, uniformly in $N$. Thus only the integral over the fixed local ball affects the power series; the complement contributes $O(e^{-d\lambda})$. [given, F2, choose]

2.1 Put $\phi=-i(\Phi-\Phi_0)$, so $\operatorname{Re}\phi=\operatorname{Im}(\Phi-\Phi_0)$ and $\phi''(0)=H$. Apply [F1] to obtain a holomorphic Morse coordinate $w=\Psi(x)$ with $\phi(x)=\tfrac12 w\cdot w$. The transformed real ball is a local contour $\Gamma$ through $0$. The transformed amplitude $ b(w)=a(\Psi^{-1}(w))\det D\Psi^{-1}(w) $ is holomorphic in a fixed polydisc and has coefficients bounded by $M R^{-|\alpha|}$ for some $M,R>0$ by [F3]–[F5]. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Differentiating the Morse identity in [F1] twice at $0$ gives $A^TA=H$, where $A=D\Psi(0)$. Taylor's formula gives $\operatorname{Re}(\phi(tv))=\tfrac12t^2v^T(\operatorname{Re}H)v+o(t^2)$; comparing with $\operatorname{Re}\phi(tv)\ge ct^2|v|^2$ and dividing by $t^2/2$ as $t\to0$ yields $v^T(\operatorname{Re}H)v\ge2c|v|^2$. For a real vector $v$, write $Av=u+iw$ with $u,w\in\mathbb R^n$. Then $|u|^2-|w|^2=\operatorname{Re}(v^THv)>0$ when $v\ne0$. In particular, the real projection on $A\mathbb R^n$ is injective, hence bijective by dimension, and $A\mathbb R^n=\{u+iKu:u\in\mathbb R^n\}$ for a real linear map $K$. For nonzero $u$, applying the strict inequality to $v=A^{-1}(u+iKu)$ gives $|Ku|<|u|$; compactness of the unit sphere gives $\|K\|<1$. The real inverse theorem [F6] makes the nonlinear contour $\Gamma$ a graph $u+i(Ku+r(u))$, with $r(u)=O(|u|^2)$. For sufficiently small $r_0$, the homotopy graphs $u+i(Ku+t r(u))$ remain in the holomorphic chart and satisfy $\operatorname{Re}(w\cdot w)\ge c_0|u|^2$ for $|u|\le r_0$, because the linear margin $|u|^2-|Ku|^2\ge(1-\|K\|^2)|u|^2$ dominates the $O(|u|^3)$ error. The homotopy $u+i tKu$, $0\le t\le1$, also has $\operatorname{Re}(w\cdot w)=|u|^2-t^2|Ku|^2\ge(1-\|K\|^2)|u|^2$. On the fixed outer boundary these bounds, together with boundedness of the transformed amplitude and Jacobian, make the integrals $O(e^{-c_1\lambda})$. [F7] and the contour statement in [F1] therefore deform $\Gamma$ to the real Gaussian contour, with only that exponential boundary term. [F1, F6, F7, step 2.1, given]

On a smaller ball $|w|\le r_0<R$, the Cauchy bound [F5] and a geometric-series estimate give $ \left|b(w)-\sum_{|\alpha|<2N}b_\alpha w^\alpha\right| \le C_2^{N+1}|w|^{2N}. $ Integrating this remainder against $e^{-\lambda|w|^2/2}$ and using $z=\sqrt{\lambda}\,w$ bounds it by $ C_3^{N+1}\lambda^{-N-n/2}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|z|^{2N}e^{-|z|^2/2}\,dz \le C_4^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}. $ For the last inequality, convexity gives $(\sum_{j=1}^n z_j^2)^N\le n^{N-1}\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|^{2N}$. Fubini factors each summand into one-dimensional Gaussian moments; integration by parts gives $M_N=(2N-1)M_{N-1}$ with $M_0=\sqrt{2\pi}$, since the polynomial times Gaussian boundary term tends to zero. Hence $M_N=(2N-1)!!\sqrt{2\pi}\le2^NN!\sqrt{2\pi}$, and the displayed integral is at most $(2n)^N(2\pi)^{n/2}N!$. Absorb this fixed-dimensional factor into $C_4^{N+1}$. The extension of the Taylor polynomial $P_{<2N}(w)=\sum_{|\alpha|<2N}b_\alpha w^\alpha$ from $|w|\le r_0$ to the full real Gaussian integral needs a separate estimate uniform in $N$. For $|w|\ge r_0$ and $k<2N$, $|w|^k\le r_0^{k-2N}|w|^{2N}$. Consequently $\int_{|w|\ge r_0}|P_{<2N}(w)|e^{-\lambda|w|^2/2}\,dw\le C_5^{N+1}\lambda^{-N-n/2}\int_{\mathbb R^n}|z|^{2N}e^{-|z|^2/2}\,dz\le C_6^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}$. The actual amplitude away from the local critical region and the contour boundary still have the exponential estimates from step 1.1 and [F1]; no extension of that amplitude outside its holomorphy neighborhood is used. Combining these estimates proves the stated normalized error for every $N$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Expand $b(w)=\sum_{\alpha}b_\alpha w^\alpha$ and group by total degree. Odd monomials integrate to zero over $\mathbb R^n$ because the Gaussian and domain are invariant under $w\mapsto-w$. Each monomial of degree $2j$ contributes a constant times $\lambda^{-n/2-j}$ by the change of variables $z=\sqrt{\lambda}\,w$. In one dimension, integration by parts gives $I_k=\int t^{2k}e^{-t^2/2}dt=(2k-1)I_{k-1}$ and $I_0=\sqrt{2\pi}$, hence $I_k=(2k-1)!!\sqrt{2\pi}$. Products give the $n$-dimensional moments. If $\alpha=2k$ and $|k|=j$, then $\prod_l(2k_l-1)!!\le(2j-1)!!\le2^j j!$; all monomials with an odd coordinate vanish. After scaling, every degree-$2j$ moment is therefore at most $C_0^{j+1}j!\lambda^{-j}$. The number of degree-$2j$ multi-indices is at most $C_n^{j+1}$ and $|b_\alpha|\le M R^{-2j}$, so the coefficient of $\lambda^{-j}$ is bounded by $C_1^{j+1}j!$. The Jacobian at zero contributes $(\det H)^{-1/2}$ on the chosen branch, and the degree-zero coefficient is $a(0)$. [F1, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ so that $N\ge\epsilon\lambda/2\ge1$, the factorial term is at most $ C^{N+1}\lambda^{-n/2}(N/\lambda)^N $ because $N!\le N^N$. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot admitting a finite regular diagram $D$ with $n$ positive crossings and no negative crossings, and let $k$ be the number of circles in its oriented resolution. Then Rasmussen’s invariant satisfies
$$
s(K)=n-k+1.
$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a positive diagram $D$ of the knot $K$.

[F1] The canonical orientation class is a basis vector in Lee homology, and its filtration level is $s_{\min}(K)$ ([[thm-lee-homology-of-a-knot-has-two-generators]], [[lem-lee-filtered-spectral-sequence-and-two-orientation-classes]]).

[F2] Rasmussen's convention is $s(K)=s_{\min}(K)+1$ ([[def-rasmussen-s-invariant]]).

[F3] In the normalized Lee complex, a state with $|v|$ one-resolutions and labels $1,X$ has quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg_q(a)$ ([[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex]]).

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is inherited through the diagram-independent definition of $s$ ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-rasmussen-s-invariant]]).

[A2] The crossing-sign convention has $n_-=0$ for a positive diagram, and its oriented smoothing at each crossing is the $0$-resolution ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]], [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]).


## Proof

**Given:** The positive diagram has $n_+=n$, $n_-=0$ and $k$ circles in its oriented resolution.

1.1 By [A2], every oriented smoothing is the $0$-resolution, so the canonical cycle lies in cohomological degree $0$. There is no chain group in degree $-1$, hence this cycle is not altered by adding a boundary. Expanding each of its $k$ circle labels $a=1+X$ or $b=X-1$ in the homogeneous basis, the unique term of least quantum degree is obtained by choosing $X$ on every circle; its coefficient is $1$ or $-1$. Its quantum degree is the state shift $n$ plus $k$ labels of degree $-1$, namely $n-k$. Therefore its induced filtration level is $s_{\min}(K)=n-k$. [A2, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 The formula [F2] for $s$ is diagram-independent under the AC$_\omega$ branch [A1]. Substitution of the value from step 1.1 gives $s(K)=n-k+1$. If $n=0$, the positive diagram is the crossingless unknot, whose oriented resolution has $k=1$, so the same calculation gives $s=0$. The state expansion itself is finite and choice-free. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume countable choice and fix a generic movie $M$ of a smooth oriented surface cobordism $\Sigma$ from an oriented link $L_0$ to an oriented link $L_1$. For each regular frame $D$, let $Kh(D)$ be the normalized integral Khovanov homology group. The empty frame has the one-term complex $\mathbb Z$ in both gradings zero, using the empty resolution and the zero-fold tensor product. Associate to a birth the unit map $\eta:\mathbb Z\to\mathcal A$, $\eta(1)=1$; associate to a death the counit $\epsilon:\mathcal A\to\mathbb Z$, $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$; and associate to a saddle the multiplication $m:\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$ when two resolution circles merge, or the comultiplication $\Delta:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ when one splits. Each local map is tensored with the identity on unaffected circles. Associate to planar isotopy the induced identification of the cube complexes. For Reidemeister moves, use the following fixed Bar-Natan constructions: the kink retractions $F_+=v-\Delta$, $G_+=e$, $F_-=u$, $G_-=w-m$; the two inverse-crossing strong retractions with degree-zero inclusion $(1,ut)^T$ and projection $(1,-se)$, with their specified reverse-order cube signs; and the third-move equivalences obtained by the explicit source- or target-cone retractions onto the common six-point residual complex. Here $u,e$ are circle birth/death, $v,w$ are punctured-torus birth/death, and the saddle letters denote the actual local bands in these constructions. Use their specified inverses for the reversed moves. Insert these formal surface matrices into the fixed planar outside of the diagram, then apply the integral Frobenius cobordism functor. Normalize a state $v$ to cochain degree $|v|-n_-$ and quantum shift $|v|+n_+-2n_-$. Fix the local coordinate identifications and orientation cases once, with the Koszul crossing-order correction $(-1)^{v(a)v(b)}$ when crossings $a,b$ are interchanged. These local maps are chosen once; composing them with an arbitrary automorphism of a complex is not an allowed change of representative. Compose the induced maps on homology in movie order and denote the result by $Kh(M):Kh(L_0)\to Kh(L_1)$, considered modulo multiplication by $-1$. This definition fixes a movie; independence from changing the movie is not included in the definition.

## Example

The original scalar model is $F(c)=c$ with exact datum $y\in\mathbb R$. Relax it by adding an unconstrained variable $z\in\mathbb R$ and using $\widetilde F(c,z)=c+z$, with penalty coordinate $P(c,z)=z$. The relaxed map satisfies the range-invariance factorization at $(0,0)$ with $K(a,b)=a+b$ and $r(c,z)=(c,z)$. For the exact datum, the unpenalized least-squares objective $J_0(c,z)=(c+z-y)^2$ has every pair with $c+z=y$ as a minimizer. For any fixed $\lambda>0$, adding $\lambda|P(c,z)|^2$ gives $J_\lambda(c,z)=(c+z-y)^2+\lambda z^2$, whose unique minimizer is $(y,0)$. This finite-dimensional example shows why an enlarged variable can require an explicit penalty; it asserts no general uniqueness result for other models.

## Statement

Let $A$ be indeterminate, $F=\mathbb Q(A)$, $q_K=A^2$, and $q_L=A^{-2}$. For every integer $N\ge1$, the concrete module, finite $R$ series, duality, pivotal comparison $G_N$, and twist $\lambda_N$ in the normalized colored Jones definition are admissible ribbon data. More precisely, take the $F$-linear category generated by all those modules under finite tensor products, chosen contragredient duals, finite direct sums, and images of module-idempotents, with all module maps as morphisms. Its braiding on weight vectors is the finite series
$$R_{X,Y}=D_{X,Y}\sum_{r\ge0}q_K^{r(r-1)/2}\frac{(q_K-q_K^{-1})^r}{[r]!}E_X^r\otimes F_Y^r,\qquad D_{X,Y}(x_h\otimes y_k)=A^{hk}x_h\otimes y_k.$$
The sum is finite on each pair. Its pivotal comparison on weight $h$ is $(-1)^h q_K^h$, and its twist on $V_N$ is $(-1)^{N-1}A^{N^2-1}I$. These give natural invertible braidings with both hexagons, both duality snakes, the balancing identity and dual compatibility of twist. In particular all colors $N$, rather than a fixed bounded range of colors, are covered.

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

Then the generator relations and coproduct in [F1] become exactly $KEK^{-1}=q_K^2E$, $KFK^{-1}=q_K^{-2}F$, $[E,F]=(K-K^{-1})/(q_K-q_K^{-1})$, $\Delta(E)=E\otimes K+1\otimes E$, $\Delta(F)=F\otimes1+K^{-1}\otimes F$. The antipodes also agree: $S(E)=-EK^{-1}$, $S(F)=-KF$. Thus this is a change of parameter and Cartan generator, not an assumption equating the two parameters. Every weight is an integer, and $E,F$ are nilpotent on every fixed generated object by its finite weight range. The finite $R$ series and all dual matrices are therefore rational matrices in $A$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix finitely many objects, module maps, and a single proposed ribbon identity involving them. Realize every image of an idempotent inside its ambient finite tensor sum. There are finitely many rational entries, denominators, weights and matrix sizes in this identity. Specialize $A=s_\ell=e^{\pi i/(2\ell)}$ for integers $\ell$ greater than every color, every weight-range width and every divided-power index which can act nontrivially. Every color specializes to $\Delta(N-1)$ in [F3]; ordinary powers divided by $[r]!$ specialize to its divided powers for all possibly nonzero indices, since those indices are below $\ell$. Larger divided powers are zero by weight range. It is consequently a full divided-power module map after specialization, not merely a small-quantum-group map. An idempotent specializes to an idempotent module map, whose image is a tilting summand. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The contragredient action and ordinary evaluation and coevaluation in the color definition are module maps by the antipode identities: the action on their composites uses $m(S\otimes1)\Delta=m(1\otimes S)\Delta=\eta\varepsilon$. The unsigned pivotal comparison is $j^+_X(x)(f)=f(Kx)$: $S^2=\operatorname{Ad}K$, and $K$ is group-like, so it is a natural monoidal module isomorphism to the double dual. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At each such specialization the finite generic series becomes exactly the one in [F2]: replacing ordinary powers by divided powers changes its coefficient to $q_K^{r(r-1)/2}(q_K-q_K^{-1})^r[r]!=q_K^{r(r+1)/2}(1-q_K^{-2})^r[r]!$. Each entry of its generic intertwining, naturality, or hexagon equation is a rational function vanishing at infinitely many distinct $s_\ell$. Its numerator polynomial has infinitely many roots and hence is zero. These identities therefore hold generically. Invertibility follows as well: the nilpotent series has constant term $1$, hence a finite geometric-series inverse on each pair, and $D$ is an invertible diagonal matrix. 4.1 Let $u$ be [F4]'s Drinfeld isomorphism, formed with the just-proved generic braiding and duality, and put $\theta^+=u^{-1}j^+$. Its tensor defect gives the balancing identity. ## Statement

Let $g\ge0$ and let $W$ be an integral $2g\times2g$ matrix satisfying
$$W-W^T=\bigoplus_{j=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
A finite construction produces a compact connected smooth oriented surface $F\subset S^3$ with one boundary component and an ordered basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ such that
$$\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)=W_{ij}.$$
Here $a_i^+$ is a sufficiently small push in the positive oriented normal direction to $F$. The construction uses a finite disk-and-band diagram, finitely many full twists and pairwise clasps, and finite local smoothing. It needs no choice axiom, abstract classification of Seifert forms, generic-projection theorem for arbitrary curves, or normal-neighborhood theorem for locally flat surfaces in four dimensions.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer $g$ and matrix $W$ with the displayed fixed skew part. Linking and surface orientation below use the usual orientation of $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$, with positive normal chosen so that positive normal followed by an oriented surface basis gives the ambient orientation.


## Proof

1.1 We first describe the finite linking calculation used in the construction. For disjoint oriented polygonal circles with a specified regular plane projection, the linking number is half the signed mixed-crossing sum. This can be proved with finite chains as follows. For the second curve $D$, extend each projected edge vertically downward from its actual height to a plane lying below both curves, and fill its resulting planar projected cycle by the finitely many oriented cone triangles from a plane point. The resulting finite two-chain has boundary $D$. Its intersections with the first curve $C$ occur exactly at the mixed crossings where $C$ is below $D$, with the usual oriented crossing signs. It therefore computes linking as the sum of that subset of signs. The full mixed sum is twice this sum: the difference between the sums where $C$ is below and above $D$ is the algebraic plane intersection of the two projected cycles, which is zero. To check the latter directly, fill one projected cycle by its finite planar cone chain and intersect the other with that chain; the signed endpoints of the resulting finite one-chain cancel. Independence of a finite spanning chain is equally finite: the difference of two such chains is a two-cycle in $\mathbb R^3$, bounded by its cone three-chain. Intersecting that three-chain with the closed curve gives a finite one-chain whose signed boundary sum is zero, so the two intersection numbers agree. Finite subdivisions and perturbations needed to avoid vertices or nontransverse affine intersections avoid only finitely many bad affine conditions; a rational point outside their union exists, for example by trying rational points in a fixed enumeration. Thus no transversality selection on an infinite family is involved. The same computation applies after small local smoothing or to parallel pushed curves, because these changes take place in disjoint boxes without introducing intersections between the two curves. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $g=0$, use an oriented disk. Otherwise start with an oriented disk and $2g$ labeled orientable rectangular bands. In the cyclic order of their attachment intervals on the disk, put the endpoints of each pair of bands $(2j-1,2j)$ in the alternating order $2j-1,2j,2j-1,2j$, and put the pairs in disjoint successive sectors. Attaching the first band of a pair splits the current boundary into two components; attaching the second joins those two, as direct traversal of the four alternating attachment intervals shows. Each pair therefore preserves one boundary component and raises genus by one. The finite relative cell calculation for the disk and bands has one degree-one generator per band and no relative degree-two cells: collapse the disk, and collapse each band across its width. The relative degree-one boundary is zero because both band ends lie in the connected disk. The pair sequence, with the disk contractible and the degree-zero inclusion an isomorphism, therefore identifies $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^{2g}$. The band cores completed by disk arcs map to its coordinate basis. Choose the disk arcs so that only paired arcs meet, once in their sector. The embedded bands can be routed through a finite regular ribbon diagram: give each band a private twist box and, for every unordered pair, give those two bands one private common box with two parallel strands. Connect these finitely many specified visits by polygonal plane arcs, avoiding the finite existing vertices and arranging transverse double crossings without triple crossings by finitely many rational perturbations. At every other diagram crossing assign one strand above the other, then lift it in a small crossing box. Distinct crossing boxes are disjoint; sufficiently narrow ribbons following these finitely many arcs, and the specified orientable attachments, give an embedded disk-band surface. Arbitrary incidental diagram crossings merely determine its initial matrix and cause no restriction. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Let $W_0$ be the positive-push matrix of this initial surface, computed by step 1.1. Its skew part has zero entries for core pairs whose disk arcs are disjoint. Indeed the annulus sweeping a core from its negative to its positive push misses the other core in that case. In the explicit normal ribbons, sliding both members of the pair $(a_i^-,a_j)$ a small equal distance in the positive normal direction identifies its linking with that of $(a_i,a_j^+)$: their normal heights stay distinct throughout, including over a disk crossing. Linking is symmetric by step 1.1, so the signed-intersection calculation gives equality of the two ordered entries. For a paired pair the sweep meets the other core once in the disk, with sign $+1$ or $-1$, so the difference of its two ordered entries is that sign. In local disk coordinates the sweep is the product of the core arc with a normal interval; its single transverse intersection has multiplicity one. Orient the second core of each pair so that this difference is $+1$. Thus $W_0-W_0^T$ is exactly the displayed standard skew matrix. This calculation is entirely within the given disk and finite ribbon chart; it does not assume a surface-classification or duality theorem. Consequently $W-W_0$ is symmetric. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In the private box of band $i$, insert one full ribbon twist with sign chosen so that the two mixed crossings between its core and its positive parallel have signed sum $+2$. Step 1.1 says this increases $(W_0)_{ii}$ by one. The opposite twist decreases it by one. Every other core and its push miss that box, so its pairings with this modification are unchanged, as are all other matrix entries. Insert the finite integer number of twists required for each $i$ to make the diagonal equal that of $W$. Full twists preserve orientability and the attachment intervals, hence the abstract disk-band surface and its one boundary component. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 In the private common box of bands $i<j$, replace the two parallel ribbon strands by the two-strand full braid whose two mixed crossings have sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. Give each ribbon its diagram framing, with no individual full twist. The two crossings between the positive parallel of the first core and the second core have signed sum $2\varepsilon$, so step 1.1 changes entry $(i,j)$ by $\varepsilon$. The same two crossings between the positive parallel of the second and the first give the same change in entry $(j,i)$. Each ribbon has no self crossing or extra rotation of its framing in this box, so its diagonal entry is unchanged. All other cores and parallels miss the box. Thus this modification changes exactly those two symmetric entries. Since the remaining difference from $W$ is symmetric with zero diagonal by steps 3.1–4.1, insert the prescribed finite number of positive or negative full braids in each pair box. None affects another pair box or previously corrected entries. The resulting surface has matrix exactly $W$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 All polygonal bends, band attachments and diagram height changes in this description lie in finitely many disjoint small coordinate boxes. Replace each polygonal bend by a smooth arc in its plane, agreeing with its incident straight pieces outside the box; a fixed smooth cutoff flat at the endpoints supplies this replacement. Along a band use the same interpolation for its two edges and framing. At a disk attachment the construction is the product of its attachment interval with a rounded planar corner, so it too has an explicit local smooth replacement. Choose the smoothing boxes and ribbon widths smaller than the minimum of the finitely many positive separations between nonincident pieces. The replacements remain embedded, retain the band parametrizations and preserve every chosen crossing sign and push-off separation. They therefore preserve the exact linking computations in steps 3.1–5.1. The resulting surface is smooth and oriented with one smooth boundary component, which is a knot in $S^3$. The band collapse still provides the displayed basis, and its positive normal is the actual oriented smooth normal. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Every list in the construction has length bounded in terms of the finite matrix entries: the bands, visits, vertices, crossings, twist counts and pair-clasp counts are finite. Rational perturbations exclude finitely many affine conditions at each of finitely many stages, and local smoothing uses an explicit cutoff and a finite minimum. No arbitrary sequence of embeddings, bases, surfaces, generic projections or normal fibers is selected. The final surface and ordered basis realize every entry of the supplied $W$ with the positive push convention in the Statement. This proves the claimed finite, choice-free realization. [given, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^1$, and let $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $0<m\le\gamma\le M<\infty$ almost everywhere. Let $\mathcal D(\Omega)=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ be the complex trace quotient and write $\dot{\mathcal D}=\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1$. Let $\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ denote the continuous conjugate-linear dual of $\dot{\mathcal D}$. For each $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ there is a unique weak solution class $[u]\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)/\mathbb C\mathbf1$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}\,dx=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The resulting solution operator $\mathscr R_\gamma:\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}\to\dot{\mathcal D}$ is bounded. Its unique representative whose boundary trace has surface mean zero solves the same weak equation. In particular, for $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$ with $\int_{\partial\Omega}f\,dS=0$, the functional $F_f([g])=\int_{\partial\Omega}f\overline g\,dS$ is admissible and defines the mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map on mean-zero $L^2$ fluxes.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, $\Omega$, $\gamma$, and $F\in\dot{\mathcal D}^{*}$ as in the statement.

[F1] The hypotheses stated above give a real coefficient with $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere; these bounds make the weak form bounded and coercive. No narrower conductivity class is used for this estimate.

[F2] On a bounded connected extension domain, subtracting the volume mean gives $\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2}\le C\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. ([[thm-poincare-wirtinger-on-bounded-connected-extension-domains]])

[F3] The trace is bounded from $H^1(\Omega)$ to $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ and the trace quotient norm is equivalent to the boundary norm; constants correspond under the quotient identification. ([[lem-ip-calderon-boundary-trace-quotient-identification]])

[F4] A bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space and a bounded conjugate-linear functional have a unique weak solution with norm at most the functional norm divided by the coercivity constant. ([[thm-lax-milgram]])

[F5] Every bounded $C^1$ domain is a Sobolev extension domain, and its compact boundary has finite positive surface measure. ([[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is used at the Poincaré and trace interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[A2] Countable Choice is used at the Lax–Milgram interface. ([[def-countable-choice]])


## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Let $V=\{v\in H^1(\Omega):\int_\Omega v\,dx=0\}$, a closed Hilbert subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$. By [F2], $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C_0\|\nabla v\|_2$ on $V$, where $C_0=(1+C^2)^{1/2}$. By [F1], the form $a_\gamma(u,v)=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}$ is bounded on $V$ and $a_\gamma(v,v)\ge m\|\nabla v\|_2^2\ge mC_0^{-2}\|v\|_{H^1}^2$. Thus it is bounded and coercive on $V$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Define $\ell_F(v)=F([\operatorname{Tr}v])$ for $v\in V$. By [F3], the quotient trace norm of $[\operatorname{Tr}v]$ is at most $C_1\|v\|_{H^1}$, so $|\ell_F(v)|\le C_1\|F\|\|v\|_{H^1}$; hence $\ell_F$ is bounded on $V$. Applying [F4] to step 1.1 gives a unique $u_0\in V$ with $a_\gamma(u_0,v)=\ell_F(v)$ for every $v\in V$. [A2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given]

3.1 For arbitrary $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ write $v=v_0+c$ with $v_0=v-v_\Omega\in V$ and $c=v_\Omega$. Gradients are unchanged by adding $c$, and $F$ acts on the trace quotient by constants, so the equation for $u_0$ on $V$ implies it for every $v\in H^1$. If $u_1$ is another solution class, subtract its volume mean to obtain $w\in V$ with $a_\gamma(w,v)=0$ for all $v\in V$; setting $v=w$ and using coercivity from step 1.1 gives $w=0$. Thus the solution is unique modulo constants. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The estimate in [F4] and step 2.1 give $\|u_0\|_{H^1}\le C_0^2C_1m^{-1}\|F\|$. The bounded trace map [F3] therefore makes the solution class in $\dot{\mathcal D}$ a bounded linear function of $F$. By [F5], the compact smooth boundary has finite positive surface measure. Subtracting the surface mean of $\operatorname{Tr}u_0$ selects one representative with boundary mean zero; this constant shift preserves the weak equation and is the only such shift. For mean-zero $f\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$, Cauchy–Schwarz and the trace bound show $F_f$ is continuous, and its zero mean makes it independent of the representative modulo constants. This proves the final assertion. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $R$ be an associative unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors, embedded as a unital subring in a division ring $K$, put $N=K/R$ as a right $R$-module, and let $C_*$ be a right $R$-module chain complex concentrated in nonnegative degrees. Supply an identification $C_0=R$. If the right ideal $\operatorname{im}(d_1)$ is principal, restriction to cycles gives an isomorphism
$$H^1(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,N))\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_1(C_*),N).$$
Neither a principal ideal domain hypothesis on $R$ nor a choice principle is required.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The specified complex and division-ring embedding. Put $Z_1=\ker d_1$, $B_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$, and $B_0=\operatorname{im}d_1=aR$ for one generator $a$.


## Proof

1.1 A degree-one cocycle is a map $f:C_1\to N$ vanishing on $B_1$, and a coboundary is a map of the form $g d_1$. Restriction of a cocycle to $Z_1$ descends to $Z_1/B_1=H_1$; coboundaries restrict to zero. Thus restriction defines the stated map. If $a=0$, then $Z_1=C_1$ and all coboundaries vanish, so the map is already an isomorphism. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $a\ne0$. Choose $z\in C_1$ with $d_1z=a$. Because $R$ has no zero divisors, $aR\to C_1$, $ar\mapsto zr$, is well-defined and a section of $d_1$. Hence $C_1=Z_1\oplus zR$. Any map $H_1\to N$ pulls back to a map on $Z_1$ vanishing on $B_1$ and extends by zero on $zR$ to a degree-one cocycle. This proves surjectivity. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 If a degree-one cocycle restricts to zero on $Z_1$, it factors as $v d_1$ for a right-linear map $v:aR\to N$. Let $v(a)=q+R$ with $q\in K$ and put $u=q a^{-1}+R$. Then $ua=v(a)$ in $N$. The right-linear map $g:R\to N$, $g(r)=ur$, extends $v$, since $g(ar)=v(a)r=v(ar)$. The cocycle is consequently the coboundary $g d_1$. This proves injectivity and the result. All selections comprise one ideal generator, one lift and one fraction representative. [step 1.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $D_+$ and $D_-$ be finite regular oriented diagrams that agree outside one crossing neighborhood and differ inside it by switching which branch is over. Let $V_+$ and $V_-$ be the Seifert matrices obtained from their oriented disk-and-band surfaces. There are corresponding integral bases in which either $V_+=V_-$ or $V_+-V_-=\pm vv^T$ for some integral column vector $v$. In particular, $\operatorname{rank}(V_+-V_-)\le1$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, two oriented knot diagrams differing at one crossing, and their Seifert disk-and-band constructions.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom used by the knot Seifert-pairing convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The Seifert construction smooths each crossing by the orientation-compatible pairing and adds one half-twisted band per original crossing. [[alg-seifert-surface-from-diagram]]

[F2] For a knot diagram, the resulting disk-and-band data can be realized as a connected compact oriented embedded spanning surface. [[lem-seifert-bands-embedded-orientable-boundary-correct]]

[F3] In an ordered integral basis, the Seifert matrix has entries $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, where $a_i^+$ is the positive normal push-off. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]


## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, the two diagrams and their prescribed crossing change.


1.1 Switching over and under does not change the oriented smoothing at the distinguished crossing. Thus [F1] gives the same Seifert circles, disk records, and bands at every other crossing. Only the distinguished band changes: its two possible half-twist directions differ by one full twist. By [F2], both disk-and-band constructions give connected embedded oriented spanning surfaces, and each surface retracts to the finite graph with one vertex per disk and one edge per band. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Let $e$ be the distinguished edge of that graph. If $e$ is a bridge, every graph cycle avoids $e$, so choose the corresponding homology basis outside the changed band; all Seifert-pairing entries are then identical. If $e$ is not a bridge, the graph with $e$ removed is connected. Choose a spanning tree of that graph; its fundamental cycles, together with the fundamental cycle using $e$, form an integral homology basis. All basis curves except the last can be represented disjoint from the distinguished band. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The crossing change is supported in a ball disjoint from every other band and disk. Hence the basis curves avoiding $e$, and their positive push-offs, have identical linking numbers before and after the change. Their pairings with the last basis curve also remain the same, because the other curve and its push-off miss that ball. The last curve passes once through the distinguished band; changing the band by a full twist adds one signed meridional turn to its positive push-off about its core, so its self-linking in [F3] changes by exactly $+1$ or $-1$. Thus only one diagonal entry changes. The matrix difference is zero in the bridge case and is $\pm vv^T$ in the non-bridge case, so its rank is at most one. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every compact Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, admits an embedding $e:M\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$, an open neighborhood $U$ of $e(M)$ and a retraction $r:U\to e(M)$. Moreover there is a finite Euclidean cubical complex $L$ with $e(M)\subseteq L\subseteq U$, so that $r|_L$ makes $M$ an actual retract of a finite CW complex. No choice principle, smooth or PL structure, triangulation of $M$, or general locally contractible-space retraction theorem is assumed.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact Hausdorff manifold.

[F1] A finite union of closed Euclidean cubes together with all their faces is a finite CW complex: the open faces are its cells, their characteristic maps are the closed cubes, and the finite closed-cover topology gives the weak topology. [[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]


## Proof

1.1 Choose finitely many chart domains $V_i$ whose smaller concentric coordinate balls cover $M$, using compactness. For boundary charts use the relatively open unit half-ball $B^n_+=\{x:|x|<1,\ x_n\ge0\}$; for interior charts use the unit ball. Denote the chart by $\varphi_i$ and arrange that the radius-$1/3$ smaller balls cover. Choose the explicit radial bump $\rho_i$ equal to $1$ at radius at most $1/3$ and zero at radius at least $2/3$, interpolating linearly in between, and extend it by zero outside $V_i$. Its support is compact in $V_i$. Define $$e(x)=\bigl(\rho_i(x),\,\rho_i(x)\varphi_i(x)\bigr)_{i=1}^s\in\mathbb R^{s(n+1)},$$ with the vector entry zero outside $V_i$. Boundedness of the chart coordinates makes these extensions continuous. If $e(x)=e(y)$, choose an index with $\rho_i(x)>0$. The equal scalar and vector entries recover $\varphi_i(x)=\varphi_i(y)$ and hence $x=y$. A continuous injection of a compact space into the Hausdorff Euclidean space is an embedding. From now on identify $M$ with its image. All choices here form one finite list. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Write an ambient point in the $i$th block as $(t_i,z_i)$. On the open ambient set $O_i=\{t_i>0,\ |z_i/t_i|<1\}$ define $$q_i(t,z)=e\bigl(\varphi_i^{-1}(p_i(z_i/t_i))\bigr),$$ where $p_i$ is the identity for an interior chart and $p_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},\max(0,x_n))$ for a boundary chart. The latter decreases norm and retracts the unit ball onto its relative half-ball. Thus $q_i:O_i\to e(V_i)$ is continuous and $q_i(x)=x$ for every $x\in M\cap O_i$. The compact sets $K_i=e(\{\rho_i\ge1/2\})$ cover $M$ and lie in $O_i$. Choose a positive $\delta_i$ with the closed $\delta_i$ neighborhood of $K_i$ contained in $O_i$; such a number exists by compactness and the open cover by small ambient balls. Put $\beta_i(z)=\max(0,\delta_i-\operatorname{dist}(z,K_i))$. Its closed support $S_i$ is compact and contained in $O_i$, and $\sum_i\beta_i>0$ on $M$. Empty $K_i$ may simply be discarded. No nearest-point selection is made: distance means the infimum of the set of distances. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 We construct successive continuous maps $r_j:D_j\to M$, where $D_j=U_j\cap\{\beta_1+\cdots+\beta_j>0\}$ and $U_j$ is an open neighborhood of $M$. In addition require the following controlled property even at points outside $D_j$: for every $x\in M$ and every neighborhood $V$ of $x$ in $M$, there is an ambient neighborhood $A$ of $x$ with $r_j(A\cap D_j)\subseteq V$. Begin with $U_0=\mathbb R^N$ and the empty map. Suppose the property holds for $r_{j-1}$. There is an open neighborhood $U_j\subseteq U_{j-1}$ of $M$ such that $$r_{j-1}(U_j\cap S_j\cap D_{j-1})\subseteq e(V_j).$$ Indeed, at $x\in M\cap S_j$ the chart $e(V_j)$ is a neighborhood of $x$, so the controlled property supplies the required ambient neighborhood. At $x\in M\setminus S_j$ an ambient neighborhood avoids the closed set $S_j$. Take the union of all open subsets of $U_{j-1}$ satisfying the displayed containment. This union contains $M$ and itself satisfies that containment. Taking the union of all admissible neighborhoods avoids selecting one for every point. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 On $D_j$ put $a=\beta_1+\cdots+\beta_{j-1}$ and $b=\beta_j$. Where $b=0$ use $r_j=r_{j-1}$; where $a=0$ use $r_j=q_j$. If $a,b>0$, both $r_{j-1}$ and $q_j$ lie in $e(V_j)$ by step 3.1, so define $$r_j(z)=e\varphi_j^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{a+b}\,\varphi_j e^{-1}r_{j-1}(z)+\frac{b}{a+b}\,\varphi_j e^{-1}q_j(z)\right).$$ The chart image is a bounded convex ball or half-ball, so the convex combination remains in it. This map is continuous where both weights are positive. At a point where $a=0,b>0$, the first coordinate vector is uniformly bounded in the unit ball and its coefficient tends to zero; the expression therefore tends to the $q_j$ value regardless of whether $r_{j-1}$ has a limit there. At $b=0,a>0$, either a neighborhood avoids $S_j$, or the point is in $S_j$ and the containment from step 3.1 puts $r_{j-1}$ in $e(V_j)$ there. Continuity of $r_{j-1},q_j$ and the bounded coordinate formula then gives the stated $r_{j-1}$ value. This proves continuity on all of $D_j$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 The controlled property also persists. At $x\notin S_j$ the map locally is the old map. At $x\in M\cap S_j$, choose a sufficiently small convex coordinate neighborhood of $\varphi_j(x)$ in the ball or half-ball whose inverse lies in a prescribed neighborhood of $x$. The old controlled property puts all defined old values in this neighborhood for ambient points sufficiently near $x$; continuity of $q_j$ and $q_j(x)=x$ puts the new values there too. Every convex blend, as well as each endpoint case, remains in that neighborhood. This proves the property at $x$. Whenever $r_j$ is defined at a point of $M$, all contributing maps have value that point, so $r_j|_{M\cap D_j}$ is the identity. Finite induction ends with $M\subset D_s$, since the sum of the weights is positive there. The continuous map $r_s:D_s\to M$ is therefore the required neighborhood retraction. The induction and neighborhood unions require no infinite selection. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 By compactness, some positive $\varepsilon$ has the closed $\varepsilon$ neighborhood of $M$ contained in the open set $D_s$: finitely many ambient balls with doubled balls inside $D_s$ give a uniform positive minimum radius. There are only finitely many grid cubes meeting the bounded compact set $M$, and their union $L$ contains $M$ and lies in $D_s$, because each such cube has diameter less than $\varepsilon$. A compact zero-manifold is finite, and the same disjoint-neighborhood construction, or a finite set of points as $L$, handles that case without dividing by $\sqrt0$. For positive dimension the construction above applies to interior and boundary charts alike. Every noncanonical datum chosen in the proof belongs to a finite chart or parameter list. Thus the asserted embedding, retraction and finite domination hold without a choice axiom. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $M=\partial\Omega$ be the compact smooth boundary in the boundary spectral setting, let $P_0$ be projection onto $L^2_0(M)$, and let $T:L^2_0(M)\to L^2_0(M)$ be Hilbert–Schmidt. Extend $T$ to $\widetilde T:L^2(M)\to L^2(M)$ by $\widetilde T=\iota_0TP_0$, where $\iota_0$ is inclusion. Then there is a unique $\kappa_T\in L^2(M\times M)$ such that
$$\widetilde T f(x)=\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)f(y)\,dS_y\quad\text{for almost every }x\text{ and every }f\in L^2(M),$$
and
$$\|\kappa_T\|_{L^2(M\times M)}=\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.$$
The kernel has zero mean in each variable: $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_y=0$ for almost every $x$, and $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_x=0$ for almost every $y$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, $M$, $P_0$, and the Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T$ in the statement.

[F1] The compact boundary $L^2(M)$ is separable and has a countable orthonormal basis; $L^2_0(M)$ is the orthogonal complement of the normalized constant. ([[lem-ip-boundary-spectral-counting-and-sobolev-scale]])

[F2] For an $L^2$ kernel on finite-measure spaces, the associated integral operator is Hilbert–Schmidt and its Hilbert–Schmidt norm equals the kernel's $L^2$ norm. ([[thm-l-two-kernels-give-hilbert-schmidt-operators]])

[F3] Fubini's theorem holds on the finite product surface measure. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is used to choose an orthonormal basis in the mean-zero Hilbert space. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[A2] Countable Choice is used for the countable eigenbasis and product-section interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])


## Proof

**Given:** The data in the statement.

1.1 Let $c_0=|M|^{-1/2}\mathbf1$ and choose a countable orthonormal basis $(c_j)_{j\ge1}$ of $L^2_0(M)$, using [A1] and separability [F1]. Extend $T$ by $\widetilde T c_0=0$ and $\widetilde T c_j=Tc_j$. The Hilbert–Schmidt condition means $\sum_{j\ge1}\|Tc_j\|_2^2<\infty$. Choose measurable representatives and define $\kappa_N(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}(Tc_j)(x)\overline{c_j(y)}$. For $i\ne j$, the summands are orthogonal in $L^2(M\times M)$ because their $y$-factors are orthogonal; Fubini [F3] gives $\|\kappa_N-\kappa_{N'}\|_2^2=\sum_{j=N'+1}^{N}\|Tc_j\|_2^2$ for $N>N'$. Thus $(\kappa_N)$ is Cauchy and converges to $\kappa_T\in L^2(M\times M)$ with $\|\kappa_T\|_2^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\|Tc_j\|_2^2=\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$. [A1, F1, F3, given, construct]

2.1 For a finite linear combination $f=\sum_{j=0}^{m}a_jc_j$, orthonormality and the definition of $\kappa_N$ give $\int_M\kappa_N(x,y)f(y)\,dS_y=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(N,m)}a_jTc_j(x)$. Passing to the limit in $N$ gives $\widetilde T f$ in $L^2(M)$. By [F2], the integral operator $K_{\kappa_T}$ is bounded on $L^2(M)$ with norm at most $\|\kappa_T\|_2$; finite linear combinations of the basis are dense, so continuity of $K_{\kappa_T}$ and $\widetilde T$ extends the equality to every $f\in L^2(M)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Since $\widetilde T c_0=0$, step 2.1 with $f=c_0$ yields $\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_y=0$ for almost every $x$. Since the range of $\widetilde T$ lies in $L^2_0(M)$, for every $f\in L^2(M)$ Fubini gives $0=\int_M\widetilde T f(x)\,dS_x=\int_M f(y)(\int_M\kappa_T(x,y)\,dS_x)\,dS_y$. The inner section is in $L^2(M)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and [F3]; its pairing with every $f$ vanishes, so it is zero almost everywhere. This proves the two zero-mean properties. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.2 If $\kappa'$ is another $L^2$ kernel for $\widetilde T$, let $q=\kappa_T-\kappa'$. For every pair of basis vectors $c_i,c_j$, the coefficient $\int_{M\times M}q(x,y)c_j(y)\overline{c_i(x)}\,dS_xdS_y$ is zero because both kernels represent the same operator. For each fixed $j$, the section coefficient $g_j(x):=\int_Mq(x,y)c_j(y)\,dS_y$ belongs to $L^2(M)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and Fubini, and its pairing with every $c_i$ is zero by the preceding product coefficient identity. Completeness of $(c_i)$ gives $g_j=0$ almost everywhere. Countable Choice supplies one conull set on which all these section coefficients vanish. For each $x$ in that set, $q(x,\cdot)$ is orthogonal to every member of the conjugate basis $(\overline{c_j})_{j\ge0}$, since $\langle q(x,\cdot),\overline{c_j}\rangle=\int_M q(x,y)c_j(y)\,dS_y=0$. The conjugates of an orthonormal basis form an orthonormal basis, so $q(x,\cdot)=0$ there. Hence $q=0$ in $L^2(M\times M)$, proving uniqueness. [A2, F1, F3, step 2.1, given]

4.1 The kernel is unique, has the prescribed zero-mean convention, and has the exact norm in step 1.1. This establishes the claimed kernel representation without relying on the reverse implication of [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $P\cup\eta\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented two-component link with unknotted axis and $\operatorname{lk}(P,\eta)=0$. Supply the disjoint closed product tubes, positive meridians and preferred zero-linking longitudes. For a smooth oriented companion knot $K$, form the untwisted infection $P(K)$ and the standard infection cobordism $E$ with oriented boundary $M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K)))$, where $M$ denotes the actual preferred zero-longitude surgery.

Let $k$ be any commutative field, $\Lambda=k[t,t^{-1}]$ with involution $\bar t=t^{-1}$, and $F=k(t)$. Use the coefficient system on $E$ sending the positive meridian of $P$ to $t$, and its restrictions to the boundary, with the standard based Hermitian form. On $M(P)$ and $M(P(K))$ these are their positive classical infinite-cyclic systems. The two inclusions give isomorphisms
$$H_1(M(P);\Lambda)\xrightarrow{i_P}H_1(E;\Lambda)\xleftarrow{i_{P(K)}}H_1(M(P(K));\Lambda).$$
Consequently $T=i_{P(K)}^{-1}i_P$ is an isometry of their classical Blanchfield pairings:
$$B_{P(K)}(Tx,Ty)=B_P(x,y).$$
With base paths through the common pattern exterior fixed as part of the peripheral data, $T[\eta]=[\mu_K]$, where the companion meridian on the infected side is oriented by the prescribed longitude-to-meridian identification. Thus a nonzero axis self-pairing remains nonzero on this companion-meridian class. For another base path the corresponding equality is conjugated by the induced power of $t$, which preserves its self-pairing. No choice axiom or finite CW model for the surgery manifolds is assumed.

**Given:** The finite smooth infection data, zero winding number, field and based coefficient systems in the Statement.

[F1] The actual collared standard infection cobordism has ordinary $H_1(E;k)=k$, with meridians of $P,K,P(K)$ mapping to $1,0,1$ in the winding-zero case. Its incoming components generate $H_2(E;k)$, and every knot zero surgery has first Betti number one over $k$. Its product construction retracts onto $M(P)\cup_{N(\eta)=V_K}M(K)$, where $V_K$ is the filling solid torus. [[lem-standard-infection-cobordisms-have-boundary-generated-second-homology]]

[F2] For a compact oriented topological four-manifold with Betti-one boundary components, PTFA fraction-field boundary-intersection rank is at most ordinary rank. A nontrivial PTFA coefficient system on a compact Betti-one manifold has zero fraction-field first homology. [[thm-ptfa-localized-boundary-intersection-rank-is-no-larger-than-ordinary-rank]], [[lem-ptfa-localization-kills-first-homology-of-betti-one-manifolds]]

[F3] If localized second homology of a compact collared four-manifold is generated by its entire boundary, the linking-form kernel on any finite union of localized-first-acyclic boundary components is isotropic. [F4] Product-collared gluing has the local-coefficient Mayer–Vietoris and pair exact sequences, including excision. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-pair-long-exact-sequences-with-local-coefficients]]

## Definition

Let $D$ be a finite set of design indices, let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$. For each $d\in D$, let $Q_d$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathsf Y$ with a specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to $\nu$, so
$$Q_d(\theta,B)=\int_B p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\nu(dy)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Define the prior-predictive density $p_d(y)=\int_\Theta p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)$. For each datum $y$ with $0<p_d(y)<\infty$, define the posterior probability measure
$$\mu_d^y(A)=\frac{\int_A p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)}{p_d(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The dominated-kernel Bayes formula makes $p_d\,d\nu$ the observation law and identifies $\mu_d^y$ as a posterior version on these positive finite evidence fibers. No posterior formula is assigned on fibers with zero or infinite evidence; their prior-predictive probability is zero.

## Example

Let the scalar parameter $u$ have prior density
$$p_0(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2},$$
and observe $y=0$ with unit-variance Gaussian noise. The exact forward map is
$G(u)=u$, while a deliberately biased numerical forward/PDE solver reports
$\widetilde G(u)=u+2$. At $y=0$, use likelihoods
$L(u)=\exp(-G(u)^2/2)$ and
$\widetilde L(u)=\exp(-\widetilde G(u)^2/2)$; the common Gaussian density
constant cancels when normalizing. Define each fixed-data posterior by
normalizing the prior times its stated likelihood. The exact posterior is
$N(0,1/2)$ and the solver posterior is $N(-1,1/2)$. For the bounded functional
$f(u)=\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,0]}(u)$, their expectations are respectively
$$\Pi(f)=\tfrac12,\qquad \widetilde\Pi(f)=\Phi_0(\sqrt2)>\tfrac12,$$
where
$$\Phi_0(t):=\int_{-\infty}^{t}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz.$$
The discrepancy is in the forward-solver stage of the posterior error budget;
this toy solver assumption makes no claim about the bias of any general PDE
discretization.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prior density, the exact and solver forward maps, the unit-variance observation noise, and the normalized prior-times-likelihood posterior convention in the Example.

[F1] The error-budget solver term compares the exact-model posterior expectation with the posterior expectation obtained from the declared numerical forward solve. [[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget]]

[F2] The standard normal density is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$, and $N(m,s^2)$ is its affine image $m+sZ$ for $s>0$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the library standard-normal law interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F3] For a bounded measurable functional, the expectation difference is at most $2\|f\|_\infty$ times the event-supremum total variation distance. [[prop-ip-bounded-posterior-functional-error]]

Its normalized density is therefore $\pi^{-1/2}e^{-u^2}$, which is $N(0,1/2)$ by [F2]. For the solver output, the prior-times-likelihood product is
$$ (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2-(u+2)^2/2}=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-(u+1)^2-1};$$

## Example

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X=Y=L^2((0,1);\mathbb R)$ with its canonical real Hilbert inner product. For $f\in L^2(0,1)$ define $T$ by the Green kernel $G(x,t)=\min(x,t)(1-\max(x,t))$, so $(Tf)(x)=\int_0^1G(x,t)f(t)\,dt$. We use the Dirichlet solution class of continuous functions $u\in C([0,1])$ satisfying $u(0)=u(1)=0$ and $u''=-f$ in distributions on $(0,1)$; the Green formula specifies its unique member. Take the truth
$$
f^\dagger(x)=x\mathbf 1_{[0,1/2]}(x)+(1-x)\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1]}(x)
$$
and exact data
$$
g^\dagger(x)=-\frac{x(4x^2-3)}{24}\mathbf 1_{[0,1/2]}(x)+\frac{(x-1)(4x^2-8x+1)}{24}\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1]}(x).

[F11] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: Absolutely integrable functions on the product of the two finite intervals may be integrated in either order.

[F12] [[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]]: A distribution on the connected interval $(0,1)$ with zero derivative is constant; applying this twice shows that a distribution with zero second derivative is affine.


## Verification

1.1 The functions $e_j(x)=\sqrt2\sin(\pi jx)$ are orthonormal on $(0,1)$ by the product-to-sum identities and direct integration. If $h\in L^2(0,1)$ is orthogonal to all of them, its odd extension to $(-1,1)$, continued periodically with period $2$, has zero constant and cosine coefficients by oddness and zero sine coefficients by the assumed orthogonality. Rescaling to the circle in [F1], every Fourier coefficient of this extension vanishes; completeness in [F2] therefore makes the extension, and hence $h$, zero almost everywhere. Thus $(e_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis, and [F7] supplies the real Hilbert structure used below. [given, A1, F1, F2, F7, construct, algebra]

1.2 For $f\in L^2(0,1)$, [F8] gives $f\in L^1(0,1)$. Since $0\le G(x,t)\le1/4$, $|Tf(x)|\le\|f\|_1/4\le\|f\|_2/4$ for every $x$, so the integral formula defines a bounded linear operator from $L^2(0,1)$ to itself. The kernel formula also gives
$$
(Tf)(x)=(1-x)\int_0^x t f(t)\,dt+x\int_x^1(1-t)f(t)\,dt.
$$
The two indefinite integrals are absolutely continuous by [F9], and [F10] gives their derivatives almost everywhere. They show that $Tf$ is continuous, has zero endpoint values, and has first derivative almost everywhere equal to the absolutely continuous function $g(x)=-\int_0^x tf(t)\,dt+\int_x^1(1-t)f(t)\,dt$, whose derivative is $g'(x)=-xf(x)-(1-x)f(x)=-f(x)$ almost everywhere. The function $(x,t)\mapsto G(x,t)f(t)\phi''(x)$ is integrable on $(0,1)^2$, so [F11] permits reversing the integrals; splitting at $x=t$ and integrating the smooth test function twice gives

=\int_0^1 f(t)\left(\int_0^1G(x,t)\phi''(x)\,dx\right)dt

Thus $(Tf)''=-f$ in distributions. If two continuous Dirichlet solutions exist, their difference $h$ has $h''=0$ in distributions. Applying [F12] to $h'$ makes $h'$ constant, and applying it to $h-cx$ makes $h$ affine; continuity identifies the distribution with its pointwise affine representative. The two zero endpoint values force $h=0$. [given, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, construct, algebra]

1.3 For every $\lambda\ge0$, the Tikhonov filter is nonnegative and satisfies $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)=\alpha/(\lambda+\alpha)\le1$ and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)=\lambda/(\lambda+\alpha)\le1$. [F4, algebra]
