## Statement

For every $0<\theta_0<\pi$ and every open interval $I\subset(0,\pi)$ containing $\theta_0$, there is an explicit integral $8\times8$ matrix $V$ with $\det(V-V^T)=1$ such that the finite Hermitian matrix
$$H_\theta(V)=(1-e^{i\theta})V+(1-e^{-i\theta})V^T$$
has signature $2$ at $\theta_0$ and signature zero for all $\theta\in[0,\pi]\setminus I$. Its signature takes only the values $0,1,2$ on $[0,\pi]$ and is invariant under $\theta\mapsto-\theta$. Moreover, its signature equals $2$ throughout an open interval containing $\theta_0$. No choice principle, classification of Seifert forms, realization by a knot, or infinite-dimensional spectral theorem is assumed.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real parameter $\theta_0$ and containing open interval $I$.

[F1] All matrices below are finite. For a finite Hermitian matrix, signature is its number of positive eigenvalues minus its number of negative eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity. Equivalently these are the positive and negative inertia indices of its Hermitian form. Invertible congruence preserves these indices by sending definite subspaces bijectively to definite subspaces; a block-diagonal sum adds them.


## Proof

1.1 The finite inertia calculations used below require no spectral theorem for an infinite-dimensional space. A nonzero Hermitian form on $\mathbb C^n$ has a vector with nonzero real value: if its diagonal values on the coordinate vectors all vanish, a nonzero off-diagonal entry is detected by a sum $e_i+e_j$ or $e_i+i e_j$. Split off the line of such a vector by subtracting its orthogonal projection, and repeat in the orthogonal complement. Finite induction gives a diagonal form with positive, negative and zero entries. If there are $p$ positive entries, the positive coordinate subspace has dimension $p$, and any subspace of dimension greater than $p$ meets the span of the nonpositive coordinates, so cannot be positive definite. Thus $p$ is the maximal positive dimension; the same argument gives the maximal negative dimension. Congruence preserves these maxima by an invertible change of coordinates, and the diagonal description proves additivity under block sum and sign reversal under negation. For a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix, its real eigenvalues are $(\operatorname{tr}C\pm\sqrt{(C_{11}-C_{22})^2+4|C_{12}|^2})/2$; their product is its determinant. Hence the trace/determinant tests used below follow explicitly. Every splitting is within a fixed finite-dimensional space. [F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 For integers $b>0$ and $a$, put $w=a-b$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&w\\w&w^2+b\end{pmatrix}$ and $V(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}A&I_2\\0&B\end{pmatrix}$. Both diagonal blocks are integral and symmetric, so $V(a,b)-V(a,b)^T=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\-I_2&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant one. Also $B$ is positive definite: its real quadratic form is $(x+wy)^2+b y^2$, and the same expression with absolute squares works over $\mathbb C$. Its determinant is $b$ and its trace is positive. All these assertions follow directly from the displayed matrices. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For $0<\theta\le\pi$ write $c=1-e^{i\theta}$ and $h=2-2\cos\theta>0$, so $|c|^2=h$. The Hermitian matrix of $V(a,b)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}hA&cI_2\\\bar cI_2&hB\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting the appropriate multiple of the lower block from the upper block, and the conjugate multiple of its column, is an invertible block congruence to $(hA-B^{-1})\oplus hB$. Its second block contributes signature two. Put $C=hA-B^{-1}$. Since $\operatorname{tr}A=0$ and $B^{-1}$ is positive definite, $\operatorname{tr}C=-\operatorname{tr}B^{-1}<0$. Direct determinant expansion, using $\operatorname{tr}(BA)=2w$ and $\det(BA)=-b$, gives $$\det C=b^{-1}\det(hBA-I_2)=b^{-1}(1-2wh-bh^2).$$ The polynomial has exactly one positive root $$s(a,b)=\frac{-w+\sqrt{w^2+b}}b.$$ For $0<h<s(a,b)$ its determinant is positive and its trace negative, so its two real eigenvalues are negative. At $h=s(a,b)$ it has one negative and one zero eigenvalue. For $h>s(a,b)$ its determinant is negative, so it has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. The signature of $H_\theta(V(a,b))$ is consequently $0,1,2$ in those three cases, respectively. At $\theta=0$ the Hermitian matrix is zero and its signature is zero. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 The positive thresholds $s(a,b)$ are dense in $(0,4)$. Indeed fix $r\in(-1,1)$ and set $a_b=\lfloor br\rfloor$ for positive integers $b$. For all sufficiently large $b$, $a_b/b<1$; put $d_b=1-a_b/b>0$. Then $$s(a_b,b)=d_b+\sqrt{d_b^2+1/b},\qquad |s(a_b,b)-2(1-r)|\le2/b+1/\sqrt b.$$ Here $|a_b/b-r|\le1/b$ and $0\le\sqrt{d_b^2+1/b}-d_b\le1/\sqrt b$, which prove the bound. For any desired positive tolerance a sufficiently large integer makes its right side smaller than that tolerance. Given any target in $(0,4)$, take $r$ to be one minus half the target; the explicit floor formula then supplies thresholds arbitrarily close to it. This is a sequence defined by a formula, without selecting any infinite family of witnesses. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The function $h(\theta)=2-2\cos\theta$ is continuous and strictly increasing from $0$ to $4$ on $[0,\pi]$: its derivative is $2\sin\theta>0$ in the interior. Choose two real angles $\alpha<\theta_0<\beta$ in $I$ and small disjoint open intervals around them whose closures are contained respectively in $I\cap(0,\theta_0)$ and $I\cap(\theta_0,\pi)$. Their $h$ images are nonempty intervals in $(0,4)$. Step 3.1 supplies a pair $(a_-,b_-)$ with threshold in the first image and a pair $(a_+,b_+)$ with threshold in the second. If desired these finite witnesses can be specified by enumerating integer pairs by increasing $|a|+b$ and then increasing $a$ and taking the first pair whose explicit threshold is in the relevant interval. Thus the corresponding unique crossing angles satisfy $\theta_-<\theta_0<\theta_+$ and lie in $I$. [given, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Define $V=V(a_-,b_-)\oplus(-V(a_+,b_+))$. Each skew block has determinant one, also after negation, so $\det(V-V^T)=1$. Its Hermitian signature is the difference of the two signatures in step 2.1. Since the thresholds are ordered, it is zero below $\theta_-$, one at $\theta_-$, two on $(\theta_-,\theta_+)$, one at $\theta_+$ and zero above $\theta_+$. It is also zero at zero. This proves all claims on $[0,\pi]$, including nonzero value at $\theta_0$ and vanishing off $I$. Finally $V$ is real, so $H_{-\theta}(V)=\overline{H_\theta(V)}$; conjugation preserves the real eigenvalues and their multiplicities, proving symmetry. The only constructions were finite matrices, explicit integer formulas and two individual integer witnesses. Thus no choice or realization theorem has been used. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with Borel law $\mu$. Let $C:B^*\to B$ be its covariance operator, let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$, and let $i:E\to B$ be the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. For every $h\in E$ and $r>0$,
$$ \mu\bigl(\{x\in B:\|x-ih\|_B\le r\}\bigr)\le \mu\bigl(\{x\in B:\|x\|_B\le r\}\bigr). $$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, HB, countable choice, a real separable Banach space $B$, a centered Borel Gaussian random element $W$, its covariance operator $C$, and its covariance-induced Hilbert space $E$ with canonical injection $i$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the finite-dimensional Gaussian-centering result used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] HB and countable choice supply the countable norming family used to recover the Banach norm from scalar coordinates. [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] $W$ is Borel measurable, each $\ell(W)$ is centered normal, and every finite vector of continuous-linear coordinates is a possibly degenerate multivariate normal vector. [[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F2] $E$ is the completion of $B^*/\ker C$, the map $i$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$, and $\ell(ih)=\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E$. [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]

[F3] There are $\ell_j\in B^*$ with $\|x\|_B=\sup_j|\ell_j(x)|$ for every $x\in B$. [[lem-separable-banach-has-countable-norming-family]]

[F4] For a nondegenerate finite-dimensional centered Gaussian vector, every bounded symmetric loss with convex sublevel sets has minimum expectation at the center. Applying this to the indicator of the complement of a closed symmetric convex set gives the Gaussian shift inequality for that set. [[lem-gaussian-centering-for-bounded-symmetric-quasiconvex-loss]]

[F5] For a finite measure, probabilities of a decreasing sequence of measurable sets converge to the probability of their intersection. [[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]


## Proof

**Proof technique:** compare finite collections of norming coordinates by finite-dimensional Gaussian centering, then pass to the norm ball by continuity from above.

1.1 Choose the norming family from [F3]. Fix $r>0$, $h\in E$, and $n\ge1$. Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Thus $a_n\perp\ker\Sigma_n$, so $a_n\in S_n:=\operatorname{ran}(\Sigma_n)$, the support subspace of $Y_n$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, choose]

2.1 In the finite-dimensional space $S_n$, the restriction of $Y_n$ is a nondegenerate Gaussian vector. Let $Q_n=[-r,r]^n$ and $D_n=Q_n\cap S_n$, a closed symmetric convex set. Since $a_n\in S_n$, the event $Y_n-a_n\in Q_n$ is the translate by $a_n$ of $D_n$ inside $S_n$. An invertible linear change of coordinates turns the centered law on $S_n$ into a nondegenerate Gaussian law and preserves symmetry and convexity of $D_n$. Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields
$$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$
If $S_n=\{0\}$, then $Y_n=a_n=0$ almost surely and the same inequality is equality. [A1, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. The sets $A_n(h)$ decrease with $n$, and [F3] gives $\bigcap_n A_n(h)=\{\|W-ih\|_B\le r\}$; likewise $\bigcap_n A_n(0)=\{\|W\|_B\le r\}$. Apply [F5] to both decreasing sequences and pass to their limits in the finite-dimensional inequalities. This proves the stated ball-mass bound. [F3, F5, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a smooth spacetime manifold of dimension $m\ge2$ with a smooth positive density, and let $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ be a scalar second-order differential operator in local coordinates. In each local chart, use the microlocal convention $D_j:=(1/i)\partial_{x_j}=-i\partial_{x_j}$ and $D^\alpha:=D_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots D_m^{\alpha_m}$. Its principal symbol $p(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=2}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha$ is real and satisfies $dp\ne0$ on $\{p=0\}\subset T^*X\setminus0$. Equip $T^*X$ with its canonical cotangent symplectic form and define the Hamilton vector field by $\iota_{H_p}\omega_{\rm can}=dp$. A null bicharacteristic is a nonzero integral curve of $H_p$ contained in $\{p=0\}$. Let $\Gamma$ be a compact phase-space segment that is an injective immersion with no repeated phase points; assume its base projection is an immersion (the no-cusp condition) and that the segment is contained in the interior of $T^*X\setminus0$. For every integer $N\ge1$, there are complex smooth functions $u_\lambda$ supported in a fixed tubular neighborhood of the base curve of $\Gamma$, with a smooth cutoff equal to one near that curve, such that the following hold as $\lambda\to+\infty$:

1. The phase has a formal transverse Taylor expansion solving the complex eikonal equation to every prescribed finite order; its transverse imaginary Hessian is positive definite along the curve and yields Gaussian decay away from the ray.
2. The amplitudes solve the transport hierarchy to the corresponding order and are realized by a Borel sum with a finite-coordinate-patch construction.
3. Write $s$ for a fixed smooth parameter on the projected curve and fix its origin. There is a smooth positive transported density $w(s)ds$, normalized by $w(0)=1$, such that the measures $|u_\lambda|^2dV_X$ converge against compactly supported smooth tests away from endpoint neighborhoods to $\int a(\pi\Gamma(s))w(s)ds$. The weight is the one determined by the leading transport equation; a general operator with complex lower-order coefficients need not give constant $w$. For the real formally self-adjoint wave operator, with parameter equal to physical time along a unit-speed spatial ray and the wave phase normalized by $|\partial_t\phi|=1$, the transport gives $w=1$.
4. For every compact set $K$ disjoint from neighborhoods of the two projected endpoints, $\|Pu_\lambda\|_{L^2(K)}=O(\lambda^{-N})$ for each requested $N$, after carrying the expansions sufficiently far. The endpoint cutoff generally produces a residual near those endpoints. In particular, if the segment extends outside a compact measurement domain and its two endpoint neighborhoods are disjoint from that domain, the residual has the asserted order throughout that domain.

The cutoff in the ambient extension is one along the portion of the ray under observation and vanishes beyond the extended endpoints. A segment wholly in the spacetime interior does not have a globally negligible endpoint residual. Its tube can be supported away from the boundary and then has zero boundary trace; a wave beam entering and exiting a measurement domain instead has its actual smooth boundary trace there. In this wave specialization, if the extended beam is zero near the required initial or terminal time, the zero-boundary energy correction on the measurement cylinder gives an exact solution with the same boundary data and an $O(\lambda^{-N})$ energy error for any requested $N$. The claim concerns an embedded segment in phase space and permits projected self-intersections.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real quadratic principal symbol, an embedded compact null bicharacteristic with immersed projection, a positive smooth density, and a requested residual order; put $h=\lambda^{-1}$ and $d=m-1$.

[F1] [[lem-ip-borel-jet-realization-and-beam-patching]] realizes compatible transverse jets uniformly on compact parameter intervals. For a curve with projected crossings, apply its single-segment construction to the embedded graph $(\pi\Gamma(s),s)$ in $X\times\mathbb R$, and then restrict to separate local branches. The chartwise jets agree on open overlaps by the jet ODE uniqueness; no extension from merely pointwise-compatible jets on a crossing union is invoked.

[F2] [[thm-local-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-for-manifold-integral-curves]] gives smooth solutions and uniqueness for the finite linear ODE systems below.

[F3] [[thm-ip-variable-metric-wave-ibvp-energy-wellposedness]] gives forward and terminal zero-boundary energy corrections on a compact wave cylinder.



## Proof

1.1 Cover the parameter interval by finitely many small overlapping intervals on which the immersed base curve is embedded. In such an interval choose coordinates $(s,y)$ with the curve $y=0$ and with $s$ its prescribed parameter. The central covector satisfies $p=0$ and $p_{\xi_s}\ne0$, since the Hamilton velocity in these coordinates is a nonzero multiple of $\partial_s$. The formal implicit equation $p(s,y,\partial_s\phi,\partial_y\phi)=0$ can thus be solved recursively for the jets of $\partial_s\phi$. This is an evolution eikonal equation in $s$, with a smooth real reduced Hamiltonian in the real variables. Its zeroth and first jet equations are exactly the given Hamilton curve (after its parameter change). Initialize the transverse Hessian by $H(0)=iI$ in the chosen transverse coordinates. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The quadratic jet equation is the matrix Riccati equation $$H'+D+BH+HB^T+HCH=0,$$ where $C,D$ are real symmetric and $B$ real, the corresponding blocks of the reduced Hamiltonian Hessian. Solve instead $Y'=B^TY+CZ$, $Z'=-DY-BZ$, $Y(0)=I$, $Z(0)=iI$. Direct differentiation gives $Y^TZ-Z^TY=0$ and $Y^*Z-Z^*Y=2iI$. If $Yv=0$ the second identity gives $0=2i|v|^2$, so $Y$ is invertible on the whole interval. Consequently $H=ZY^{-1}$ is symmetric, solves the Riccati equation, and $$\operatorname{Im}H=(Y^{-1})^*Y^{-1}>0.$$ Compactness gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds. At an overlap transform all jets by the coordinate chain rule, carry these initial data to the next chart, and use ODE uniqueness. Positivity is unchanged by real coordinate change and persists on the finite cover. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For transverse degree $k\ge3$, differentiating the reduced eikonal equation $k$ times gives a finite linear ODE for the degree-$k$ phase jet: its highest jet enters linearly, with coefficients determined by the Hessian and the first derivatives of the reduced Hamiltonian; the inhomogeneous terms involve only lower jets and derivatives of the symbol. This follows by the product rule: terms containing a highest derivative of $\phi$ can have only one such factor, and the degree-$k+1$ derivative cancels against differentiation along the central Hamilton curve. Thus solve successively for every degree using [F2], matching all jets on overlaps. Apply [F1], or its explicit shrinking-cutoff series, to realize them. This yields a smooth phase with eikonal defect flat on each branch and $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ after shrinking the transverse tube. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Define $T_\phi$ to be the coefficient of $h^{-1}$ in the exact conjugation identity $$P(e^{i\phi/h}a)=e^{i\phi/h}(h^{-2}p(x,d\phi)a+h^{-1}T_\phi a+Pa).$$ It is a first-order operator with derivative part $p_\xi(x,d\phi)\cdot D$, so its coefficient of $\partial_s$ on the ray is nonzero. Solve $T_\phi a_0=0$ and $T_\phi a_j=-Pa_{j-1}$ for $j\ge1$ to infinite transverse order. The central $a_0$ equation is a scalar homogeneous ODE with nonzero initial value, hence has nonvanishing exponential solution. For each successive transverse degree and amplitude index the differentiated equations are linear ODEs with already known right sides, by the same cancellation of derivatives along the curve as in step 3.1. Realize these jets by [F1]. The separate asymptotic series $a(x;h)\sim\sum_{j\ge0}h^ja_j(x)$ is realized by $\sum_jh^ja_j(x)\eta(h/\delta_j)$, with $\eta=1$ near zero and $\delta_j\downarrow0$ chosen so its $C^k$ tails are summable for every fixed $k$ and have the required $h$ asymptotic bounds. Explicitly, for each $j$ make $\delta_j<2^{-j}$ and $\delta_j^{j/2}(1+\|a_j\|_{C^j})<2^{-j}$; for fixed $k,J$, terms $j\ge\max(k,2J+2)$ are then $O(h^J)$ in $C^k$. Only finitely many earlier terms remain. This proves the full transport and Borel realization. [F1, F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 On an embedded branch take $u_h=h^{-d/4}e^{i\phi/h}a(x;h)$ and a fixed transverse cutoff. For a flat defect $r$, Taylor's formula gives $|D^\alpha r|\le C_{k,\alpha}|y|^k$ for every $k$. Scaling $y=\sqrt h z$ and using $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ shows $$\|h^{-d/4}|y|^ke^{-c|y|^2/h}\|_{L^2}\le C_kh^{k/2}.$$ Every application of $P$ loses at most two powers of $h$. Choose $k$ and the amplitude order large enough to dominate that loss and any requested $N$. Derivatives of the transverse cutoff are supported at fixed positive distance from the ray and are $O(h^\infty)$ by Gaussian decay. Thus the residual is $O(h^N)$ away from longitudinal endpoint cutoffs; at endpoints the commutator with a longitudinal cutoff remains, and no vanishing assertion is made there. This also proves uniform $L^2$ boundedness on each branch. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 To patch, use the compatible phase and amplitude jets constructed above and a finite partition in the curve parameter. On the overlap of adjacent descriptions, their phases and amplitudes differ by flat terms, so after multiplication by $h^{-d/4}e^{i\phi/h}$ their difference and any fixed number of derivatives are $O(h^N)$ for every $N$, by step 5.1. Derivatives of the partition cancel because its sum is one on each branch; their remaining flat differences have the same bound. Nonadjacent branches meeting at a projected crossing have distinct covectors: otherwise the phase-space curve would repeat a point. Compactness separates those covectors uniformly off a small neighborhood of the parameter diagonal. Mixed products therefore tend to zero: integrate by parts against the nonzero difference of the two real phase gradients, shrinking crossing neighborhoods so it remains bounded below. Each integration gains $h$, while each transverse Gaussian derivative loses at most $h^{-1/2}$ in its integral bounds; arbitrarily many integrations give arbitrary decay. Away from crossings ordinary Gaussian decay applies. Thus patching preserves the residual, positivity, and the sum of the branch mass limits, including at projected self-intersections. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty simple Riemannian background of dimension $n\ge2$ with smooth strictly convex boundary, no conjugate points, and nontrapping geodesics. Fix $x_0\in\partial M$. For an inward unit vector $\omega\in T_{x_0}M$ with $g(\omega,\nu_{out})<0$, let $\gamma_{x_0,\omega}$ be the unit-speed geodesic starting at $(x_0,\omega)$, and let $\tau(x_0,\omega)>0$ be its first positive boundary-exit time. Define
$$\mathcal D_{x_0}=\{s\omega: g(\omega,\omega)=1,\ g(\omega,\nu_{out})<0,\ 0<s<\tau(x_0,\omega)\}\subset T_{x_0}M,$$
and define $E_{x_0}:\mathcal D_{x_0}\to M^\circ$ by $E_{x_0}(s\omega)=\gamma_{x_0,\omega}(s)$. Then $E_{x_0}$ is a diffeomorphism. In particular every interior point is joined to $x_0$ by a unique minimizing geodesic, the function $r_{x_0}(y)=d_g(x_0,y)$ is smooth on $M^\circ$, and on each ray tube it satisfies $|\nabla_g r_{x_0}|_g=1$. The no-return extension of $M$ across its boundary is complete, and each outward or tangent geodesic launched from the boundary leaves $M$ permanently.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The simple compact connected manifold and the boundary basepoint $x_0$ in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-simple-riemannian-background]] gives strict convexity, nontrapping, and absence of endpoint-zero nontrivial Jacobi fields. The geodesic ODE and its smooth dependence are supplied by [[thm-local-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-for-manifold-integral-curves]].

[F2] [[lem-ip-simple-manifold-no-return-extension]] gives a complete exterior extension, with no return after exit.

[F3] [[prop-compact-local-homeomorphism-is-finite-covering]] turns a local homeomorphism from a nonempty compact Hausdorff domain to a connected Hausdorff target into a finite covering. The target $M$ is path-connected because manifolds are locally path-connected ([[prop-topological-manifolds-are-locally-compact-and-locally-path-connected]]) and connected locally path-connected spaces are path-connected ([[thm-connected-and-locally-path-connected-implies-path-connected]]); $B_{x_0}$ is path-connected by its closed-ball model. Thus [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]] applies: a covering with simply connected total space is regular and its deck group acts transitively on each fibre. [[thm-uniqueness-of-lifts-from-a-connected-space]] makes a deck transformation fixing one point the identity.

[F4] [[thm-brouwer-fixed-point-theorem]] gives a fixed point for every continuous self-map of a closed ball.

[F5] [[thm-hopf-rinow]] gives a minimizing geodesic in the complete exterior between any two points. [[prop-length-dominates-endpoint-distance]] compares its length with distance.

[F6] [[thm-differential-of-the-exponential-map-in-terms-of-jacobi-fields]] identifies $d(\exp_{x_0})_v(w)$ with $J(1)$ for the Jacobi field along $t\mapsto\exp_{x_0}(tv)$ satisfying $J(0)=0$ and $D_tJ(0)=w$. Its Countable Choice hypothesis is included in the statement.

[F7] [[cor-the-tangent-space-of-an-n-manifold-has-dimension-n]] gives $\dim T_{x_0}M=n$, and [[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]] gives an orthonormal basis for $g_{x_0}$. These coordinates identify the unit sphere and closed unit ball in $T_{x_0}M$ with the Euclidean unit sphere and closed unit ball, which are compact by [[cor-euclidean-closed-balls-and-spheres-are-compact]]. The boundary-tangent unit sphere is the closed subset $\{\omega:g(\omega,\nu_{out})=0\}$ of that compact unit sphere, so it is compact by [[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]. This is the sphere used for the uniform bound in step 1.1. Every sequence of inward unit directions has bounded coordinates in $\mathbb R^n$; [[cor-bolzano-weierstrass-in-rn]] gives a convergent subsequence. Continuity of the finite-coordinate quadratic norm and of $\omega\mapsto g(\omega,\nu_{out})$ puts its limit on the unit sphere in the closed inward hemisphere. Thus the subsequence conclusion used in step 2.1 is supplied separately from topological compactness.



## Proof

1.1 Choose a smooth boundary defining function $\rho$ positive inside. At the boundary, $\nabla\rho$ is a negative multiple of $\nu_{out}$; hence for a tangent unit vector $\omega$, strict convexity gives $(\rho\circ\gamma_\omega)''(0)=\operatorname{Hess}\rho(\omega,\omega)<0$. Compactness of the tangent sphere from [F7] makes this bound uniform near tangency. For a nearby inward direction, put $a=d\rho_{x_0}(\omega)>0$. Taylor's formula factors the boundary equation as $\rho(\gamma_\omega(s))=s(a+sB(\omega,s))$, with $B<0$ uniformly near tangency. The implicit function theorem gives the first positive exit $\tau(\omega)$ there, with $\tau/a$ extending continuously and positively to tangent directions. Every other exit is transverse: a first exit with zero normal derivative would have $\rho=0$, $\rho'=0$, $\rho''<0$, forcing $\rho<0$ immediately before the exit. Thus all inward exits vary smoothly, and $\tau\to0$ at the equator. [F1, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 These exit times are uniformly bounded. Otherwise take inward unit directions $\omega_j$ and increasing lengths tending to infinity with no exit before those lengths. Compactness [F7] gives a convergent subsequence of directions, and continuity of $\omega\mapsto g(\omega,\nu_{out})$ puts the limit in the closed inward hemisphere. Step 1.1 excludes a tangent limit. Smooth dependence then gives a limiting inward geodesic that remains in $M$ for every positive time. It enters $M^\circ$ immediately. If it had a first later boundary contact at $t_0$, then $\rho'(t_0)>0$ would force $\rho<0$ just before $t_0$, $\rho'(t_0)<0$ would force $\rho<0$ just after $t_0$, and $\rho'(t_0)=0$ together with strict convexity would force $\rho<0$ just before $t_0$. Each contradicts that the limit stays in $M$. Thus a positive-time shift is a geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ that never reaches $\partial M$, contrary to nontrapping. Define $$B_{x_0}=\{s\omega:\omega\text{ inward unit},\ 0\le s\le\tau(\omega)\},$$ including $0$ and tangent endpoints only as $0$. Identify the inward normal with the last Euclidean coordinate and compare this radial set with the closed ball of radius one centred at the inward normal, whose radial length is $2\omega_n$ on the inward hemisphere. The radial map multiplies by $\tau(\omega)/(2\omega_n)$. Step 1.1 makes this ratio extend positively and continuously to the equator, so the radial map and its inverse are continuous also at zero. Hence $B_{x_0}$ is homeomorphic to a closed $n$-ball and compact by [F7]. [F1, F7, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 In the complete exterior of [F2], the exponential map $E(v)=\exp_{x_0}(v)$ is smooth on a neighborhood of $B_{x_0}$. Fix $v=s\omega\ne0$ in that set and let $\alpha(t)=\exp_{x_0}(tv)$, $0\le t\le1$. By [F6], if $dE_v(w)=0$, the Jacobi field $J$ with $J(0)=0$ and $D_tJ(0)=w$ has $J(1)=0$. Decompose $w=cv+w_\perp$ with $g(w_\perp,v)=0$. The radial Jacobi field is $J_\parallel(t)=ct\dot\alpha(t)$, so $J_\parallel(1)$ is nonzero when $c\ne0$. The Jacobi field $J_\perp$ from $w_\perp$ remains orthogonal to $\dot\alpha$: for $f(t)=g(J_\perp(t),\dot\alpha(t))$, the Jacobi equation gives $f''(t)=-g(R(J_\perp,\dot\alpha)\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)=0$, since metric compatibility makes $R(J_\perp,\dot\alpha)$ skew-adjoint in its last two slots; also $f(0)=f'(0)=0$. Thus $J_\perp(1)$ is orthogonal to the radial vector. If $J(1)=0$, orthogonality forces $c=0$ and $J_\perp(1)=0$. For $w\ne0$ this is a nonzero Jacobi field with endpoint zeros; reparametrizing $\alpha$ by arclength gives a unit-speed geodesic segment in $M$, contradicting [F1]. Hence $dE_v$ has trivial kernel. At $v=0$, [F6] on the constant geodesic gives $dE_0=I$. On the radial boundary $s=\tau(\omega)>0$, transversality from step 1.1 identifies $B_{x_0}$ locally with the inverse image of $M$ under this inverse chart, so the restricted map is a local homeomorphism of manifolds with boundary. The same is true at $0$: in a small normal neighborhood the inverse image of $M$ is precisely the short inward radial segments; tangent and outward rays immediately leave by strict convexity, and inward directions with very small exit time have already left. The exterior no-return property excludes extra portions of a ray in this local description. Thus $E:B_{x_0}\to M$ is a local homeomorphism everywhere. [F1, F2, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F3] to this compact radial ball [F7]. It is a finite covering of $M$. The ball model contracts to its centre by straight-line homotopy, so $B_{x_0}$ is simply connected and [F3] makes the covering regular. If a fibre had two points, transitivity would supply a nonidentity deck transformation of $B_{x_0}$. Conjugate it by the ball homeomorphism of step 2.1. By [F4] it has a fixed point, and by uniqueness of lifts in [F3] a deck transformation with a fixed point is the identity, a contradiction. Every fibre therefore has one point. Interior inverse charts show that $E$ restricted to $\mathcal D_{x_0}$ is a smooth diffeomorphism onto $M^\circ$. This proves global injectivity without a path-space Morse theorem. [F3, F4, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 A minimizing exterior geodesic from $x_0$ to $y\in M^\circ$ exists by [F5]. It cannot leave $M$ and return, by [F2]; it must start inward, since an outward or tangent launch never enters $M$. It is therefore one of the radial segments just shown unique. Its length equals exterior distance and, being contained in $M$, equals intrinsic distance as well. To compute the metric in polar coordinates, vary the unit initial direction. The resulting Jacobi field $J$ has $J(0)=0$ and $g(D_sJ(0),\dot\gamma(0))=0$. Metric compatibility and the Jacobi equation give $(g(D_sJ,\dot\gamma))'=0$, and hence $(g(J,\dot\gamma))'=0$ with zero initial value. Thus the radial vector has unit length and is orthogonal to every angular vector. Consequently $r_{x_0}=s$ is smooth in the interior and $|\nabla r_{x_0}|_g=1$. Completeness and no return are exactly [F2]. [F1, F2, F5, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. The restriction of representations of $\pi_1(E_K)$ to the peripheral torus gives an eigenvalue locus in $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ with algebraic Zariski closure. Its one-dimensional reduced image components are exactly the curve components used in $A_K(M,L)$; isolated image points contribute no curve factor. Radical elimination of the representation, trace and eigenline coordinates from the finite presentation incidence equations, followed by retaining precisely the one-dimensional irreducible components, yields the Laurent ideal of that curve union, whose square-free primitive generator is $A_K$ up to $\pm M^aL^b$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a finite knot-group presentation, marked peripheral words $\mu,\lambda$, and the definition of $A_K$ as the reduced union of one-dimensional eigenvalue-image closure components.

[F1] Matrix determinant and relator equations for the specified presentation have integer coefficients; inverse letters are replaced by adjugates ([[lem-sl2-representation-variety-is-affine]]).

[F2] A finite list of word traces gives the actual closed character-quotient model; equal irreducible characters are conjugate, while reducible characters record diagonal semisimplifications ([[lem-sl-two-character-trace-coordinate-model]]).

[F3] Finite affine incidence charts give the exact radical projection ideal by contraction, followed by a separate selection of dimension-one components. Stable sets and their selected components descend to rational radical ideals ([[lem-finite-affine-incidence-projection-and-curve-component-selection]]).

[F4] The full eigenvalue-image closure is stable under all field automorphisms fixing $\mathbb Q$, by applying them to the actual presentation matrices and common eigenvector ([[lem-knot-boundary-eigenvalue-locus-defined-over-q]]).

[F5] A finite reduced rationally defined union of Laurent plane curves has a square-free primitive integer-coefficient generator unique up to $\pm M^aL^b$ ([[lem-laurent-algebraic-curve-has-principal-equation]]).


## Proof

1.1 **Two finite eigenline charts.** Write the generator matrices as in [F1] and evaluate the two peripheral words by the same polynomial adjugate rule; call their matrices $U(A)$ and $V(A)$. Work over $R=\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$. In one chart put $v=(1,z)^T$ and in the other put $v=(z,1)^T$. In each impose all determinant and presented-relator equations together with the four scalar equations $U(A)v=Mv$ and $V(A)v=Lv$. These give finite ideals $J_1,J_2$ of polynomial extensions of $R$ with integer coefficients. Every common eigenline has a vector in at least one chart: divide by its first nonzero coordinate, using the second chart if its first coordinate is zero. Conversely any solution has a nonzero displayed vector and hence the required common eigenline. Their projected union is therefore exactly $\mathcal E_K$ of the definition, including repeated eigenvalues, scalar matrices and nonsemisimple peripheral matrices. No global eigenvector choice is made. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Trace coordinates introduce no extra image.** Choose the finite words $w_j$ of [F2]. If trace coordinates are used, append variables $t_j$ and equations $t_j=\operatorname{tr}(w_j(A))$ to both charts. These right sides are integer polynomials by [F1]. Every original chart point has exactly one such trace tuple, and forgetting that tuple gives exactly the original chart; thus appending and eliminating it changes neither the projected point set nor its ideal. The eigenvalue relation is independent of the representative of a character: for irreducible representations [F2] gives conjugacy, which carries common eigenlines with their eigenvalues; for reducible representations use an invariant-line basis. The peripheral matrices are then upper triangular and commute. Their possible joint eigenvalue pairs are precisely the two diagonal pairs, with coincident pairs counted once. To verify this last assertion, if one diagonal pair differs, one of the two matrices has distinct eigenvalues; its two eigenspaces are preserved by the commuting other matrix, giving both pairs. If neither differs, all common eigenvalues are the single repeated pair, and the original invariant line supplies it. Diagonal semisimplification consequently preserves exactly these pairs. Thus quotienting creates no additional peripheral eigenvalue pairs; the matrix incidence calculation already computes the same locus. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Radical elimination and the required selection.** Apply [F3] to the two finite charts, with the optional trace equations from step 2.1. It gives $I(\overline{\mathcal E_K})=(\sqrt{J_1}\cap R)\cap(\sqrt{J_2}\cap R)$. Decompose this closed set into its finite maximal irreducible components and retain exactly those of dimension one. Their union is exactly $V_K$ in the definition of $A_K$, so the intersection of their prime vanishing ideals is precisely $I(V_K)$. An isolated image component is not selected; no assumption that raw elimination removes it is used. The same operation discards a component of any other dimension if one occurs, without needing a separate dimension bound for the full peripheral image. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Primitive equation.** By [F4] the point set $\mathcal E_K$ is stable under every automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$. The component-selection part of [F3] therefore gives a radical rational structure on $I(V_K)$, not merely on the ideal before selection. By [F5] its finite reduced curve union has a square-free primitive integer Laurent generator, unique up to $\pm M^aL^b$. This is $A_K$ by its defining normalization. The construction retains the full-AC branch inherited from [F2]–[F5] and makes no choice of a global eigenline section or of a closed projection image. This proves all asserted elimination and normalization claims. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth nontrivial knot $K$, its chosen exterior $E_K$, and a properly embedded disk $D$ whose boundary $c=\partial D$ is essential on $T_K$.

[F1] The Axiom of Choice is the assertion that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F2] The boundary torus has a basis $[\mu],[\lambda]$ for which $[\mu]$ generates $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ and the kernel of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$; the preferred longitude has degree one under projection to the oriented core ([[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]], Statement; [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]], Definition).

[F3] Essential simple curves on a torus with the same primitive homology class up to orientation are isotopic on the torus ([[lem-essential-curves-on-torus-with-same-primitive-class-are-isotopic]], Statement).

[F4] Under countable choice a smooth knot has Seifert genus zero exactly when it is smoothly ambient isotopic to the unknot ([[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]]). Full AC in [F1] supplies countable choice by restriction to any countable family.

[F5] A compact smooth boundary-preimage disk in the compact smooth exterior can be made neat by a smooth isotopy of embeddings fixing its boundary pointwise. Only the resulting disk, not a smooth ambient extension at an original tangency, is needed. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]


## Proof

1.1 Under the full-AC hypothesis [F1], the supplier in [F2] applies. Since $c$ is essential on the torus, it is nonseparating: a separating simple curve on a genus-one surface cuts off a disk on one side and is null-homotopic. Cutting the torus along $c$ therefore gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. An embedded arc joining its two boundary circles closes after regluing to a loop meeting $c$ transversely once. The algebraic intersection is therefore $\pm1$, so $[c]$ is primitive in $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Because $c=\partial D$, its image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero. By [F2], write $[c]=q[\lambda]$ for an integer $q$. Since both $[c]$ and $[\lambda]$ are primitive, $q=\pm1$. Orient $c$ to make $[c]=[\lambda]$. By [F3], $c$ is isotopic on $T_K$ to a chosen simple representative of the preferred longitude. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In product coordinates $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, the curve $c$ has core degree one by [F2], so its torus class is $(1,k)$ for an integer $k$. The graph $\gamma_k(t)=(e^{it},e^{ikt})$ has that class. By [F3], choose a smooth isotopy $c_s(t)=(u_s(t),z_s(t))$ on the boundary torus from $c$ to $\gamma_k$, stationary near its final time after smooth reparametrization. This isotopy need not trace an embedded annulus on the torus itself. Instead choose a smooth strictly decreasing radius $r(s)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ with nonzero derivative, and use $(s,t)\mapsto(u_s(t),r(s)z_s(t))$ in the tube. Distinct $s$ have distinct radii, while each fixed-$s$ curve is embedded; moreover the time derivative has nonzero radial component and is independent of its circle tangent. This gives a smooth embedded annulus with outer boundary exactly $c$ and inner boundary the radius-$1/2$ copy of $\gamma_k$. Continue it inward by $(r,t)\mapsto(e^{it},r e^{ikt})$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. The stationary final curve makes the collars agree; the inward annulus is smooth and regular even at $r=0$ and has core boundary $K$. The resulting annulus lies otherwise in the interior of $N(K)$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 If the given disk is only boundary-preimage embedded, first replace it using [F5] by a neat smooth disk in $E_K$ with the same boundary $c$. The annulus of step 3.1 has nonzero inward radial derivative at $c$ on the tube side. The resulting proper disk $D$ on the exterior side and this annulus on the tube side meet only along $c$. Their union is an embedded disk with boundary $K$; smoothing the corner along $c$ in a product collar leaves that boundary fixed. Thus $K$ bounds a smooth disk, which is a genus-zero Seifert surface. Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F4], so [F4] makes $K$ ambient isotopic to the unknot, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore no such disk $D$ exists. [F1, F4, F5, given, step 3.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

## Statement

For every finite ASCII input string, the BMW braid-closure algorithm parses the
form `n;ell;word`, where `n` and `ell` are canonical decimal natural numbers
(`0`, or a nonzero decimal digit followed by zero or more decimal digits), and
`word` is empty if $\ell=0$ or is exactly $\ell$ comma-separated tokens of the
form `i+` or `i-`, with `i` a canonical decimal natural number. There is no
whitespace or trailing character. It returns `REJECT` exactly when the string
fails this syntax, the parsed value of $\ell$ differs from the actual number of
letter tokens, the parsed strand count is $n=0$, or some letter index fails
$1\le i<n$. For every other input, the algorithm terminates after finitely
many basis-code searches, algebra operations, and skein reductions, and returns exactly
$$-(-1)^c a^{-w}d^{n-1}\tau_n(\beta).$$
Here $w$ is the determinant writhe of the oriented closure, $c$ is its
component count, and $\tau_n$ is the normalized scalar closure trace. No
asymptotic complexity bound is asserted.

[F4] For each fixed $n$, the matching tangles form a finite basis of the tangle skein algebra ([[lem-bmw-descending-tangle-spanning]], [[lem-bmw-closure-pairing-independence]]).

[F5] The BMW generators map multiplicatively to the crossing and cup-cap tangle generators ([[lem-bmw-presentation-tangle-evaluation-is-well-defined]], [[def-dubrovnik-tangle-skein-algebra]]).

[F6] The Artin word generators are the positive geometric half twists; each contributes $+1$ to determinant writhe, its inverse contributes $-1$, the word exponent sum is their signed sum, and the closure components are the cycles of the strand permutation ([[def-markov-conjugation-and-stabilization-moves]], [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]], [[def-exponent-sum-of-a-braid]], [[def-closure-of-a-geometric-braid]]).

## Statement refuted

In $\mathbb R^2$ with $u\cdot v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2$, take the real measurement family $\Phi=(a_1,a_2)$ with $a_1=(1,0)$ and $a_2=(0,1)$, and define its intensity data by $I_\Phi(x)=((a_1\cdot x)^2,(a_2\cdot x)^2)$. The partition $S=\{1\}$ has neither side spanning $\mathbb R^2$. The signals $x=(1,1)$ and $z=(-1,1)$ satisfy neither $z=x$ nor $z=-x$, but $I_\Phi(x)=I_\Phi(z)$.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space and let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space. Let $K:X\to H$ be bounded and linear, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $Z$ be a jointly Gaussian centered family indexed by $H$, linear into $L^2$ with covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(k)]=\langle g,k\rangle_H$. For each $x\in X$ define $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$. A continuous linear feature is a map $\phi\in X^*$, where $X^*$ is the continuous dual of $X$. By the Riesz representation theorem there is a unique $h_\phi\in X$ with $\phi(x)=\langle x,h_\phi\rangle_X$ for every $x\in X$. The feature is **exactly linearly estimable by one probe** if some $\Phi\in H$ makes the statistic $Y_x(\Phi)$ unbiased for $\phi(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Writing $R(K^*)=\{K^*\Phi:\Phi\in H\}$ for the adjoint range, this holds exactly when $h_\phi\in R(K^*)$. Every such probe has variance $\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$. This definition concerns one-probe unbiased linear estimators; it does not identify membership in $\overline{R(K^*)}$ with exact estimability.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Real Hilbert spaces $X,H$, a bounded linear map $K:X\to H$, an isonormal white-noise experiment with $\epsilon>0$, and a continuous linear feature $\phi(x)=\langle x,h_\phi\rangle_X$.

[F1] In the isonormal experiment, $\mathbb E_xY_x(\Phi)=\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle_H$ and $\operatorname{Var}_x(Y_x(\Phi))=\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$ for every fixed $x\in X$ and $\Phi\in H$. [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]]

[F2] The adjoint satisfies $\langle Kx,\Phi\rangle_H=\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X$. [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]

[F3] Every continuous linear functional on a real Hilbert space has a unique representing vector $h_\phi$ with $\phi(x)=\langle x,h_\phi\rangle_X$. [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by [F2] and [F3]. [[def-countable-choice]]


## Proof

1.1 Fix a probe $\Phi\in H$. By [F1] and [F2], whose supplier hypotheses are recorded in [A1], its mean at parameter $x$ is $\langle x,K^*\Phi\rangle_X$ and its variance is finite, equal to $\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$. If it is unbiased for every $x$, then $\langle x,K^*\Phi-h_\phi\rangle_X=0$ for every $x\in X$. Taking $x=K^*\Phi-h_\phi$ gives $K^*\Phi=h_\phi$, so $h_\phi\in R(K^*)$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, if $h_\phi\in R(K^*)$, use [A1] to choose $\Phi\in H$ with $K^*\Phi=h_\phi$. Equations [F1] and [F2] then give $\mathbb E_xY_x(\Phi)=\langle x,h_\phi\rangle_X=\phi(x)$ for every $x$, and [F1] gives its finite variance $\epsilon^2\|\Phi\|_H^2$. Hence this probe is an exact one-probe estimator, proving both directions and the variance assertion. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, choose, algebra] ∎

For $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=2$, and $f(2)=0$, both $\tau_1f$ and $Rf$ have the same Fourier magnitude data as $f$, while neither equals $f$ or $-f$.

## Statement

$$\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}},\qquad \|b-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|a\|_{W^{1,3}})\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}.$$
All constants are independent of the higher norm of $a$.

Given a finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an action $\tau$ of $\Gamma$ on $SU(2)$ by constant unitary conjugations, suppose $\gamma^*a=d\tau_\gamma(a)$ and $\gamma^*\lambda=d\tau_\gamma(\lambda)$. Then $u(\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(u(x))$ and $h(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(h(x))$. A representation into $PU(2)$ supplies such a conjugation action; no lift of that representation to $SU(2)$ is required.

Adding the three bounds and using step 6.1 proves the claimed estimate for $b-a$, with $C$ independent of $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **Prescribed finite equivariance.** Orthogonal pullback preserves the Laplacian, codifferential, means and all the domain norms. Constant unitary conjugation preserves matrix products, the Frobenius norm and the exponential. Therefore the transformation $u(x)\mapsto d\tau_\gamma^{-1}(u(\gamma x))$ preserves $X$ and commutes with $T$ when $a,\lambda$ have the stated equivariance; this uses the equivariant inverse of [F1]. The zero starting iterate is invariant, so every iterate and its limit are invariant. Exponentiation gives the assertion for $h$. A central unitary scalar acts trivially by conjugation, which explains why a $PU(2)$ action suffices. The existence, uniqueness, estimates and boundary compatibility are all supplied in steps 5.1–7.1; full AC is inherited as stated in [F5]. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $k$ be a commutative field and let $H\trianglelefteq G$ be a normal subgroup with torsion-free abelian quotient $G/H$. If $k[H]$ has no zero divisors, then $k[G]$ has no zero divisors. The group extension need not split; neither finite generation of $G/H$ nor an order on all of $G$ is assumed.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $k$, normal subgroup $H\trianglelefteq G$, and torsion-free abelian quotient $A=G/H$.

[F1] Group-ring elements have unique finite expansions, multiplication is $k$-bilinear with $[g][h]=[gh]$, and each $[g]$ is a unit ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

[F2] Every finitely generated torsion-free abelian group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ for some finite $r$ ([[lem-finitely-generated-torsion-free-abelian-freeness-without-choice]]).

[A1] The ring $k[H]$ has no zero divisors.


## Proof

**Given:** Two nonzero elements $f,g\in k[G]$ and [A1].

1.1 Let $B$ be the subgroup of $A$ generated by the images of the finite supports of $f$ and $g$. It is finitely generated, torsion-free and abelian, so [F2] identifies it with $\mathbb Z^r$. Transport the lexicographic order from $\mathbb Z^r$ to $B$. This is a total order invariant under addition. No order on the whole quotient or on $G$ is needed. Let $X,Y\subseteq B$ be the finite quotient supports of $f,g$. Choose lifts $t_x\in G$ for the finitely many elements of $X\cup Y\cup(X+Y)$, using the same lift for any repeated element. By grouping terms in each coset, [F1] gives unique expressions $f=\sum_{x\in X}r_xt_x$ and $g=\sum_{y\in Y}s_yt_y$ with $0\ne r_x,s_y\in k[H]$. Distinct cosets have disjoint group bases, so these grouped coefficients are nonzero. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 For these lifts put $\alpha_x(s)=t_xst_x^{-1}$ on $k[H]$ and $h_{x,y}=t_xt_yt_{x+y}^{-1}\in H$. Normality makes $\alpha_x$ a ring automorphism, with inverse conjugation by $t_x^{-1}$. Direct multiplication gives $(r_xt_x)(s_yt_y)=r_x\alpha_x(s_y)h_{x,y}t_{x+y}$. This is the crossed-product multiplication on the finite supports. The factor $h_{x,y}$ is retained and is a unit; it is not assumed to be $1$. Its compatibility with iterated multiplication is inherited from associativity in $G$. Thus the calculation applies to a nonsplit extension. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $x_0=\max X$ and $y_0=\max Y$. Every other pair $(x,y)$ satisfies $x+y<x_0+y_0$: if $x<x_0$, then $x+y\le x+y_0<x_0+y_0$, and if $x=x_0$ but $y<y_0$, addition invariance gives the same strict inequality. Hence the coefficient of $t_{x_0+y_0}$ in $fg$ is the single term $r_{x_0}\alpha_{x_0}(s_{y_0})h_{x_0,y_0}$. It is nonzero by [A1], invertibility of $h_{x_0,y_0}$ and injectivity of $\alpha_{x_0}$. By disjointness of coset bases, $fg\ne0$. Since $f,g$ were arbitrary, $k[G]$ has no zero divisors. Only finitely many lifts were chosen, so the proof introduces no choice axiom. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X,Y$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be open, and let $F:U\to Y$ be Fréchet differentiable at every point with $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$ continuous in operator norm. Fix $x_0\in U$ and $r>0$ such that $\overline B_{2r}(x_0)\subseteq U$, and suppose an exact solution $x^\dagger\in\overline B_r(x_0)$ satisfies $y=F(x^\dagger)$. Assume $\|F'(x)\|\le1$ for every $x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ and that, for some $0\le\eta<1/2$,

$$
\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)-F'(x)(x-\widetilde x)\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x)-F(\widetilde x)\|_Y
$$

for every $x,\widetilde x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. This is a uniform two-point hypothesis with the derivative based at the first point. Assume Countable Choice so that the bounded derivatives have Hilbert adjoints. For $\delta\ge0$ and $y^\delta\in Y$ with $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$, set $x_0^\delta=x_0$ and define the ideal Landweber sequence by

$$
x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+F'(x_n^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)).
$$

Let $\tau>2(1+\eta)/(1-2\eta)$. For $\delta>0$, let $N(\delta,y^\delta)$ denote the first $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with $\|y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y\le\tau\delta$, if it exists. Put $d_0=\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X$ and $c_\tau=1-2\eta-2(1+\eta)/\tau>0$. Then the following hold.

1. For every update before the first discrepancy stop, writing $R_n^\delta=\|y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta)\|_Y$, the squared-error estimate is

   $$
   \|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le R_n^\delta\bigl(2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)R_n^\delta\bigr).
   $$

   In particular, the iterates are Fejér monotone relative to $x^\dagger$ up to the stop: their distance to $x^\dagger$ does not increase. Here Fejér monotonicity means exactly this nonincrease of distance to the stated solution.

2. If $\delta>0$, the first discrepancy index exists and

   $$
   N(\delta,y^\delta)<C\delta^{-2},\qquad C:=1+\frac{d_0^2}{c_\tau\tau^2}.
   $$

   A run of the finite-budget algorithm with budget $M\ge N(\delta,y^\delta)$ returns `stopped` at this first index; if $M<N(\delta,y^\delta)$, it returns `budget_exhausted` at $M$.

3. For exact data ($\delta=0$ and $y^\delta=y$), the ideal sequence is defined for every $n$, satisfies

   $$
   (1-2\eta)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2\le d_0^2,
   $$

   and converges strongly to some $\bar x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$ with $F(\bar x)=y$. No finite stopping index is claimed in the exact-data case.

4. For noisy data ($\delta>0$), the ideal stopped iterates converge uniformly over the admissible noise ball to that same exact-data limit:

   $$
   \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\ \sup_{\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta}\|x_{N(\delta,y^\delta)}^\delta-\bar x\|_X=0.
   $$

   For finite-budget runs this conclusion concerns outputs only when their budgets reach the first discrepancy indices. The theorem asserts neither a convergence rate nor that $\bar x$ is an $x_0$-minimum-norm solution.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** All hypotheses in the Statement. For any current iterate $u$ in the outer ball, write $A=F'(u)$ and $q=y^\delta-F(u)$. The update is $u^+=u+A^*q$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: the Axiom of Countable Choice, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is assumed. No stronger form of choice is assumed.

[A2] The data satisfy $y=F(x^\dagger)$ and $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$.

[A3] The closed outer ball lies in $U$, $x^\dagger$ is within distance $r$ of $x_0$, $F'$ is continuous in operator norm on $U$, and the derivative bound and uniform two-point tangential-cone inequality in the Statement hold on that ball.

[F1] [[alg-ip-nonlinear-landweber-discrepancy]]: the iteration is $x_{n+1}^\delta=x_n^\delta+F'(x_n^\delta)^*(y^\delta-F(x_n^\delta))$ and the discrepancy check is made before the finite-budget check.

[F2] [[def-ip-tangential-cone-condition]]: at a base point $x$, the local TCC bounds $\|F(x+h)-F(x)-F'(x)h\|_Y$ by $\eta\|F(x+h)-F(x)\|_Y$. The theorem assumes this exact orientation uniformly for pairs in the outer ball.

[F3] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]] and [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]: $\langle Au,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*v\rangle_X$ and $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ for every bounded Hilbert-space operator $A$.

[F4] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the real inner product is symmetric and $\|u\|_X^2=\langle u,u\rangle_X$; the corresponding expansion is $\|u+v\|_X^2=\|u\|_X^2+2\langle u,v\rangle_X+\|v\|_X^2$.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$.

[F6] [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]: $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$ in each real Hilbert space.

[F7] [[def-hilbert-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $X$ for the induced norm converges in $X$.

[F8] [[def-series]] and [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]]: a series with nonnegative real terms and bounded partial sums converges, and its tails tend to zero.

[F9] [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the real field is complete and its natural numbers are unbounded above.

[F10] [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]: every nonempty set of natural indices has a least member.

[F11] [[def-operator-norm]]: for every bounded linear $T$, $\|Tu\|\le\|T\|\,\|u\|$.

[F12] [[def-ip-nonlinear-forward-map]]: a real-Hilbert forward map is $F:U\to Y$ on an open domain, and exact solutions satisfy $F(x^\dagger)=y$.

[F13] [[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]: each Fréchet derivative is a bounded real-linear operator, and differentiability on $U$ defines the derivative map $F':U\to\mathcal B(X,Y)$.


## Proof


1.1 Fix a current point $u$ and any exact solution $z$ in the outer ball, and set $e=u-z$, $R=F(u)-y^\delta$, and $w=F(u)-F(z)-F'(u)e$. The uniform TCC gives $\|w\|_Y\le\eta\|F(u)-F(z)\|_Y$. Since $y=F(z)$, $y^\delta-F(u)+F'(u)e=y^\delta-y-w$, so by the noise bound and the triangle inequality, $\|y^\delta-F(u)+F'(u)e\|_Y\le\delta+\eta\|F(u)-y\|_Y\le(1+\eta)\delta+\eta\|R\|_Y$. [given, A2, A3, F2, F6, algebra]

1.2 The update has $e^+=e+A^*(y^\delta-F(u))$. Expanding its squared norm and using the adjoint identity yields $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2=2\langle y^\delta-F(u),Ae\rangle_Y+\|A^*(y^\delta-F(u))\|_X^2$. Since [F13] makes $A$ a bounded operator, [F11] gives $\|A^*(y^\delta-F(u))\|_X\le\|A^*\|\,\|R\|_Y=\|A\|\,\|R\|_Y\le\|R\|_Y$. [A1, A3, F3, F4, F11, F13, algebra]

2.1 Write $Ae=-(y^\delta-F(u))+(y^\delta-F(u)+Ae)$. By [F5] and step 1.2, $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2\le-\|R\|_Y^2+2\|R\|_Y\,\|y^\delta-F(u)+Ae\|_Y$. Substituting step 1.1 gives the stated one-step estimate $\|e^+\|_X^2-\|e\|_X^2\le\|R\|_Y\bigl(2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y\bigr)$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F5, algebra]

3.1 If $\delta>0$ and $\|R\|_Y>\tau\delta$, then $2(1+\eta)\delta-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y<0$ by the strict lower bound on $\tau$, so the squared error decreases. For exact data $\delta=0$, the same bound is $-(1-2\eta)\|R\|_Y^2\le0$ for every residual, including zero. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Put $c_\tau:=1-2\eta-2(1+\eta)/\tau$, which is positive by the strict hypothesis on $\tau$. For each $n<N(\delta,y^\delta)$, the residual is greater than $\tau\delta$; step 2.1 then gives $\|x_{n+1}^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le-c_\tau(R_n^\delta)^2$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 For exact data, step 2.1 gives $\|x_{n+1}-x^\dagger\|_X^2-\|x_n-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le-(1-2\eta)\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2$ for every $n$. Summing the first $K$ inequalities telescopes and yields $(1-2\eta)\sum_{n<K}\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y^2\le d_0^2-\|x_K-x^\dagger\|_X^2\le d_0^2$. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The initial point satisfies $\|x_0-x^\dagger\|_X=d_0\le r$. At every update before the noisy stop, or at every exact-data update, step 3.1 keeps $\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X\le d_0$; consequently $\|x_n^\delta-x_0\|_X\le\|x_n^\delta-x^\dagger\|_X+d_0\le2r$. Induction therefore keeps every iterate needed by the recurrence in the declared outer ball and proves Fejér decrease relative to $x^\dagger$. [given, A3, step 3.1, F1, F6, induction]

4.2 Suppose $\delta>0$ and the discrepancy test never succeeds. Summing step 3.2 over the first $K$ updates telescopes, while every residual exceeds $\tau\delta$, so $K\tau^2\delta^2<\sum_{n<K}(R_n^\delta)^2\le d_0^2/c_\tau$ for every natural $K$. The Archimedean property in [F9] supplies a natural $K>d_0^2/(c_\tau\tau^2\delta^2)$, contradicting this bound. Hence the first stopping index is finite. [given, step 3.2, F9, assume-contra, choose, algebra]

4.3 The partial sums of the nonnegative residual-square series are bounded by step 3.3. By [F8] the series converges, its tails tend to zero, and its terms tend to zero; thus $\|F(x_n)-y\|_Y\to0$ and the claimed infinite-series bound holds. [step 3.3, F8, algebra]

4.4 Let $e_j:=x_j-x^\dagger$, $a_j:=\|e_j\|_X^2$, and $\rho_j:=\|F(x_j)-y\|_Y$. The sequence $a_j$ is nonincreasing by step 3.1. Hence $\Delta_j:=a_j-a_{j+1}\ge0$, and the partial sums satisfy $\sum_{j<K}\Delta_j=a_0-a_K\le a_0$. Applying [F8] again shows that the tail sums $D_n:=\sum_{j\ge n}\Delta_j$ tend to zero. [step 3.1, step 3.3, F8, algebra]

5.1 If $d_0>0$, the same telescoping through the finite first index gives $N(\delta,y^\delta)\tau^2\delta^2<d_0^2/c_\tau$, hence $N(\delta,y^\delta)<C\delta^{-2}$. If $d_0=0$, then $x_0=x^\dagger$ and the initial residual is at most $\delta<\tau\delta$, so $N=0$ and the same bound holds for the stated positive $C$. By [F1], a budget reaching $N$ returns the first stop, while a shorter budget returns `budget_exhausted`. [given, A2, step 3.2, step 4.2, F1, algebra]

5.2 Fix $m\ge n$ and choose $k\in\{n,\ldots,m\}$ minimizing the finite set of residuals $\rho_j$; [F10] supplies a least index among minimizers. For $n\le j<m$, put $A_j=F'(x_j)$, $w_j=F(x_j)-y-A_je_j$, and $v_{j,k}=F(x_j)-F(x_k)-A_j(x_j-x_k)$. The uniform TCC gives $\|w_j\|_Y\le\eta\rho_j$ and $\|v_{j,k}\|_Y\le\eta\|F(x_j)-F(x_k)\|_Y\le\eta(\rho_j+\rho_k)\le2\eta\rho_j$. Since $A_je_k=\bigl(F(x_j)-y-w_j\bigr)+\bigl(F(x_k)-F(x_j)+v_{j,k}\bigr)=F(x_k)-y-w_j+v_{j,k}$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle y-F(x_j),A_je_k\rangle_Y|\le\rho_j(\rho_k+\|w_j\|_Y+\|v_{j,k}\|_Y)\le(1+3\eta)\rho_j^2$. [given, A3, step 4.1, F2, F5, F10, choose, algebra]

5.3 For any fixed finite number of executed updates, the noisy iterates converge to the exact iterates as $\delta\to0$ along data sequences whose discrepancy stop occurs no earlier. Indeed, the update map $(x,z)\mapsto x+F'(x)^*(z-F(x))$ is continuous: $F$ is continuous by Fréchet differentiability, $F'$ is continuous by hypothesis, and [F3] together with [F11] gives operator-norm continuity of the adjoint action. Induction from the common initial point proves the fixed-index assertion. [A3, F1, F3, F11, F13, step 4.1, induction, algebra]

6.1 The exact update gives $e_{j+1}-e_j=A_j^*(y-F(x_j))$. Summing this identity and using [F3] shows $\langle e_k-e_m,e_k\rangle_X\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j=k}^{m-1}\rho_j^2\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$, and likewise $\langle e_k-e_n,e_k\rangle_X\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\rho_j^2\le(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$. [step 5.2, F3, algebra]

7.1 Real inner-product expansion gives $\|e_m-e_k\|_X^2=2\langle e_k-e_m,e_k\rangle_X+a_m-a_k\le2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2$, since $a_m\le a_k$. It also gives $\|e_k-e_n\|_X^2=2\langle e_k-e_n,e_k\rangle_X+a_n-a_k\le2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2+D_n$, because $a_n-a_k=\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\Delta_j\le D_n$. [step 4.4, step 6.1, F4, algebra]

8.1 By the triangle inequality, $\|e_m-e_n\|_X\le\sqrt{2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2}+\sqrt{2(1+3\eta)\sum_{j\ge n}\rho_j^2+D_n}$, which tends to zero uniformly in $m\ge n$ by steps 4.3 and 4.4. Thus $(e_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness of $X$ gives $x_n\to\bar x$. By Fréchet differentiability at $\bar x$, $F(x_n)-F(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)(x_n-\bar x)+o(\|x_n-\bar x\|_X)$, so boundedness of $F'(\bar x)$ implies $F(x_n)\to F(\bar x)$; step 4.3 gives $F(\bar x)=y$. step 4.1 and the triangle inequality give $\|x_n-x_0\|_X\le2r$, so passage to the limit gives $\bar x\in\overline B_{2r}(x_0)$. [step 4.1, step 4.3, step 4.4, step 7.1, F6, F7, F12, F13, A3, algebra]

9.1 Suppose the uniform noisy-data conclusion fails. Then some $\varepsilon>0$ and, for every $j$, a positive $\delta_j<1/j$ and admissible datum $y_j$ can be selected so that the stopped iterate is at least $\varepsilon/2$ from $\bar x$; [A1] supplies this countable selection from the nonempty bad-data sets. Let $N_j=N(\delta_j,y_j)$. Passing to a subsequence, either $N_j$ is a fixed integer or $N_j\to\infty$: a bounded sequence of natural indices has a value occurring infinitely often, and an unbounded one has an increasing subsequence chosen recursively by least indices. [A1, F10, step 8.1, choose, assume-contra]

9.2 In the fixed-index case, write $N_j=N$. Step 5.3 gives $x_N^{\delta_j}\to x_N$. Fréchet differentiability at $x_N$ and boundedness of $F'(x_N)$ imply $F(x_N^{\delta_j})\to F(x_N)$. The discrepancy test and noise bound give $\|F(x_N^{\delta_j})-y\|_Y\le\tau\delta_j+\delta_j$, so $F(x_N)=y$. The exact update at $x_N$ is then zero, so $x_n=x_N$ for every $n\ge N$ and therefore $x_N=\bar x$. Step 5.3 now gives $x_N^{\delta_j}\to\bar x$, contradicting the selected distance lower bound. [A2, step 8.1, step 5.3, F1, F12, F13, algebra]

9.3 In the case $N_j\to\infty$, choose $L$ with $\|x_L-\bar x\|_X<\varepsilon/4$ by step 8.1. For all sufficiently large $j$, $N_j\ge L$ and step 5.3 gives $\|x_L^{\delta_j}-x_L\|_X<\varepsilon/4$. Each noisy iterate before its stop stays in the outer ball by step 4.1, and $\bar x$ lies there by step 8.1; applying the one-step estimate of step 2.1 with the exact solution $\bar x$ makes the noisy iterates Fejér monotone relative to $\bar x$ up to $N_j$. Hence $\|x_{N_j}^{\delta_j}-\bar x\|_X\le\|x_L^{\delta_j}-\bar x\|_X<\varepsilon/2$, again contradicting the selected lower bound. [A3, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 8.1, step 5.3, F6, algebra]

10.1 Both subsequence cases contradict the failure assumption in step 9.1. Therefore the supremum over all data satisfying $\|y^\delta-y\|_Y\le\delta$ tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. [step 9.1, step 9.2, step 9.3, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$
v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3)
=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).
$$


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A regular positively oriented ideal tetrahedron in $\mathbb H^3$.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]] specifies the upper half-space model; a normalized tetrahedron with vertices $0,1,\infty,\omega$, $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, is regular.

[F2] [[lem-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-parameter-relations]] proves that this tetrahedron has all dihedral angles $\pi/3$.

[F3] [[lem-ideal-orthoscheme-volume]] gives $\operatorname{Vol}(\mathcal O_\zeta)=\frac12\Lambda(\zeta)$ for the explicit region $\mathcal O_\zeta$ in upper half-space.

[F4] [[lem-lobachevsky-fourier-expansion-and-pi-third-bound]] gives the absolutely convergent series for $\Lambda(\pi/3)$.


## Proof

1.1 Apply a Euclidean similarity of the boundary plane, extended by the same scaling of height, sending the circumcircle of the three finite ideal vertices to the unit circle centered at $0$; this upper half-space isometry fixes $\infty$. The three vertices become points $p,q,r$ on that circle and remain equilateral. Hence $(0,0)$ lies in the interior of their triangle, so the vertical ray from $(0,0,1)$ to $\infty$ lies inside the tetrahedron. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 On the unit-hemisphere face, draw the perpendicular arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to its three edges and the arcs from $(0,0,1)$ to $p,q,r$. Cone the six resulting sectors to $\infty$. Because the vertical ray lies in the tetrahedron, the six simplices have disjoint interiors and cover the tetrahedron; their common faces have three-dimensional volume zero. Each simplex has two finite vertices and two ideal vertices. Its three right dihedral angles come from the perpendicular cuts; among its other angles, two equal the corresponding original tetrahedron edge angle $\zeta$ and the third is $\pi/2-\zeta$. The tetrahedron is regular, so [F2] gives $\zeta=\pi/3$ for each of the six simplices. [F2, given, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Normalize one simplex by a hyperbolic isometry so its ideal vertices are $\infty$ and $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$ and one finite vertex is $(0,0,1)$. The three right angles place the projected right-angle vertex at $(\cos\zeta,0)$: the two legs are horizontal and vertical. The angle at the origin is $\zeta$, so the other ideal point has coordinates $(\cos\zeta,\sin\zeta)$. The projected triangle is the intersection of the half-planes $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$, $x\le\cos\zeta$ and $y\le x\tan\zeta$. The unit hemisphere through $(0,0,1)$ has equation $x^2+y^2+t^2=1$, and the tetrahedral side is above it. Thus the simplex is exactly $\mathcal O_\zeta$ from [F3] with $\zeta=\pi/3$. [F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 By [F3], each of the six simplices has volume $\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Their interiors are disjoint and their union is the tetrahedron up to faces of volume zero, so additivity gives $\operatorname{Vol}=6\cdot\frac12\Lambda(\pi/3)=3\Lambda(\pi/3)$. Substitution of the absolutely convergent series in [F4] gives the second displayed expression; absolute convergence follows by comparison with $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
